Here, two zonal trans-basin transects (outbound and inbound) across the Arctic Ocean from August to October 2025, collecting continuous underway data at 1,271 stations spanning 19 degrees of latitude (65.1°N to 84.2°N) across six hydrographically distinct sea regions. Analyses revealed striking seasonal reversals in environmental gradients: in late summer, surface temperature decreased poleward from 6.3°C in the Pacific-Arctic Region to −0.4°C in the Eurasian Basin, while salinity increased from shelf to basin; in early autumn, the highest temperature (4.6°C) shifted to the Chukchi Sea shelf and salinity increased westward. Notably, dissolved inorganic nitrogen concentrations in the Pacific-Arctic region increased 33-fold from late summer to early autumn, alongside 3.4-fold and 5.6-fold increases in phosphate and silicate, respectively. Stoichiometric ratios exhibited equally strong seasonal and spatial variation: N:P ratios reached 8.1 in the Pacific-Arctic Region, while Si:N ratios peaked at 308.9 in the East Siberian Sea, indicating severe nitrogen limitation across most Arctic shelf regions. A novel phytoplankton bloom risk assessment framework based on integrated nutrient concentrations and stoichiometric matching to the Redfield ratio (N:P:Si = 16:1:15), classifying all stations into four risk tiers and identifying discrete high-risk zones in the Pacific-Arctic region and the East Siberian Sea. This study delivers the most comprehensive high-resolution dataset of Arctic surface environmental properties to date and offers a robust, management-oriented tool for predicting phytoplankton bloom dynamics under accelerating climate change.

title: Revealing hidden structural regimes in fluvial stage–discharge relationships using time-series imaging
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Jiarui Zhang, Shenliang Chen, Yaoshen Fan, Hongyu Ji, Taihuan Hu, Jianbin Chen
abstract: Stage–discharge relationships in alluvial rivers are widely recognized as nonstationary, yet it remains unclear whether their long-term variability is truly unstructured or instead organized into a finite set of recurrent structural regimes. This study addresses this issue using 75 years of daily stage and discharge records from the Lijin hydrological station on the lower Yellow River. We develop a physics-guided time-series imaging framework that integrates Markov Transition Field (MTF) encoding, dual-branch convolutional representation learning, derivative-based physics-guidance encoding, and hierarchical clustering to classify annual stage–discharge behavior within a fused structural space. Results demonstrate that annual stage–discharge dynamics do not vary as a smooth continuum but recur as a limited set of identifiable structural regimes. Relative to the non-physics-guided framework, the physics-guided framework reorganizes interannual similarity into less fragmented and more hydraulically consistent structural groups, albeit with a larger weighted mean within-cluster distance—indicating that geometric compactness alone does not guarantee physically meaningful partitioning. Distinctions among regimes manifest primarily in state persistence, cross-seasonal reconnection, and hysteretic coupling between stage and discharge. Inter-regime contrasts concentrate in a small number of cross-seasonal hotspot transition windows, indicating that nonstationarity is organized via specific seasonal pathways rather than being uniformly distributed across the year. Feature-attribution analysis further reveals that transition-structure metrics contribute more strongly to regime classification than magnitude-based hydrological indicators, while physics-derived features function primarily as a structural refinement layer rather than the primary source of regime separation. These insights may support adaptive management and structural monitoring in regulated river systems, while providing a potential transferable methodological paradigm for comparable fluvial systems worldwide.

title: An improved Green-Ampt infiltration model of depth-dependent initial soil water content and its experimental verification
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Zheng-Long Cai, Jin Li, Yong-Dong Meng, Xiu-Wen Li, Wei-Jie Zhang, Bin Tian, Jia-Wen Zhou
abstract: Rainfall infiltration analysis is essential for evaluating slope stability. Conventional Green-Ampt models assume homogeneous soil or presume specific functional forms of the initial water content distribution, limiting their applicability to heterogeneous slopes. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes a generalized improved Green-Ampt model that accommodates arbitrary distributions of initial soil water content by numerically solving the governing equation with the Newton-Cotes formula, and further incorporates the moisture-driven variation of hydraulic conductivity during infiltration. The model is validated through an indoor rainfall infiltration experiment on a physical slope model monitored by the high density electrical resistivity tomography (ERT). The results show that the depth-dependent distribution of initial soil water content governs the water storage capacity, whereas the moisture-driven variation of hydraulic conductivity mainly affects the seepage process after the onset of surface ponding. The calculated wetting front depths agree well with the experimental measurements, confirming the accuracy of the improved model and extending the Green-Ampt framework to practical rainfall infiltration analyses of slopes.

title: Scaling properties and classification of urban drainage networks in an Asian megacity
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Hyeonju Kim, Soohyun Yang
abstract: Urban drainage networks (UDNs) are critical infrastructure for public health and the mitigation of flood risk. As UDNs age and expand in scale and complexity, their structural properties are adapted to cope with new needs. Self-similarity of the structure of such drainage networks has been proposed as a naturally self-organized and optimal state of such systems but it remains unclear whether self-similarity is a universal feature of UDNs globally and how to interpret any differences in scaling from the classical scaling as seen in rivers. To address this, we analyzed 221 UDNs (3,942 km) in Seoul. We assessed three classical scaling metrics describing the spatial organization of river networks i.e., Hortonian scaling ratios, the power-law relationship between main-channel length and drainage area, and the area-exceedance probability distribution. While the latter two metrics had similar power-law scaling, UDNs showed a wider range of the power-law exponent in the length-area relationship and a lower power-law exponent in the area-exceedance probability distribution as compared to rivers. Just 50.2% of UDNs (68.5% of total length) satisfied Hortonian scaling invariance. Employing these ratios as criteria, we grouped UDNs and found that their structural properties are associated with sewershed size and commercial area ratio. Moreover, UDNs with scaling more similar to that of rivers had a lower side-to-main pipe-size ratio. These findings provide a systematic diagnosis of scaling heterogeneity across a large set of UDNs within a single megacity and offer a preliminary screening approach for identifying UDNs that may warrant further hydraulic assessment.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution and concentration of global meteorological drought from a three-dimensional object-based perspective
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Heng Wang, Fuqiang Wang, Chong-Yu Xu, Heng Zhao, Shengzhi Huang, Huan Yang, Honglu Zhang, Lanbo Cui, Yutian Du
abstract: Drought is a major hydroclimatic hazard, but conventional local or regional indicators can obscure how individual drought events connect and evolve across space and time. Here we track global meteorological drought as three-dimensional (3-D) objects using the 6-month Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI-06) for 1901–2024. We identify 5,822 objects across global land. Compared with early 20th-century levels, the annual drought-object count declined by approximately 20%, whereas the annual total area–duration (AD) increased by about 40%. The 10% of objects with the highest AD account for 75.5% of total AD and 77.0% of cumulative severity. The objects fall into four recurring morphological types, with Type III comprising 19.0% of objects but contributing 50.1% of total AD. Most objects are precipitation-dominant, but the mean relative contribution of atmospheric evaporative demand (AED) is 7.28 percentage points higher in the top 10% by AD than in the remaining objects. Together, these results indicate that global meteorological drought burden is increasingly concentrated in fewer, larger, and longer-lived events, highlighting the value of connected drought-object metrics for drought monitoring and water-resource risk assessment.

title: Efficient and high-precision urban flood forecasting model combining numerical weather prediction with real-time correction
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Guangzhao Chen, Jingming Hou, Yan Li, Yuan Hu, Yanhong Wang, Xinxin Pan, Jiahao Lv, Baojun Guan
abstract: Urban flood forecasting is a crucial measure of reducing flood disaster risk, enabling early forecasting of flood events and informing emergency dispatch. However, traditional urban flood forecasting techniques face several challenges, including limited lead time and insufficient forecast accuracy. This work integrates NWP model with a hydrological–hydrodynamic model to construct an urban flood forecasting framework that can leverage GPU architecture to achieve efficient computation, thereby delivering high-resolution forecasts with extended lead time. Precipitation forecast data are generated from the NWP model, aiming to extend the forecasting horizon. Additionally, a rainfall real-time correction method is proposed to further enhance the reliability of rainfall forecast. The GPU-accelerated hydrological-hydrodynamic model is driven by the forecast rainfall data, and fine topographic data are employed to accurately represent the complex urban surface characteristics. This approach achieves high-precision urban flood forecasting without compromising computational efficiency. In a typical rainfall-flood event, the total rainfall forecast error after real-time correction is reduced from 2.8 mm to 0.6 mm, with the NSE values for forecast water levels exceeding 0.90. Additionally, the maximum water depth APE error is reduced to 4.2%, and the RMLSE error decreased to 0.002, demonstrating an improvement in the accuracy of both rainfall and flood forecasts. Meanwhile, within a simulation domain comprising 2.71 million grid cells, the urban flood forecasting model completed a 1 h inundation scenario forecasting with an average runtime of 2.12 min. Compared to traditional simulations executed on a CPU, the use of GPU acceleration technology increased the computational efficiency by a factor of 68.4, demonstrating high computational efficiency. This research effectively extends the lead time and enhances accuracy compared to traditional methods, thereby improving cities’ disaster prevention capabilities under extreme climate conditions.

title: Drivers and controls of salinization in prairie ponds
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Michael Mensah, Andrew Ireson, Bruno Soares, Zohra Zahir, Ryan Rimas, Britt Hall, Kerri Finlay
abstract: High sulphate (SO4 2−) concentrations in ponds can support distinctive aquatic communities but can also promote salinization and disrupt aquatic ecosystem functioning, with implications for livestock watering. These contrasting effects are widespread across pondscapes of the Northern Great Plains, yet the interacting biophysical, limnological, and hydrological controls on SO4 2− dynamics remain underexplored. We investigated SO4 2− dynamics across upland soils, water columns, and sediments of prairie ponds comprising naturally occurring wetlands and artificially constructed dugouts (small, excavated water-storage ponds) spanning gradients in salinity, depth, upland vegetation cover, and hydrological setting. Wetlands exhibited higher SO4 2− concentrations in water and sediment than dugouts, consistent with differences in pond morphology, hydrological connectivity, and longer-term solute accumulation. Hydrological setting was strongly associated with pond SO4 2− concentrations, with discharge systems generally exhibiting higher concentrations than recharge systems. Across pondscapes, sediments had the highest SO4 2− concentrations, followed by upland soils and the water column, highlighting sediments as an important long-term SO4 2− reservoir. Structural equation modelling further identified hydrology, sediment and soil SO4 2−, soil organic matter, total dissolved nitrogen, and water depth as important predictors of pond salinization. Upland vegetation cover was negatively associated with SO4 2− desorption, suggesting a potential role in limiting solute mobilization, although its contribution appeared secondary to hydrological and geochemical controls. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of hydrological setting, pond morphology, and long-term SO4 2− storage in regulating salinization across prairie pondscapes and provide insights into processes that may influence the suitability of ponds as livestock-water resources.

title: Hydrologically constrained genetic programming for interpretable rainfall–runoff model discovery: A process–informed machine learning approach
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Naila Matin, Herath Mudiyanselage Viraj Vidura Herath, Abhishek Saha, Lucy Marshall, Vladan Babovic
abstract: Advances in machine learning have improved rainfall–runoff prediction, but integrating these capabilities with interpretable, process-based model structures remains an open challenge. This study seeks a middle ground between conceptual hydrological modelling and modern data-driven prediction by automating model structure discovery while retaining interpretability and hydrological consistency. We introduce HydroXGP (Hydrological Model eXplorer using Genetic Programming) to reduce reliance on legacy model choices and subjective a priori structural assumptions by learning model structure directly from data during optimization. The framework evolves models from a modular, process-based component library adapted from the open-source MARRMoT toolbox, making the search process-informed through reusable flux and routing components and hydrologically constrained by enforcing mass balance during simulation. GP jointly optimizes model structure and parameters, while each discovered model remains explicit and interpretable. Evaluation on the CAMELS-US dataset showed that a proof-of-concept test in a snow-dominated basin achieved strong performance over the out-of-sample test period (NSE=0.849), and, when transferred to a hydrologically similar basin, the learned structure retained useful predictive skill (NSE=0.724). Across 18 basins (one representative basin per U.S. hydrologic region), median NSE reached 0.702, generally outperforming the mean performance of an ensemble of conceptual benchmark models while remaining competitive with some regional LSTM baselines. The findings support a modelling perspective in which structural hypotheses can be revisited and adapted as new data, diagnostics, or environmental signals become available, enabling basin-specific configurations that evolve in response to changing information rather than relying on a single fixed template.

title: Toward AI-driven digital twins for metropolitan floods: A conditional latent dynamics network surrogate of the shallow water equations
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Phillip Si, Yuan Qiu, Omar Sallam, Jeremy Feinstein, Ziang He, Eugene Yan, Peng Chen
abstract: AI-driven flood digital twins demand fast hydrodynamic surrogates for ensemble forecasting and observation assimilation. Yet even GPU-accelerated two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers still require ∼ 55 minutes per 96 -hour run on a ∼ 4.2 -million-active-cell metropolitan basin (the Des Plaines River basin at 30 m resolution), making such workloads prohibitive at native resolution. We present the Conditional Latent Dynamics Network (CLDNet): a low-dimensional latent neural ODE driven by rainfall, paired with a coordinate-based decoder conditioned on static terrain (elevation, slope, Manning roughness) that reconstructs depth and discharge at arbitrary query points. Pointwise decoding decouples memory from grid size and handles irregular watersheds natively, enabling metropolitan-scale training on a single compute node and direct queries at exact gauge coordinates without raster snapping. We evaluate CLDNet on a synthetic 250,000 -cell Texas benchmark and on a new Des Plaines case study of 94 real-rainfall Stage IV storms whose reference simulator we validate against United States Geological Survey (USGS) gauges during the April 2013 flood-of-record (Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency 0.57–0.94 on mean-recentered water-surface elevation). CLDNet reduces the relative root-mean-squared error of an unconditional baseline by 1.7–2.3 × , outperforms regular-grid VAE–ConvLSTM and FNO baselines on the Texas benchmark (both presuppose a Cartesian grid and do not apply to the irregular Des Plaines watershed), reaches a critical success index of ≈ 81 % at the 0.5 m inundation threshold, and produces a full 96 -hour basin-wide forecast in ∼ 29 seconds—a ∼ 115 × speedup. Finally, we demonstrate that CLDNet’s compact latent state supports online observation coupling: using the Latent Dynamics Ensemble Score Filter (LD-EnSF), we assimilate water-depth observations at gauge locations into the surrogate’s latent dynamics and recover a mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.69 against USGS observations at six held-out gauges, from − 1.03 for the rainfall-perturbed open-loop forecast, realizing the observation-update step required of an AI-driven flood digital twin.

title: Unearthing dominant controls of precipitation – streamflow interaction using information theory and explainable AI in large-sample hydrology
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Siva Sai Syam Nandikanti, Maheswaran Rathinasamy
abstract: Understanding the interaction between precipitation (P) and streamflow (Q) across different hydrological regions is essential for the comprehensive interpretation of the catchment’s behaviour. The present study quantifies the strength of the P–Q interaction using the information-theoretic metric Transfer Entropy (TE) across the Conterminous United States. Daily precipitation, streamflow and 38 other variables related to hydrologic, climatic, soil and vegetation characteristics for 554 catchments were analysed. To identify the dominant factors influencing the TE values at the continental and regional scales, Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were employed. The Conterminous US is delineated into homogeneous regions using the Gaussian Mixture Model clustering technique, using TE values and the continental-scale dominant factors as input attributes. The dominant factors governing the P-Q interaction at each cluster are also determined. The results exhibit that the spatial variability in TE is delineated into eight distinct regimes, with the lowest and Highest P-Q interactions observed in mountainous snow-dominated regions and humid catchments, respectively, indicating the dominance of storage components and rainfall, respectively. The SHAP analysis further reveals that the combination of variables regulates P-Q interactions across clusters, with runoff timing, flow signatures, vegetation dynamics, and snow fraction emerging as important controls in different regions. Overall, the findings demonstrate that P-Q interactions vary systematically across hydroclimatic settings and are governed by region-specific combinations of climatic, hydrologic, and physiographic factors.

title: Groundwater response to ice loading as a potential contributor to glacier surge dynamics at Hispar Glacier, Karakoram
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Shuting Ji, Guoliang Wang, Zhenzhong Zeng, Zhilin Guo, Xiuyu Liang
abstract: Basal water contributions to glacier surging remains poorly understood due to complex basal hydrology and multiple potential water sources, where groundwater may play an important role. Here we develop an analytical poroelastic groundwater flow model to examine whether changes in ice loading induce upward groundwater flux through subglacial sediments, thereby potentially increasing basal water pressure and accelerating glacier sliding. Using the DEM-derived thickness-change record, the model predicts downward groundwater flow during ice thickening and exfiltration toward the glacier bed during thinning. Contrary to the expectation that thicker ice promotes faster motion through greater driving stress, glacier velocity increased as ice thickness decreased during the 2014–2016 surge of Hispar Glacier in the Karakoram. Meanwhile, modeled flux maxima occur near the June and December 2015 peaks in a nearby Sentinel-1-derived surface-velocity record, which varies inversely with ice thickness changes. This first-order temporal agreement may indicate groundwater exfiltration as a basal-water source that could raise water pressure and facilitate sliding. Groundwater may therefore be an overlooked component of glacier-bed coupling and surge dynamics, and further investigation is needed to confirm the relationship.

title: Pollution loads and redox-controlled geochemical processes drive contrasting nitrate and ammonium accumulation in shallow groundwater of the Songnen Plain
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Mingxin Zhang, Yanjia Chu, Baonan He, Qiwen Xia, Jiangtao He, Mengmeng Wu
abstract: Groundwater contamination by nitrate and ammonium poses a persistent threat to water security and public health. Although their behavior has been widely studied, quantifying how external loading, hydrochemical conditions, and hydrogeological settings shape their relative dominance remains challenging in a heterogeneous shallow aquifer system. Here, 1,026 shallow groundwater samples from the Songnen Plain and multi-source environmental data were analyzed to evaluate the spatial patterns, source-related factors, and controlling conditions of nitrate-N (NO3-N) and ammonium-N (NH4-N). Both species occurred across the two hydrogeologically defined subregions but showed contrasting dominant exceedance patterns. NO3-N exceedance was concentrated in the high plain (46.8%), whereas NH4-N exceedance was more frequent in the low plain (30.2%). PMF and GNMF results suggested that NO3-N exceedance was mainly associated with agricultural and industrial source-related factors, with model-derived grouped contributions of 57.5–62.5%. In contrast, NH4-N was linked to mixed organic-related and natural geochemical factors, with model-derived grouped contributions of 59.0–70.5%. Grouped XGBoost-SHAP importance analysis identified pollution-load-related variables as the dominant predictors of nitrate accumulation (72.4%), whereas NH4-N showed a more distributed predictor structure involving pollution-load-related variables (54.5%), redox-sensitive hydrochemical indicators (29.0%), and hydrogeological settings (16.5%). PLS-SEM results were consistent with contrasting accumulation pathways: nitrate enrichment was associated with anthropogenic inputs under oxic conditions favoring nitrification and nitrate persistence, while ammonium enrichment was favored in low-lying, organic-rich, and reducing settings where nitrification may be limited. These findings provided a model-supported comparison of nitrate and ammonium dominance in shallow groundwater.

title: Hybrid physics–AI modeling in hydrogeology: a review of concepts, applications, and challenges
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Daniele Secci, Valeria Todaro, J. Jaime Gómez-Hernández
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping hydrogeological modeling. The question is whether hybrid physics–AI approaches can reconcile the explanatory power of process-based models with the flexibility and speed of machine learning. We try to answer this question with a concept-driven review which traces the progression from purely data-driven approaches to emerging modeling paradigms incorporating physical knowledge. We show that hydrogeological modeling is moving beyond a simple opposition between mechanistic simulators and black-box algorithms toward a continuum of physics–AI integration, including theory-guided machine learning, physics-informed neural networks, physics-aware architectures, neural operators, generative models, and differentiable programming. Applications across key hydrogeological domains are reviewed, followed by a discussion of current limitations and barriers to operational deployment, including data requirements, transferability across hydrogeological settings, verification and validation, uncertainty quantification, and issues of trust. We conclude that hybrid physics–AI modeling should not be understood as a replacement for hydrogeological theory, but as an emerging methodological framework in which physical laws, numerical simulation, and machine learning are combined to produce models that are faster, more interpretable, more robust, and more useful for decision-making in groundwater science and management.

title: Hierarchical source-zone inversion and century-scale transport interpretation of landfill-derived groundwater contamination
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Yang Chen, Yun Chen, Haijian Xie, Zhenxing Shi, Yunmin Chen, Jiawei Wu, Minmin Luo, Yong Xu, Shuang Zhao, Lili Zhu
abstract: Identifying source zones of landfill-derived groundwater contamination is challenging when multiple pollutants coexist, monitoring data are sparse, and source geometry is uncertain. This study developed a hierarchical framework linking multivariate screening, analytical inversion, and transport-constrained numerical modelling. Monitoring data for 24 pollutants were screened by significance testing, cluster analysis, and principal component analysis, from which an Aggregate Pollutant Concentration (APC) index was derived. Analytical APC-PSO inversion reduced the area-searching reference from 0.360 to 0.153 km2, and PTNS-PSO refinement defined a 0.108-km2 numerical search area, representing approximately 69.9% contraction rather than independently validated source geometry. Across 50 fixed-setting APC-PSO runs, reconstruction MSE ranged from 0.007 to 0.015, and the nominal 90% source-center dispersion ellipse had semi-axes of 99.3 and 52.7 m. Alternative APC constructions shifted the source centers by 23.4–39.8 m. A controlled analytical semi-synthetic benchmark produced configuration-dependent median mean source-location errors of 36.9–118.5 m. Conditional century-scale simulations showed that COD and chloride co-varied as early leachate indicators, whereas ammonia nitrogen and Pb exhibited persistent co-migration; ethylbenzene showed stronger spatial variability. Engineered barriers reduced concentration amplitudes without eliminating localized leakage, and fault-related migration remained important. Analytical and deterministic hydraulic-conductivity sensitivity tests characterized selected scenario dependence. The framework supports candidate-zone prioritization and pathway- and timescale-based monitoring, subject to source non-uniqueness and the prescribed hydrogeological conditions.

title: Hydrologic and biogeochemical controls on stochastic water and pollutant dynamics in stormwater ponds
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Kuan-Ying Lee, Jacques C. Finlay, Benjamin D. Janke, Anthony J. Parolari, Xue Feng
abstract: Stormwater ponds are a critical part of urban infrastructure for flood mitigation and pollutant removal. They may experience increasing external and internal pollutant loading under climate change, compromising their performance. To evaluate the impact of climate change on pond performance, a coupled stochastic model of stormwater pond water and pollutant dynamics was developed. This study examined the effects of climate variability through stochastic runoff inputs that drive stochastic outflows and incorporated the effects of internal biogeochemical processes on pollutant dynamics via first-order reaction kinetics. Concise analytical solutions for the probability distributions of pond water depth and for the mean pond pollutant concentration were derived. The model was validated in two stormwater ponds in the Twin Cities, Minnesota: USA, Alameda Pond (AP) and Church Pond (CP), using measured total phosphorus concentrations, one of the primary targets for water quality treatment by ponds. Under the 2018 climate conditions, the internal reaction rates for total phosphorus in AP and CP were −0.0146 [ d a y − 1 ] and −0.0022 [ d a y − 1 ] , respectively, indicating that AP was a stronger sink for total phosphorus. Compared with AP, CP showed greater variation in total phosphorus concentration. Finally, under the 2050 and 2090 climate scenarios, the projected concentration trends indicated that reduced internal consumption caused a nonlinear increase in concentration. These results suggest that internal reactions predominantly control pond function in the consumption or release of redox-sensitive pollutants, and regular pollutant removal, such as street sweeping in the watershed and pond dredging, can improve pond function and resilience to climate change.

title: Effect of land reclamation on denitrification processes in intertidal zones of beach aquifers
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Wenjin Song, Chunhui Lu, Huiqiang Wu, Jian Luo
abstract: Biogeochemical processes in intertidal aquifers regulate the nutrient levels of groundwater that ultimately discharges into the marine environment. Most previous studies of intertidal reactivity have focused on natural beach aquifers, while the impact of coastal land reclamation on these processes remains largely unknown. This study investigated the denitrification in an intertidal aquifer modified by land reclamation using a two-dimensional variable-density groundwater flow and reactive transport model. Simulations were performed for a range of reclaimed soil permeabilities, along with different beach slopes and tidal amplitudes after land reclamation. The results show that the heterogeneity introduced by reclamation induces significant changes in the extent and distribution of denitrification hotspots, whereby higher reclaimed soil permeability results in a larger denitrification zone and thus a greater nitrate removal efficiency. Sensitivity analyses indicate that nitrate removal efficiency is most influenced by tidal amplitude, followed by reclaimed soil permeability and beach slope. These findings provide insights into how land reclamation affects the biogeochemical functions of beach aquifers, with important implications for the coordinated management of coastal land reclamation, groundwater nutrient fluxes, and the health of marine ecosystems.

title: AnytimeHydroTwin: A deployment-valid inference-orchestration layer for AI-driven hydrological digital twins
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Yue Zhu, Qingyang Liu
abstract: When does a water-quality nowcast need a process-resolving model, and when is the previous observation enough? Across eleven regimes on three tidal-estuarine systems, the answer is set by the signal, not the model. Estuarine pH and dissolved oxygen are persistence-dominated everywhere (lag-1 autocorrelation ρ 1 = 0.978 – 0.9998 ): a high-fidelity (HF) neural nowcaster beats the previous observation in none of the nine such regimes. Only Sacramento Delta 15-min turbidity genuinely decorrelates ( ρ 1 = 0.819 ), reflecting episodic sediment resuspension, and it alone rewards HF ( Δ NSE = 0.158 ). Variability is not the discriminant—the two highest-variance regimes are persistence-dominated—giving an operational screen: above ρ 1 ≈ 0.99 , an expensive nowcaster will not repay its compute. We exploit this with AnytimeHydroTwin, an inference-orchestration layer rather than a full digital twin, whose deployment-valid pre-HF causal gate reads only observations available before the HF forward pass, so a skipped HF call is a real compute saving, not a post-hoc blend ratio. The gate is itself paid every step: an HF-invocation rate is not a compute saving, and we account for it in full. Our headline is a leakage-clean nested-split evaluation on Sacramento turbidity—NSE parity with HF-only, Δ KGE = + 0.020 at 3.15 % HF, an estimated + 31 % to + 80 % end-to-end wall-clock saving from measured component latencies—closed for the two LSTM headline regimes, open for the TCN stress case and ancillary CAMELS variant. On the nine persistence-dominated regimes it safely defers to lag-1 ≥ 95 % of the time. This regime classification is robust across the three backbone families we evaluate (TCN, LSTM and Transformer): the structure reflects the signal more than the learner.

title: Benthic water exchange drives inorganic carbon export via paleochannels in deltaic seas
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Runze Zhang, Guangquan Chen, William C. Burnett, Shibin Zhao, Tristan McKenzie, Honghai Zhang, Haowei Xu, Wen Liu, Tianyi Zhu, Xiaoyi Guo, Jia’ning Zhang, Miaomiao Zhang, Shuyang Huang, Chunmei Jiang, Zenghui Zhu, Shuo Ren, Ran An, Xiaopeng Lv, Sihui Liu, Zhigang Yu
abstract: Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD, m-to-km scale) and cm-scale porewater exchange (PEX) are important benthic water flow processes that regulate nutrient and inorganic carbon dynamics in coastal seas. Partitioning SGD and PEX is useful for accurately quantifying their water and solute contributions. This is particularly important in deltaic systems underlain by well-developed, yet understudied, paleochannels. Here we employ an optimized multi-radium mass balance model to distinguish SGD from PEX and quantify the dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), total alkalinity (TA), and CO2 fluxes in the Yellow River deltaic seas. Benthic water exchange hotspots were identified in the southern estuary, where the combined SGD and PEX fluxes were 3–6 times greater than those in the northern region. The extensive paleo-river channel network in the south may facilitate SGD. More spatial heterogeneity was observed during the wet season, with total SGD and PEX fluxes approximately twice those in the dry season. PEX dominated the total benthic water flux, exceeding SGD by a factor of 2–4 across regions and seasons. Both SGD and PEX contributed substantially to inorganic carbon export, especially during the wet season. Lateral exports of SGD- and PEX-driven HCO3 – and CO3 2– fluxes exceeded vertical sedimentary carbon burial by 2–4 times on average. Considering the potential offset from CO2 emission and CaCO3 precipitation, SGD and PEX still represent important carbon sink contributor in the Yellow River delta. We propose that benthic exchange processes should be considered in future assessments of coastal carbon sinks.

title: Proposal for using daily thermal amplitude to estimate reference evapotranspiration without relative humidity
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Iulo Pessotti Moro, Sidney Sara Zanetti, Roberto Avelino Cecílio, José Eduardo Macedo Pezzopane
abstract: The FAO-56 Penman-Monteith (PM) method is the standard for estimating reference evapotranspiration (ET o), but its application is frequently limited by the scarcity of relative humidity data. In these cases, assuming the dew point temperature (T dew) is equal to the minimum temperature (T min) is a common practice; however, it ignores the physical reality of dry environments, leading to overestimations of the actual vapor pressure (e a) and biases in ET o. Since atmospheric humidity acts by moderating temperature variations, the daily thermal amplitude (TA) serves as a consistent physical indicator of the hygrometric state of the atmosphere. Based on this premise, this study aims to propose and validate a new method to estimate T dew as a function of T min and TA, aiming to calculate e a and ET o in data-limited scenarios. The method was calibrated and evaluated using daily meteorological data from 584 automatic stations across different Brazilian climates. The model’s performance was compared to the standard PM method. The proposed general approach systematically reduced estimation errors and mitigated systemic biases in a large part of the studied territory, outperforming traditional methods. However, in regions with extreme hygrometric conditions, such as severe water deficit, there was an inferior performance when compared to humid regions. The incorporation of the daily thermal amplitude eliminates the subjectivity of arbitrary correction factors. This approach provides a physically consistent and easily applicable alternative for estimating ET o in regions without relative air humidity data, supporting water resources management and irrigation planning.

title: A grid-informed physics-guided graph deep learning framework for interpretable distributed daily streamflow prediction
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Zhonghui Guo, Dehua Mao, Chang Feng, Ting Wang, Yishu Li
abstract: Watershed refined management requires accurate, spatially explicit, and physically interpretable frameworks for distributed daily streamflow prediction. However, process-based models (PBMs) may be constrained by structural assumptions and parameterized process representations, whereas data-driven models (DDMs) often lack physical consistency and hydrologically interpretable spatial dependencies. We developed a Grid-informed Physics-Guided Graph Deep Learning (GPGDL) framework that integrates GSWAT-derived hydrological representations with a GraphSAGE-BiLSTM model. GSWAT, a grid-based implementation of the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), provides grid-resolved upstream–downstream routing for constructing a weighted directed hydrological graph, together with process information for the gauging-station nodes. The framework was evaluated for multi-site daily streamflow prediction at 15 gauging stations in the Xiangjiang River Basin. The residual-learning configuration implemented within GPGDL achieved the best overall testing performance among the evaluated benchmark and ablation models. Its testing-period mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and coefficient of determination (R2) values were 0.754 and 0.771, respectively. Additional diagnostic experiments comparing GSWAT- and SWAT-based guidance showed that framework performance was jointly influenced by the quality of simulated intermediate hydrological information and the corresponding spatial graph representation. Graph-based interpretation (node, edge, and feature levels) indicated that streamflow prediction relied on a compact and hydrologically meaningful subgraph concentrated in the mid- to upper-basin region, and that the learned spatial dependencies were consistent with the basin’s confluence structure and runoff-routing processes. Overall, the proposed GPGDL framework demonstrates that grid-informed PBM-derived topological priors and hydrological process variables can serve as structured knowledge for graph deep learning, providing a promising pathway for coupling PBMs with DDMs and advancing physics-guided deep learning for interpretable watershed prediction.

title: Conditional normalizing flows: a generative framework for probabilistic streamflow forecasting
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Mingyang Liu, Zhongmin Liang, Jianfei Zhao, Yiming Hu, Binquan Li, Jun Wang
abstract: This study develops an end-to-end probabilistic streamflow forecasting framework that combines a gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder with a conditional normalizing flow (CNF). Rational quadratic spline transformations are used to learn an explicit conditional streamflow density and generate predictive quantiles within a unified trainable framework. The framework was first evaluated in a one-day-ahead regional experiment using a shared model across Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies (CAMELS) catchments and was subsequently examined in a 1- to 4-day case study in the Tunxi catchment. In the CAMELS experiment, the deterministic performance of CNF was comparable to that of the other frameworks, and 92.0% of catchments exceeded both the deterministic-skill and interval-reliability diagnostic thresholds. For CAMELS catchments where test-period high flows exceeded the training-period maxima, CNF remained among the leading frameworks in both deterministic and probabilistic performance. In the Tunxi experiment, CNF achieved the highest deterministic skill at the 1- to 3-day lead times and the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS; 12.189–48.044 m3/s) and highest containing ratio coefficient (CRC; 0.9718–0.9976) across all four lead times. A matched long short-term memory (LSTM) backbone control further showed comparable overall performance between LSTM-CNF and an LSTM-based quantile regression neural network (LSTM-QRNN), with LSTM-CNF showing slight advantages in average point-forecast accuracy and CRC. These results demonstrate that CNF provides an end-to-end optimized, explicit, and flexible conditional-density representation while maintaining predictive performance competitive with the comparison frameworks.

title: A hybrid smoothed particle hydrodynamics framework for modelling erosion in deformable riverbank
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Guodong Ma, Annan Zhou, Ha H. Bui
abstract: Riverbank erosion is an important geomorphological process that significantly influences river morphology, ecological systems, and infrastructure stability. Existing morphodynamic modelling approaches are generally unable to fully reveal the underlying hydro-mechanical mechanisms governing riverbank erosion because of the lack of suitable numerical models capable of simultaneously modelling free-surface flow, seepage, soil deformation, and large-deformation failure processes. This study proposes a hybrid smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) framework to address the challenging coupled riverbank erosion processes. The proposed fully coupled SPH framework is first validated through benchmark problems involving submerged soil column consolidation, submerged deformable landslide motion, and wave-scouring-induced landslide failure. Subsequently, a field-scale riverbank erosion simulation is conducted to demonstrate the capability of the proposed approach and to investigate the hydro-mechanical mechanisms governing riverbank erosion and retreat. The results show that repeated wave fluctuations induce long-term seepage erosion near the riverbank surface, resulting in progressive mass loss and degradation of soil strength. Continuous erosion causes undercutting and stress deterioration within the bank, eventually leading to instability of the overhanging riverbank and subsequent block collapse. The collapsed soil mass is further fluidized and eroded by cyclic wave action, producing repeated cycles of erosion, collapse, and retreat that progressively reshape the riverbank geometry. The proposed SPH framework provides a promising hydro-mechanical modelling tool for investigating complex riverbank erosion processes involving strong fluid-soil interaction and large deformation.

title: The overlooked role of plant hydraulics in shaping groundwater recharge projections
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Xue-Yan Zhang, Yuan Qiu, Zhi Li, Xubin Zeng, Guo-Yue Niu
abstract: Groundwater resources in the western U.S. are increasingly stressed by climate change and growing water demand, yet vegetation processes remain poorly represented in projections of groundwater recharge. Here, we quantify the influence of plant hydraulics on projected recharge using the Noah-MP land surface model with advanced representations of plant hydraulics and soil hydrology. Historical simulations are evaluated against a USGS recharge product, Budyko-based water balance constraints, observed runoff, and GRACE terrestrial water storage anomalies over 1980–2018, demonstrating the model’s ability to capture large-scale hydrologic behavior. We project recharge for 2070–2099 under the SSP3–7.0 scenario using WUS-D3 simulations driven by three global climate models spanning a range of projected temperature and precipitation changes. Relative to 1980–2018, ensemble-mean recharge averaged across the western U.S. decreases by 20.0 %, with the largest reductions occurring in mountainous regions. To isolate the influence of plant hydraulics, we conduct sensitivity experiments that replace the explicit plant hydraulics representation with a traditional soil moisture-based plant water stress function. Averaged across the western U.S., neglecting plant hydraulics increases projected recharge by an amount equivalent to 10.1 % of historical recharge, while the mean absolute plant hydraulics effect reaches 38 % of the inter-GCM spread. Without plant hydraulics, stronger plant water stress suppresses warm-season transpiration, leaving more soil water available to enhance recharge primarily during winter and spring. These findings demonstrate that plant hydraulics can substantially affect recharge projections, highlighting the need to better represent vegetation–hydrology interactions in assessments of future groundwater resources.

title: Joint prediction of river discharge and suspended sediment load through a physics-informed capacity-supply decomposition framework
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Can Ding, Shicheng Li, Nanbo Tang, Zhong Tian
abstract: River discharge (RD) and suspended sediment load (SSL) are inherently coupled in river systems, yet existing data-driven models often fail to explicitly represent their physical linkage, which limits physical interpretability and may reduce robustness under extreme conditions. To address this issue, this study proposes a physics-informed capacity-supply decomposition (PCSD) framework for joint prediction of RD and SSL. The key idea is to reformulate SSL prediction as a sequential decomposition problem, in which sediment load is expressed as the product of a discharge-dependent transport-capacity term and a supply-related modulation term. In this way, RD prediction and SSL prediction are linked within a physically meaningful sequential structure. To further enhance physical consistency, several constraints were incorporated into the framework, including monotonic constraints in the RD branch, as well as discharge-sediment envelope, low-flow threshold, and proxy-supervision constraints in the sediment branch. The framework was evaluated in the Beijiang River Basin, China, using daily hydro-meteorological data from 1991 to 2010, and was compared against several benchmark data-driven models. Results showed that the proposed framework maintained high RD prediction accuracy while achieving the best point-estimate performance for SSL among the evaluated models. For one-step SSL prediction, PCSD achieved the best overall performance, with RMSE, NSE, R 2, and KGE of 195 kg/s, 0.89, 0.90, and 0.94, respectively. Its advantage was especially evident under extreme flood conditions, where it reproduced major sediment peaks more accurately than all benchmark models. Additional multi-lead-time experiments showed that PCSD retained SSL prediction skill across 1–7-day forecasting horizons and consistently outperformed decomposition-based and conventional data-driven benchmarks. These results suggest that the proposed decomposition framework provides a physically interpretable approach with strong predictive performance for coupled hydro-sediment prediction.

title: Hydrogeochemical relationship between large river and adjacent aquifer controls nitrogen accumulation and transformation in riparian zone
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Haichuan Sun, Qi Zhu, Luguang Liu, Yan Li, Yuhang Liang, Gohar Murad Khan, Yize Wang, Zhang Wen, Hui Liu
abstract: Nitrogen behavior in large-river riparian aquifers is difficult to predict because lateral river-groundwater exchange and vertical connectivity between phreatic groundwater (PGW) and confined groundwater (CGW) are highly heterogeneous. This study investigated how the Yangtze River (YR), a representative of a large river, and its lateral PGW and CGW jointly regulate nitrogen distribution and transformation in three riparian profiles with contrasting hydrogeochemical properties: Jiangling (JL), Jianli (JLX), and Honghu (HH). Groundwater-level monitoring, hydrochemistry, and multiple isotope tracers (δ2H-H2O, δ18O-H2O, δ15N-NO3 −, δ18O-NO3 −, and δ15N-NH4 +) were integrated to identify hydrological connectivity, nitrogen distribution, sources, and transformation pathways. The results show that: (1) large-river riparian aquifers have strong lateral and vertical connectivity heterogeneity. The CGW response distance to the YR decreased from approximately 10 km in JL to 5 km in JLX and 2 km in HH, while PGW-CGW leakage fluxes varied from 209.4-1012.2 m3/d in JL to −141.2–154.2 m3/d in HH, under the hydrological conditions of this study; (2) distinct hydrogeochemical variables controlled nitrate and ammonium accumulation. Connected and relatively oxic pathways favored NO3 −-N enrichment in JL, with maximum concentrations of 11.81 mg/L in PGW and 11.95 mg/L in CGW. In contrast, weak flushing, reducing confined groundwater, favored NH4 +-N accumulation, reaching 8.43 mg/L in JLX-CGW and 4.76 mg/L in HH-CGW; and (3) nitrogen transformation was regulated by the interaction between river-driven oxygen supply and confined-aquifer reducing capacity. Nitrification and nitrate accumulation dominated in connected oxic zones, while organic nitrogen mineralization and ammonium preservation dominated in reducing confined groundwater. These findings provide a connectivity-redox framework for identifying nitrate-transport and ammonium-preservation zones in large alluvial river basins, supporting nitrogen pollution assessment and groundwater protection in layered aquifer systems.

title: Dynamic risk assessment of water inrush from coal seam roof by coupling numerical modeling of groundwater flow and static risk model: a case study in Southwest China
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Enyang He, Xinyang Luo, Hongbin Zhan, Juan Fan, Quanrong Wang
abstract: Spatial distribution of groundwater is a critical factor in the risk assessment model of water inrush in a coal mine. However, it is assumed to be time independent in previous models (e.g., multi-year average water level), which is named the static risk model (SRM) in this study. Actually, groundwater level fluctuates seasonally and is also affected by anthropogenic activities. This study integrates transient groundwater flow modeling into the SRM framework to evaluate the impact of groundwater level dynamics on water inrush risk. The proposed model incorporates 10 key controlling factors, including carbonate rock thickness, carbonate rock proportion coefficient, coal seam thickness, aquitard thickness, aquifer thickness, distance to rivers, groundwater level, precipitation, spring density, and distance to faults. The weights of these factors are determined using a combination of the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) for subjective weighting and the entropy weight method (EWM) for objective weighting, with game theory (GT) applied to derive the optimal integrated weights for a comprehensive risk assessment. The risk is categorized into five levels, and normal cloud model is employed to calculate the membership degree of each spatial unit to each risk level. The membership degrees are integrated using a centroid method to derive a continuous risk grade, enabling continuous risk grading at the raster-cell scale that conventional discrete classifications cannot achieve. The new model is applied to the Longfeng Coal Mine in southwestern China. Results indicate that the risk index is significantly influenced by groundwater level fluctuations. Specifically, the spatial patterns during the normal season are generally similar to those in the dry season, whereas more pronounced variations are observed during the wet season. Under increased precipitation recharge, groundwater levels rise moderately, leading to enhanced hydraulic conditions and an appreciable increase in overall risk. Quantitatively, the dynamic model identifies an approximately 61.8% larger high-risk zone during the wet season compared to the static model, demonstrating that traditional assessments systematically underestimate water-inrush risk under seasonal groundwater fluctuations. Furthermore, the risk centroid shifts southeastward by approximately 423.56 m from the dry to the wet season, revealing that elevated hydraulic gradients not only intensify local hazards but also drive directional risk migration along preferential structural pathways. The integration of continuous risk grading with transient hydraulic simulation enables the model to characterize the temporal evolution of risk across different hydrological periods, thereby informing dynamic mine surveillance and seasonally tailored prevention and control strategies.

title: Fourier spectral heuristic indices for streamflow complexity and predictability
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Francisco Javier Frau, Dragutin T. Mihailović, Slavica Malinović-Milićević, Vijay P. Singh
abstract: This research investigates the complexity, temporal organization, and chaotic dynamics of streamflow by introducing two novel heuristic indices derived from Fourier spectral analysis and comparing them with Kolmogorov complexity (KC), its derivatives, and the Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LE). The proposed indices are the Participation of Non-seasonal Frequencies (PNSF) and the Standard Triperiod Index (STP). These indices are applied to monthly streamflow records from rivers in the Mendoza Basin, Argentina, and the continental United States. The results show that PNSF characterizes the redistribution of non-seasonal spectral participation associated with streamflow variability, whereas STP quantifies temporal organization related to dominant seasonal cycles, providing complementary information for distinguishing hydrological regimes. Significant correlations between the proposed indices and established complexity measures indicate that PNSF and STP complement existing information-theoretic and nonlinear dynamical frameworks. Although the proposed indices do not directly quantify the defining properties of chaos or predictability, they provide additional descriptors of spectral regularity and temporal organization that are associated with complex hydrological dynamics. Future research will further validate these indices and evaluate their applicability across diverse hydrological conditions.

title: Balancing subsurface complexity and model simplicity: How much spatially distributed field data is needed to simulate streamflow in a subalpine critical zone
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Aniket Gupta, Jean-Martial Cohard, Alix Reverdy, Romain Biron, Catherine Coulaud, Hervé Denis, Marc Descloitres, Thierry Dumont, Stéphane Garambois, Basile Hector, Jean-Pierre Vandervaere, Didier Voisin
abstract: Representing subsurface heterogeneity in spatially-distributed hydrological models is particularly challenging, as geological and geophysical data are often sparse and infrequent. Hydrologists face two main challenges in subsurface characterization: determining the necessary depth and detail for accurate flow modeling, and developing cost and time-effective methods to capture subsurface heterogeneity. In this study, we conducted preparatory geological and geophysical surveys to investigate subsurface structures and develop conceptual models for the studied catchment. We began with a simple single-layer subsurface model based on initial field investigations and progressively refined it into a more complex three-layer model that incorporates geological, geophysical, and hydraulic properties measured in the field. These conceptual subsurface models were used to inform a 3D hydrological model applied to a 15.28 ha subalpine catchment at Lautaret Pass. Results show that both the three-layer homogeneous and three-layer heterogeneous models perform best, yielding comparable results for runoff (KGEnp = 0.89, 0.91), soil moisture (MAPE = 0.23, 0.22), and evapotranspiration (MAPE = 6.65, 6.60). The three-layer model introduces an active regolith layer at an optimal depth, which is responsible for storing and releasing infiltrated water. We argue that conceptual homogeneous models can meet hydrological objectives, provided they are grounded in reliable geological and geophysical field data. However, we also show that the heterogeneous model performs slightly better in capturing snowmelt amplitude, baseflow, evapotranspiration, and surface heterogeneities. These results highlight how cost and time-effective geophysical methods that capture vertical heterogeneity can be leveraged to upscale critical zone processes.

title: Subsurface processes of Li isotopic fractionation: A study of groundwater at the semi-arid Lake Qinghai catchment, NE Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Yadan Hu, Yang Cao, Fei Zhang, Li Deng, Zhangdong Jin
abstract: Riverine lithium isotopic composition (δ7Li) has been widely used as a tracer for continental silicate weathering. Groundwater could have critical influences on continental rivers and marine Li budget, but the subsurface processes of Li isotopic fractionation remain unclear. This study systematically investigates δ7Li signatures of shallow groundwater within the Lake Qinghai catchment, northeastern Tibetan Plateau. Our results show significant variability in δ7Li of shallow groundwater, ranging from ∼5‰ to ∼27‰. Brackish groundwater generally exhibits higher δ7Li values relative to fresh groundwater, except for two samples characterized by very low δ7Li. Higher δ7Li values in brackish groundwater suggest more secondary phase formation associated with longer water–rock interaction times, leading to more 6Li incorporation into clays and larger isotopic fractionation, consistent with overall higher TDS. Lower δ7Li values in fresh groundwater are consistent with shorter water–rock interaction times, which would limit secondary mineral formation and suppress Li isotopic fractionation. Very low, rock-like δ7Li values in brackish groundwater reflect congruent weathering of silicate rocks. Similar to surface waters, water–rock interaction time may be an important control on Li isotope fractionation in groundwater. Importantly, the remarkable range of δ7Li values in shallow groundwater from this tectonically active catchment indicates that within a single basin, groundwater δ7Li is not systematically high or low and even encompasses the full range of riverine δ7Li. These findings provide new insights into the potential influence of subsurface δ7Li on interpretations of weathering processes in continental river basins.

title: The effect of macropore flow on nitrogen migration and transformation in layered media structure bioretention systems
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Chunbo Jiang, Yizhuo Gou, Junpeng Zhang, Jiayu Gao, Jiake Li
abstract: Macropore flow, a manifestation of preferential flow, strongly affects water and solute transport in bioretention media, but previous studies have often relied on short-term experiments, influent and effluent measurements, or homogeneous media simulations. To address these limitations, this study combined three seasonal experimental phases in pilot-scale systems that had operated for seven years, post-experiment X-ray computed tomography (CT) analysis of the internal macropore network, and HYDRUS-3D dual-porosity simulations of homogeneous and layered media. Effluent Cl− concentrations varied more widely in the homogeneous system than in the layered systems, consistent with flow redistribution caused by local saturation at the coarse–fine interface. The ANOVA results show that seasonal factors have a significant impact on breakthrough time and average effluent Cl− concentration, while the medium structure has a significant effect on breakthrough time. Using the total influent ammonium mass as the denominator, the mean fractions across summer, autumn, and winter were 4.89% unreacted, 7.91% soil adsorbed, 1.58% present as intermediate products, 5.28% immobilized by microorganisms, 12.54% nitrified, 14.80% taken up by plants, and approximately 53% assigned to the mass-balance residual attributed to gaseous losses. Overall, seasonal effects were more widespread, with all seven fractions significantly affected (P 0.95) and solute transport (R2 > 0.71 and NSE > 0.65), providing satisfactory performance for comparative scenario analysis. The simulation results predict that the coarse-over-fine layered structure can more effectively utilize the adsorption capacity of the filter media under various inflow conditions.

title: Decoding dissolved oxygen dynamics using ensemble machine learning models: insights across multi-regional rivers
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Wang Jing, Ali Omran Al-Sulttani, Raad Z. Homod, Ricky Anak Kemarau, Sajjad Firas Abdulameer, Iliass Naouadir, Omer A. Alawi, Billel Salhi, Mehvish Bilal, Zaher Mundher Yaseen
abstract: Dissolved oxygen (DO) is a key indicator of river water quality (RWQ) as it reflects aquatic ecosystem health, microbial and biological activity, and the balance of physicochemical processes within river systems. The study evaluates ensemble machine learning (ML) models to predict DO in the Brisbane River (Australia), the Piabanha River (Brazil), and two river systems in Hong Kong. Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient-Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Extra Trees (ET), and Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT) models were developed using hierarchical feature combinations to assess model robustness under varying input dimensionality. Results indicated that the RF model achieved the best generalization performance for the Australian dataset, with a coefficient of determination (R2 = 0.87) during the testing phase, whereas the ET model achieved the best performance in Brazil (R2 = 0.95). In the case of Hong Kong, the ET model achieved the highest performance (R2 = 0.94) at Pai Min Kok, whereas the LightGBM model showed consistent performance at Kai Tak River (R2 = 0.85–0.86). Further, research results indicated that complete multivariate predictor sets generally improved ML model prediction accuracy. Overall, the ensemble models effectively captured the nonlinear variability of DO across diverse river systems, demonstrating their potential for data-driven river water quality assessment and prediction.

title: Anthropogenic activities dominate dissolved organic matter dynamics via direct rather than nutrient-mediated pathways in a karst river
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Yuekai Ding, Jing Zhang, Rui Liu, Maofei Ni, Weihua Yuan
abstract: As a major reactive carbon pool in aquatic ecosystems, dissolved organic matter (DOM) is highly sensitive to anthropogenic disturbances. However, the specific anthropogenic pathways regulating DOM dynamics remain poorly constrained, particularly in environmentally sensitive karst river systems. Here, we combined optical characterization with partial least squares path modeling to disentangle the seasonal linkages between anthropogenic activities and riverine DOM dynamics. We show that anthropogenic activities influenced DOM primarily through direct inputs, deviating from the nutrient-mediated pathways commonly reported in non-karst rivers. This dominance persisted across seasons despite substantial variability in nutrient conditions. Notably, population was associated with increased DOC and enhanced DOM humification, whereas mines were associated with DOC and chromophoric DOM enrichment, revealing that anthropogenic organic carbon in karst rivers may be propagated primarily through transport rather than nutrient-driven transformation. Building on this pattern, we propose a conceptual segmented DOM accumulation–consumption framework, in which direct anthropogenic inputs favor DOM preservation and accumulation, whereas stronger nutrient-mediated regulation promotes DOM transformation and consumption. Our findings highlight that anthropogenic activities should be explicitly considered as key regulators of carbon fate in karst river systems.

title: Partitioning groundwater and porewater reveals seasonal controls on nutrient export to a chronically eutrophic bay
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Haowei Xu, Shibin Zhao, Natasha T. Dimova, Wen Liu, Disong Yang, Runze Zhang, Miaomiao Zhang, Shuyang Huang, Jianing Zhang, Sihui Liu, Tianyi Zhu, Xiaoyi Guo, Bochao Xu
abstract: Coastal eutrophication caused by excess nutrient inputs has increased worldwide. Of the nutrients sources to coastal ocean, benthic advective pathways, including large-scale submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) and centimeter-scale porewater exchange (PEX), remain the most uncertain relative to surface inputs such as rivers. In particular, the biogeochemical signatures and spatiotemporal variability of individual subsurface flows are poorly understood. Here, we present monthly field observations from January 2022 to April 2024 to assess seasonal dynamics of nutrient loading from different benthic advective processes and their ecological impacts in a chronically eutrophic semi-enclosed bay. We found that longer porewater residence times promoted ammonium and silicate accumulation, alongside the attenuation of nitrate and nitrite in the intertidal sandy aquifer. PEX dominated benthic advection, with enhanced water and solute fluxes during wet seasons driven by intensified hydrodynamic forcing and biological activity. Despite covering 41% of dissolved silicate sources to the entire bay. By altering the magnitude and stoichiometry of nutrients, PEX and SGD exports likely exacerbate phosphorus deficiency. Partitioning the contributions of individual benthic advective pathways to long-term nutrient dynamics is key to mitigate coastal eutrophication.

title: Geodetic constraints on regional scale mountain bedrock aquifer properties
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Matthew J. Swarr, Donald F. Argus, Zachary H. Hoylman, Brett J. Oliver, W. Payton Gardner
abstract: Groundwater in mountainous, fractured-bedrock systems is increasingly recognized as a critical component of water storage and transmission, yet characterizing the hydraulic properties of these systems remains challenging due to sparse observations. Here, we use estimates of groundwater storage change in the Sierra Nevada and Cascades mountain ranges over the last two decades derived from Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) observations of vertical surface displacement to estimate mountain-range-scale effective groundwater hydraulic parameters. We estimate mountain-range-scale hydraulic conductivity and specific yield by fitting models of groundwater storage change to GNSS-derived storage estimates during groundwater discharge periods. We estimate hydraulic conductivity (7.03 × 10−6 m/s and 5.1 × 10−5 m/s) and specific yield (0.063 and 0.15) for the Sierra Nevada and Cascades, respectively, which align with published values based upon their unique bedrock lithologies. The relatively high hydraulic conductivities within each region indicate that fractured and/or weathered bedrock strongly influences the storage and release properties of these regional groundwater systems. The estimated characteristic drainage lengths of 727 m for the Sierra Nevada are consistent with average channel spacing of both perennial and intermittent streams, while the characteristic drainage length of 984 m for the Cascades is consistent with the average spacing of perennial streams only, indicating differing connections between surface water and groundwater within each region. This new method demonstrates the utility of geodetic observations in studying mountain groundwater systems and may provide improved constraints on large-scale simulations of mountain groundwater flow, furthering our understanding of these systems.

title: Quantifying carbon export at the porewater–surface water interface in native saltmarshes under restoration contexts
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Yuda Chen, Shiqing Sun, Jinqiu Du, Fenfen Zhang, Dan Wu, Jianan Liu, Yibang Zhang, Jinzhou Du, Xiaogang Chen

title: Root water uptake estimation and associated ecohydrological functions based on distributed moisture storage dynamics in soil-weathered bedrock profiles
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Yang Qiu, Zekang He, Zhiqiang Yin, Dongmei Han, Ling Peng, Aifang Jin, Chuanming Ma, Lei Zhao, Xianfang Song
abstract: Root water uptake (RWU) is a key process linking subsurface moisture redistribution and the atmospheric water cycle. However, it is difficult to quantitatively simulate under strong heterogeneity of the medium or a lack of hydraulic parameters, especially for weathered bedrock. Therefore, we developed a non‑parametric, observation‑driven diagnostic framework that integrates mass conservation with water‑demand allocation to infer layer‑wise flux and RWU across soil and weathered bedrock profiles. We further applied it in two larch plantation plots underlain by sandstone and tuff. It clearly reversed the layer-wise moisture dynamics driven by freeze-thaw cycles, infiltration, and transpiration. Then, the RWU sourced from different layers were estimated. Although soil moisture supported the dominant water source for the shallow-rooted larch plantation (over 90%), RWU from the weathered bedrock layer still cannot be ignored. The weathered sandstone moisture provided about 7.85% and 3.25% RWU (based on lower-bound estimations) during the growing and post-growing seasons, respectively, whereas it was about 1.13% and 4.88% from weathered tuff. Additionally, this framework can also estimate the layer-wise vertical drainage flux. It was verified that the weathered bedrock layers act as deep moisture buffers during the wet season and provide stable water retention during the dry season. Our study provides a reproducible computational framework for simulating moisture transport and RWU in profiles where parameters are difficult to obtain or where the medium heterogeneity is strong. Our results also highlighted that incorporating bedrock moisture dynamics into evapotranspiration frameworks is essential for improving assessments of drought resilience and guiding water‑limited afforestation strategies.

title: Nitrate transport and transformation in riverbeds under vegetation-induced hyporheic exchange
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Siyi Zhang, Kaiwen Zhang, Yuhang Tian, Hexiang Chen, Xinyi Luo, Guangqiu Jin
abstract: Flow around emergent vegetation creates spatial pressure differences along the riverbed surface, but the resulting effects on nitrate delivery and transformation in the hyporheic zone remain insufficiently quantified. A three-dimensional model was developed to couple overlying flow, pore water flow, and reactive solute transport in a permeable riverbed. The results show that vegetation altered solute transport from shallow diffusion near the sediment surface to advective exchange driven by pressure gradients. Compared with the flat bed, vegetation increased nitrate influx into the bed by about 7 orders of magnitude under the reference conditions, while total denitrification was 6.8 times that in the flat-bed case. The difference in nitrate influx between the flat-bed and vegetated cases varied with background hydraulic gradient and flow velocity. Streamwise spacing (Sx ) mainly affected the solute transport pathway length in the pore water and the residence time. Shorter Sx promoted oxygen supply and nitrification near the surface, whereas larger Sx increased the residence time and expanded anoxic zones favorable for denitrification. The nitrate consumption fraction at Sx = 20 cm was 1.79 times that at Sx = 3 cm. Spanwise spacing mainly affected the exchange rate and oxygen penetration. Higher flow velocity increased nitrate influx and reaction rates, but reduced nitrate consumption fraction because pore water returned to the surface water before nitrate reduction was complete. These results indicate that nitrate removal in riverbeds with vegetation is not determined by the exchange rate alone. Péclet (Pe) − Damköhler (Da) analysis showed that high Pe favored nitrate supply, while high Da indicated a longer residence time relative to the characteristic time scale of DOC oxidation. The most favorable condition occurred when nitrate supply and residence time were both maintained. At low flow velocity and wider vegetation spacing, residence time was longer (Da = 1536.7, Pe = 5.7) and the nitrate consumption fraction was the highest. Under high velocity and dense spacing, nitrate supply was high (Pe = 472.8), but nitrate consumption fraction was lowest because the residence time was short (Da = 16.4). Power-law regressions described the relationships among Reynolds number, vegetation spacing, nitrate influx, nitrate consumption rate, and consumption fraction. This study explains how hyporheic exchange induced by vegetation affects nitrate transport and transformation in riverbeds by altering nitrate supply, residence time, and reaction conditions.

title: Drought recurrence across China under diverse ENSO and IOD modes (1941–2023)
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Zhenchen Liu, Wen Zhou, Bo Tong, Zhiyong Wu, Hao Yin
abstract: El Niño‑Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) strongly modulate extreme droughts across China. When particular ENSO/IOD modes recur, extreme droughts can repeatedly occur within consistent regions and seasons, a phenomenon defined herein as “ENSO/IOD‑related drought recurrence”. Although this phenomenon suggests predictable drought responses, the underlying characteristics and physical mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aims to systematically characterize ENSO/IOD‑related drought recurrence over China and reveal its associated physical drivers. Based on historical extreme drought events for 1941‑2023, we adopt an event‑based ENSO/IOD classification system, and apply the newly proposed three‑dimensional Drought Recurrence Index (DRI) to identify recurrent drought groups. Linear baroclinic model and ocean‑atmosphere coupling sensitivity experiments are further used to diagnose circulation responses forced by typical SSTA patterns. Our analyses show that approximately 75% of the identified extreme drought events are associated with specific ENSO/IOD modes, among which ∼ 53% occur during the developing phases of El Niño or La Niña. Distinct response asymmetry exists: developing‑phase El Niño triggers near‑immediate drought responses within two months, whereas La Niña produces large‑scale, persistent droughts with lags longer than five months. Eight groups of recurrent droughts are further distinguished. Summer‑autumn droughts over northern China during El Niño development represent the most frequent recurrence pattern, while compound La Niña‑negative IOD modes drive cross‑seasonal and cross‑regional recurrent drought events. Model experiments reproduce these asymmetric drought responses under representative summertime El Niño, autumn positive‑IOD, and cross‑seasonal La Niña SSTA forcing. These results provide an important reference for developing long‑term drought prediction systems incorporating ENSO/IOD signals.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for hydrodynamic inversion and discharge estimation in river flows over complex bed topography
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Congfang Ai, Yuxiang Ma, Junzheng Li, Jiajie Song, Jiaxiang Sun
abstract: Accurate estimation of river discharge and internal hydraulic states remains a fundamental challenge in hydrological monitoring, particularly when observations are limited and key flow variables cannot be directly measured. In this study, we develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN)-based framework for hydrodynamic inversion and discharge estimation in river flows over complex bed topography under limited observations. The proposed approach embeds the Serre–Green–Naghdi (SGN) equations into the neural network training process to enforce physical consistency while assimilating limited observations, such as water-depth or bottom-pressure-head observations. Within this framework, hydraulic states and river discharge can be reconstructed, and bed topography can be inferred when discretized bed-elevation data are available. The unified inverse formulation is implemented in three task-specific configurations for different observation types and bed-information conditions. For prescribed continuous and smooth bed profiles, water-depth or bottom-pressure-head observations are utilized to reconstruct hydraulic states and estimate discharge.
