Human activities, particularly water use and population density, dominated drought recovery in three sub‑basins, whereas climate and vegetation factors controlled recovery in the fourth. This framework enhances the accuracy and spatial resolution of drought recovery assessments and provides quantitative support for adaptive water management under a changing environment.

title: Strategies for correcting nonstationary resistivity–water content relations in time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Jianguo Liu, Simone Gelsinari, Andrew van de Ven, Matthias Leopold, Sally Thompson
abstract: Time-lapse Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) provides an attractive framework for quantifying spatially distributed water-content dynamics, yet quantitative interpretation remains limited by uncertainty in the petrophysical relationship between resistivity ( ρ ) and volumetric water content ( θ ). This uncertainty is distinct from that associated with lithological heterogeneity, measurement resolution, or inversion artefacts, and can arise from temporal variability in the ρ – θ relationship itself. We examine two approaches for representing this nonstationary behaviour: a particle-filter data-assimilation framework that requires continuous or periodic co-located water-content observations from an independent sensor system to dynamically calibrate time-varying petrophysical parameters, and a machine-learning model that predicts θ from resistivity-based predictors together with auxiliary environmental information, including surface water content and contact resistance, after training. Synthetic experiments indicate that the imposed time-varying petrophysical scaling coefficient, a ( t ) , and saturation exponent, b ( t ) , can be recovered with low trajectory error across the tested ranges of parameter amplitudes, frequencies, and resistivity-noise levels. Applications at two sandy vadose-zone sites in Western Australia show that data-assimilation-based dynamic calibration of the petrophysical relationship substantially improves consistency between ERT-derived water-content reconstructions and the co-located water-content observations assimilated by the particle filter. The particle-filter reconstructions should therefore be interpreted as assimilation-constrained dynamic reconstructions that evaluate the benefit of updating the ρ – θ relationship through time relative to a stationary petrophysical calibration. The data assimilation framework provides a direct depiction of how the relationship evolves through time, capturing gradual seasonal shifts as well as extended periods of relative stability. Machine learning offers a practical alternative when sufficient and representative data are available. The observed variability in the effective petrophysical relationship covaried with near-surface environmental and electrode-contact conditions, as indicated in part by contact-resistance diagnostics. We interpret these associations as empirical and installation-specific, rather than as evidence that contact resistance is an intrinsic soil property or an independent causal control. Accounting for temporal variability in the petrophysical relationship improves the interpretability and reliability of quantitative time-lapse ERT analyses.

title: A digital twin framework for real-time probabilistic forecasting of permeable pavement performance
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Jose Brasil, Marcus Nóbrega Gomes Jr., Drew W. Johnson, Athanassios T. Papagiannakis, Eduardo Mario Mendiondo, Marcio Hofheinz Giacomoni
abstract: Low Impact Development (LID), such as permeable pavements, mitigates some of the urban runoff effects. Their hydrologic response can be enhanced with real-time forecasting and management. Digital Twins (DT), which integrate physical models with sensor data, offer a solution, yet require methods to handle uncertainties in model inputs and observations. This study presents a DT framework for permeable pavement systems that couples a one-dimensional, explicit-state hydrologic model with a Particle Filter (PF) data assimilation scheme. The framework assimilates real-time underdrain outflow observations to refine model states and provide probabilistic forecasts. Uncertainty characterization revealed that sensor measurement error depends on the underdrain outflow, while rainfall forecast error from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh model is a function of the magnitude of the rainfall event. The DT framework was evaluated against a baseline model using field data from four permeable pavement types. The data assimilation approach reduced the ensemble forecast error by an average of 20%, as measured by the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS), with positive skill scores in 96.2% of forecast events. The deterministic performance of the PF ensemble median, evaluated by Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), also exceeded that of the baseline model. The data assimilation framework yielded more accurate forecasts than a deterministic modeling approach and is computationally efficient for operational deployment. However, outflow forecast accuracy is constrained by the structural limitations of the baseline model, evidenced by poor prediction interval coverage during some high-intensity events, highlighting areas for future model development.

title: Improving and evaluating the performance of change detection methods for soil moisture retrieval using Sentinel-1A over a forest-dominated mountainous study area in Beijing, China
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Haotian Cai, Nan Ye, Rui Tong, Fuqiang Tian, Jingan Lin, Yao Zhuang
abstract: Surface Soil Moisture (SSM) plays a crucial role in the development of natural disasters over mountainous areas, particularly in triggering flash floods caused by precipitation following antecedent rainfall. Numerous spaceborne SSM products can be used in flood models for forecasting and early warning of flash flood events. In recent decades, passive microwave remote sensing has been widely acknowledged as the most accurate technique for global SSM mapping. However, its spatial resolutions are limited to the order of 10 km from space. While Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and optical sensors onboard satellites can enhance the spatial resolution of passive microwave SSM data or directly retrieve high-resolution SSM, the accuracy of SSM products is adversely affected by ground geometry and vegetation coverage over mountainous areas. In this study, the Advanced Change Detection method for Mountainous areas (ACD_M) was developed as an attempt to adapt the ACD framework for high-resolution SSM retrieval over forest-dominated mountainous areas using multi-temporal repeat orbit Sentinel-1A SAR data. ACD_M incorporates two key adaptations into the ACD framework. First, the Helsinki University of Technology (HUT) forest backscattering model was introduced to consider volume scattering in the ACD_M. Second, the SMAP passive microwave 9-km SSM product was downscaled, and pixel-wise SSM constraints were derived from local spatial variability to account for mountainous heterogeneity. The ACD_M was evaluated over a forest-dominated mountainous study area in northern Beijing, China. SSM with a spatial resolution of 25 m was retrieved from Sentinel-1A L1 radar backscatter data and subsequently validated using time series of ground SSM measurements from a monitoring station network for the period from January 2020 to May 2024. The ACD_M was also inter-compared with the existing short-term change detection methods, demonstrating superior overall retrieval accuracy. Compared to ACD, the ACD_M demonstrated higher and more stable retrieval accuracy, with an increase of 0.011 in R and a reduction of 0.022 cm3/cm3 in Bias. Furthermore, the potential for further enhancing the retrieval accuracy of the ACD_M by optimizing model constraints was explored. For instance, the mean R increased by 0.018 and the RMSE decreased by 0.008 cm3/cm3 after introducing a statistical relationship between geographical factors and SSM in the upper constraints. ACD_M showed limitations under high SSM conditions, indicating that caution is required when applying the retrieved SSM to near-saturated or flash-flood-related hydrological conditions.

title: A graph-based surrogate modeling framework for large-scale spatial optimization of low-impact development layouts in urban pluvial flood mitigation
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Qiming Cheng, Jiayue Zhu, Ye Rao, Zhen Liu, Fei Liu, Yixin Mu, Kaifeng Wang, Yao Chen
abstract: The increasing frequency of extreme weather events, coupled with anthropogenic modifications to urban land surfaces, has significantly exacerbated urban flooding. Low-impact development (LID) strategies have therefore been widely advocated as a primary approach for mitigating urban pluvial flood, the effectiveness of which highly dependents on the spatial layout of LID facilities and their construction costs. However, this multi-objective optimization approach faces formidable challenges. Existing approaches to LID spatial allocation optimization often fail to effectively balance cost-benefit heterogeneity across diverse configurations and become computationally intractable when applied to urban drainage systems characterized by numerous sub-catchments, complex hydraulic network topologies, or both. To address these challenges, we propose the GraphicSWMM framework, a deep learning surrogate model driven by real-world physical priors. Trained via an end-to-end architecture, this framework integrates a novel sampling strategy with advanced dimensionality reduction techniques. These methodological innovations collectively alleviate the dimensionality bottlenecks inherent in large-scale spatial optimization tasks. Empirical validation across two real-world urban regions confirms that GraphicSWMM consistently outperforms existing approaches and exhibits potential for transferability to regions with different climatic conditions. In urban catchments characterized by high-resolution drainage networks and constrained budgets, the proposed model achieves a 481.1-fold acceleration in computational efficiency compared to conventional workflows, while simultaneously reducing flood discharge volumes by 45.0% and inundation areas by 38.3%. This framework serves as a robust decision-support tool that balances flood mitigation performance with construction costs, facilitating more resilient urban drainage systems.

title: A knowledge-constrained improved Mean Flow method for planar sedimentary facies interpretation
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Xu Yang, Shaoqun Dong, Xu Bai, Junkun Quan, Tao Xu, Sai Yao, Lianbo Zeng, Mingxuan Han, Naiyang Sun, Huangshuai Kong
abstract: Planar sedimentary facies interpretation conditioned on well data remains challenging because the limited spatial coverage of wells makes lateral continuity difficult to preserve. To address this, a knowledge-constrained improved Mean Flow (K-iMF) method is proposed, integrating data-driven velocity-field learning, variogram-regularized training, and variogram-guided candidate selection. Multi-directional variogram discrepancies regularize velocity-field learning during training. During inference, the fixed U-Net maps independently sampled latent variables in parallel and retains the candidate with the lowest discrepancy score. The method was evaluated on a fluvial facies dataset from the Hailar River system and a delta-front microfacies dataset from the Songliao Basin. Among the evaluated methods, K-iMF achieved the highest accuracy and F1-score on both datasets. Relative to iMF, K-iMF increased accuracy from 95.7% to 97.0% and F1-score from 90.9% to 93.8% on the fluvial dataset. On the delta-front dataset, accuracy increased from 84.5% to 88.8% and F1-score from 67.2% to 77.4%. The anisotropic variograms more closely reproduced the reference ranges and sills, while pixel-wise variance remained non-zero along facies boundaries, indicating that spatial consistency was improved without collapsing the stochastic realizations. Compared with the diffusion model, K-iMF achieved higher predictive performance while requiring less than 1/290 of its testing time. In blind well tests, the method achieved accuracies of 80% and 78% for the two datasets, respectively. Predictive performance improved and variability decreased as the number of conditioning wells increased, with both trends more pronounced for the delta-front dataset. Overall, K-iMF improves predictive performance and directional spatial consistency while retaining stochastic variability and efficient inference.

title: Enhancing river flow prediction accuracy in data scarce catchments using a time varying ensemble deep learning approach
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Angel I. Tumushabe, Seith N. Mugume, Johanna Sörensen
abstract: Ensemble deep learning (EDL) methods offer an effective way to reduce model structural uncertainty and improve the reliability of river flow predictions, especially in catchments with limited data. This study evaluated the performance of a Time-Varying Dynamic Model Averaging (TV-DMA) ensemble for integrating heterogeneous machine learning and deep learning architectures, including FFNN, 1D-CNN, LSTM, CNN-LSTM and Diff-FFNN-LSTM models, for river flow prediction in two hydrologically distinct, data-scarce tropical catchments in the Upper White Nile Basin. Results show that the heterogeneous, first-order differential processing Diff-FFNN-LSTM model consistently achieved the highest individual-model river flow predictive performance (NSE ≥ 0.980), due to its ability to stabilise non-stationary river flow time series by mitigating boundary effects associated with decomposition methods, thereby improving representation of rapid flow transitions. Additionally, the TV-DMA resulted in more superior performance in both the Semliki (NSE = 0.910; PBIAS = −0.42%) and Tochi (NSE = 0.831; PBIAS = −0.34%) catchments when compared to the Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) ensemble (Semliki: NSE = 0.848; PBIAS = −0.20% and Tochi: NSE = 0.710, PBIAS = −18.86%). BMA and TV-DMA also improved computational efficiency by 98–98.4% and 77–81%, respectively, relative to the process-based HEC-HMS model. The findings highlight the principal value of TV-DMA’s dynamic update of individual model weights based on predictive error distributions, which enhances river flow predictive performance, particularly in the rainfall-runoff-dominated Tochi catchment. This EDL approach can improve the accuracy and efficiency of river flow modelling and support the development of flood forecasting and early warning systems in data scarce regions.

title: Emergence of macroscopic hydraulic behaviors from data: a hybrid physics-AI universal differential equation framework for spatio-temporal soil moisture dynamics
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Wenrui Yuan, Shi Hu, Chaoyang Du, Chesheng Zhan

title: Water quality data imputation based on spatial neighborhood-aware and error-adaptive dynamic fusion model
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Xinwei Fang, Zhonglian Jiang, Lei Liu, Xuejun Feng, Jianqun Guo
abstract: Marine water quality data frequently suffer from missing values, undermining the reliability of data analysis and the scientific basis for environmental management decisions. To enhance the completeness and accuracy of water quality data imputation, a Spatial Neighborhood-aware and Error-Adaptive dynamic Fusion (SN-EAF) imputation model has been proposed. It improves the spatial perception capability by constructing enhanced spatial neighborhood information features, employs multiple base imputation models with error predictors to assess sample-level prediction errors, and eventually achieves personalized data fusion through dynamic weighting. Experimental results demonstrate that, for salinity indicator, the proposed model achieved mean R 2 values of 0.913 (Missing Completely at Random) and 0.868 (Continuous Block Missing), while the RMSE was reduced by 12.1%–28.2% and 17.4%–30.1% approximately, compared with the best-performing base model. The model adaptively adjusts the weights of base models according to the spatial distribution characteristics of water quality parameters, with error-prediction R 2 values ranging from 0.759 to 0.909 for three representative base models under two data missing scenarios. It consistently outperforms the contrast methods across four additional water quality indicators (Dissolved Oxygen, Total Nitrogen, Particulate Organic Carbon and Chlorophyll-a) and 19 distinct data missing scenarios. The results verify its robustness in complex marine monitoring applications and provide a promising tool for intelligent imputation of marine water quality indicators. The present study shares valuable insights into the data imputation and marine environmental management.

title: Moderate litter biomass benefits soil water replenishment in semiarid grasslands
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Yang Luo, Kemiao Li, Jie Zhang, Bingcheng Xu
abstract: Litter plays a crucial role in rainfall redistribution and hydrological cycles, and understanding its hydrological effects is of great significance for ecological management and restoration. Decades of vegetation restoration on the Loess Plateau have resulted in accumulated litter, which has further influenced regional ecohydrology and sustainable grassland restoration. To elucidate grassland litter interception capacity and its role in regulating runoff and infiltration, plot-scale experiments were conducted using immersion and simulated rainfall (10, 20, and 40 mm) methods. Three ground litter types (Bothriochloa ischaemum, Stipa bungeana, and Artemisia gmelinii) and the standing litter of A. gmelinii were evaluated across four biomass gradients (0, 100, 200, and 300 g m−2). The results showed that the interception capacity quantified via simulated rainfall was 2.54 to 6.82 times higher than that of immersion method. Litter type, biomass, and rainfall amount significantly influenced the proportion of interception, runoff, and infiltration. Ground litter of A. gmelinii exhibited significantly higher interception and infiltration proportions than B. ischaemum and S. bungeana. As litter biomass increased, the interception proportion rose consistently, whereas the soil infiltration proportion increased initially, then decreased. Increases in rainfall amount were partitioned mainly into the proportion of surface runoff. Litter thickness was the strongest predictor of interception, whereas soil bulk density and initial soil water storage were the main predictors of runoff and infiltration. Among the tested levels, approximately 100 g m−2 produced the greatest soil water replenishment, whereas higher biomass increased litter interception. These findings suggest that litter accumulation during long-term restoration may reduce effective rainfall and that maintaining moderate litter biomass could improve soil water replenishment in semiarid grasslands.

title: Predicting root-zone soil moisture using a small sample deep learning approach
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Yalin Xie, Jing Tian, Yongqiang Zhang, Xuanze Zhang, Longhao Wang, Haoshan Wei, Xian Wang, Zixuan Tang
abstract: Estimating root-zone soil moisture (RZSM) under sparse in-situ observations is closely related to the broader Prediction in Ungauged Basins (PUB) challenge. This study introduces a novel application of the Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) for predicting RZSM using small sample sizes (fewer than 10,000) and evaluates its robustness under extreme data sparsity conditions. Using five-fold spatial cross-validation conducted at the grid-cell level, TabPFN was trained on sampled data, while the baseline models (RF, XGBoost, CatBoost and Tabular ResNet) were trained on both sampled and full datasets. All models were evaluated on full test sets to ensure a consistent benchmark. Our results indicate that under extremely sparse training conditions (one sample per grid), TabPFN achieves the highest prediction accuracy (R = 0.726 ± 0.002; RMSE = 0.069 ± 0.0004; MAE = 0.053 ± 0.0003), improving correlation by 2.5–9.2% and reducing prediction errors by 2.6–9.8% compared to benchmark models. In time-specific modeling, where separate models were constructed for each day, week, and month, its performance advantage was broadly maintained across changing hydro-climatic states and under consistent temporal aggregation. Its performance also remained relatively stable as training grid density decreased, including when fewer than 40% of the available training grids were used. These results demonstrate that TabPFN enables robust RZSM prediction using small samples and provides a practical tool for drought monitoring and water assessment in data-scarce or poorly monitored regions.

title: Organic carbon dynamics in a subtropical watershed: hydrological processes and land use controls
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Guan-Zhou Lin, Li-Chi Chiang
abstract: Land use and hydrological processes jointly influence soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and riverine organic carbon (OC) export in subtropical watersheds. This study employed the SWAT-C model to quantify SOC storage and the export of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and particulate organic carbon (POC) in the Wu River Basin, Taiwan, during 2012–2017. Model calibration against observed total organic carbon (TOC) fluxes achieved robust performance (NSE ≥ 0.7), supporting its applicability for representing watershed-scale and seasonal carbon transport in high-energy, data-scarce basins. Simulations estimated mean annual DOC and POC exports of 10.4 and 6.9 kg ha−1 yr−1, respectively, with SOC stocks ranging from 155 to 294 t ha−1 (mean: 224 t ha−1), based on soil profile depths defined by the soil-layer data incorporated into the SWAT-C model. The results reveal pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity, with annual OC export varying by more than one order of magnitude across subbasins. Irrigated paddy fields functioned as significant carbon sinks, whereas bare land and rainfed croplands on steep slopes emerged as major POC source areas. More than 60% of annual OC export occurred during the wet season (June–September), and the peak export months (July–August) contributed over 30% of annual POC export and over 20% of annual DOC export. These results indicate that wet-season hydrological conditions strongly regulate seasonal carbon mobilization, without implying precise event-scale simulation. Overall, the findings demonstrate how hydrological routing and land-use intensity interact to modulate SOC retention and riverine OC export. This study offers a scientific basis for targeted erosion control and enhanced SOC sequestration to strengthen watershed resilience and sustainable management in subtropical monsoon regions.

title: Artificial interventions temporarily influence bacterial community spatial patterns along a natural river continuum
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Han Gao, Yujia Zhai, Yanci Zhang, Hongjie Wang, Baoshan Cui
abstract: River networks increasingly connect natural and engineered reaches, yet spatial variation in nearshore sediment bacterial communities across these connected habitats remains poorly resolved. This study investigated the spatial dynamics of bacterial communities in nearshore surface sediments along the natural-artificial continuum of the Daqing River Basin during the dry season. Alpha diversity was 22.58% lower at the estuary than in the upstream reach. Assembly metrics, network topology, and source assignments also varied among sampled reaches. At the confluence, the median source assignment to the engineered channel was 24.2%, compared with 15.1% assigned to the upstream river; farther downstream, the upstream river was the largest identified source (38.4%). This study elucidates bacterial community dynamics in complex river–lake systems and supports prioritizing natural hydrological connectivity conservation for ecosystem health in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region.

title: Long-term monitoring of lake dynamics across the Yangtze River Basin using multi-source altimetry fusion
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part A Author(s): Yong Wang, Yulin Gong, Yinghong Jing, Xiaojun She, Shanlong Lu, Yao Li
abstract: The Yangtze River Basin (YRB) contains numerous natural lakes whose water level fluctuations are typically an order of magnitude smaller than those of managed reservoirs, posing a major challenge for high-resolution, long-term monitoring. To address this limitation, we developed a multi-source satellite altimetry fusion algorithm to enhance the detection of subtle water level variations and integrated it with long-term optical observations to enable consistent basin-scale monitoring. These resulting records are compiled into the YRB Lake Dynamics (YLD) dataset, which provides monthly time series of lake area, water level, and lake water storage variations from 1990 to 2023. The YLD dataset delivers an enhanced water level product derived from multi-source altimetry fusion for 883 lakes (accounting for >99% of total lake area). It establishes robust area–elevation (A–E) relationships for 440 lakes (>90% of total lake capacity), with a mean coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.76. Validation against in situ observations from 12 lakes demonstrates strong agreement in reconstructed dynamics, with a mean correlation coefficient (CC) of 0.73, a mean root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.73 m, and a normalized RMSE (NRMSE) of 14.05%. Over the past three decades, approximately 70% of large lakes within the basin have contracted, driving declines in total lake area and water storage at rates of 16.07 ± 6.95 km2 yr⁻1 and 144.28 ± 44.11 Mm3 yr⁻1, respectively. In contrast, about 61% of small lakes have expanded, accompanied by a mean water level rise of 1.65 ± 0.50 cm yr⁻1. Spatially, a distinct pattern of “shrinkage in the middle reaches and expansion in the upper and lower reaches” emerges, indicating the combined influence of climate change and human activities across different hydrological regions. Overall, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of multi-source altimetry fusion for high-resolution monitoring of lakes with subtle water level variations, thereby providing a transferable methodological framework and a long-term dataset for investigating lake dynamics in similar systems worldwide.

title: Curie point depth (CPD) and thermal anomaly of the Rukwa Rift Basin, SW Tanzania from aeromagnetic data
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Obeid Saitabau Lemna
abstract: Curie point depth (CPD) variations across the Rukwa Rift Basin, southwestern Tanzania, were estimated from aeromagnetic data using 2D radially averaged power spectrum analysis. The results reveal pronounced lateral variations in CPD, ranging from 14 km and 33 km, corresponding to estimated surface heat flow values of 51 - 119 mWm-2. A NW – SE trending zone of shallow CPD ( 69 mWm-2) is observed in the southern part of the Rukwa Rift Basin, indicating elevated geothermal gradients and surface temperatures. In contrast, deeper CPD values (26 - 33 km) and lower heat flow (51 – 69 mWm-2) characterise the adjacent Precambrian basement and the northwestern margin of the basin. These spatial variations are interpreted to reflect spatial differences in crustal thermal structure and the degree of regional thermal demagnetisation, potentially associated with asthenospheric upwelling during crustal and lithospheric extension. The observed thermal anomalies in the southern Rukwa Rift Basin may be linked with inherited lithospheric heterogeneities, including pre-existing basement fabrics that could have acted as preferential pathways for upward migration of hot fluids from the lower lithosphere. If such controls are present, the resulting thermal perturbations may have contributed to localised thermal weakening and strain localisation during rift development. These findings provide new insights into the thermal structure and geodynamic evolution of the Rukwa Rift Basin and suggest that inherited lithospheric heterogeneities may have influenced the spatial distribution of thermal anomalies and the evolution of this segment of the western branch of the East African Rift System, however, further geological and geophysical evidence is required to substantiate this interpretation.

title: Temperature and velocity dependent drift-flux model for gas–liquid flow in geothermal systems
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Adolph Bravo, Erlend Straume, Samuel Scott, Andri Stefánsson
abstract: Multiphase gas–liquid flow governs mass and energy transport in geothermal reservoirs, wellbores, and surface facilities. Because direct resolution of interfacial fluid dynamics is generally impractical, simplified approaches such as drift-flux formulations are widely used to predict fluid-phase behavior including phase slip and void fraction. However, most commonly used correlations were developed for air–water and oil–gas systems under near-ambient conditions, introducing uncertainty in their applicability to geothermal environments where fluid properties vary strongly with temperature. In this study, the performance of widely used drift-flux correlations was evaluated using 421 measurements obtained from water–N2 and water–NaCl–N2 experiments conducted in the Geothermal-Flowloop (GFL) at the University of Iceland under conditions of 20–180 °C and 1–20 barg. Void fraction was determined by gamma densitometry, and the results were compared with predictions from classical drift-flux formulations. At ambient temperatures (20–30 °C), the existing models reproduced the measurements well, and comparison with two independent flow-loop datasets confirmed the consistency of the data. However, all major correlations progressively overpredict void fraction with increasing temperature and total superficial velocity, indicating that important temperature- and flow-dependent effects are not adequately represented. To address these deficiencies, a modified drift-flux model was developed from the Zuber–Findlay framework. Analysis of the experimental data showed that phase slip increases systematically with decreasing liquid viscosity and increasing superficial velocity. Accordingly, the classical drift-velocity expression was reformulated using normalized liquid viscosity and total superficial velocity, and a transition function was additionally introduced to extend applicability across different flow regimes. The resulting formulation substantially improves agreement with experimental observations across the full range of temperatures, flow velocities, and void fractions, reducing systematic void-fraction overestimation, lowering RMSE from 0.20 to 0.05 at 180 °C, and reproducing the observed thermal and flow-rate trends. The results demonstrate that explicit incorporation of temperature-dependent fluid properties and flow-dependent slip behavior is important for accurate multiphase flow modelling in geothermal systems and provide an extended drift-flux framework applicable to high-temperature gas–liquid flows.

title: Heat transfer performance of HDD‑installed horizontal ground heat exchangers: influence of subsurface stratigraphic structure under low-groundwater-flow conditions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Koutaro Tsubaki, Retsu Harada
abstract: Horizontal ground heat exchangers (GHEs) installed using the Horizontal Directional Drilling (HDD) method offer a cost‑effective alternative to vertical systems in regions with fragile geological formations such as Japan. When placed within permeable aquifer layers, these systems may benefit from groundwater‑induced convective heat transfer; however, the actual influence of groundwater flow on horizontally installed GHEs remains insufficiently understood. This study experimentally investigates the heat transfer performance of two HDD‑installed horizontal GHEs of different lengths under both heating and cooling conditions in Saga City, Japan. The subsurface at the installation depth consists of alternating clay and coarse sand layers, and a nearby boring survey indicates that the heat exchangers traverse the boundary between these strata. Measured heat transfer rates were compared with theoretical predictions based on the Kelvin line‑source model to estimate the effective thermal conductivity of the surrounding soil. The north heat exchanger exhibited thermal conductivities of 1.0–1.2 W/(m·K), whereas the south exchanger showed higher values of 1.6–2.9 W/(m·K), reflecting strong geological heterogeneity along the horizontal installation path. Analysis of Nusselt and Fourier numbers revealed no clear enhancement due to groundwater flow, consistent with previously reported low groundwater velocities in the region. These findings indicate that subsurface stratigraphic heterogeneity plays a dominant role in the thermal performance of horizontal GHEs, while the influence of groundwater flow remains limited under low-velocity conditions. The results provide practical guidance for the design and installation of HDD-based horizontal ground heat exchangers in heterogeneous subsurface environments.

title: Preliminary observations from a decameter-scale field test of fracture thermal energy storage: Initial and induced in-situ stress and its impact on fluid flow
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Leon Hibbard, Dana Sirota, Matthew Ingraham, Joseph Pope, Taylor Myers, Jeffrey Burghardt
abstract: We present preliminary data, results, and analysis from the first decameter-scale test of fracture thermal energy storage. The test took place at the Sanford Underground Research Facility 1250 m underground in an amphibolite test bed comprising five boreholes connected by a stimulated fracture network. The system was “charged” by injecting hot water in the central borehole while producing from the others, and subsequently “discharged” by injecting ambient temperature in the peripheral boreholes while producing from the center borehole. During the charging phase more than 60% of the injected water was recovered but during the discharging phase recovery rates were less than 10%. Significant compressive stress heterogeneity on the fracture network (> 4 MPa difference) existed between boreholes before hot water injection and was exacerbated (up to ∼ 9 MPa) during hot water injection. We observed a strong correlation between the compressive stress gradient on the fracture network and the injection impedance between boreholes. Our results suggest that adding thermal energy to our system induced poroelastic and thermoelastic effects that exacerbated existing compressive stress heterogeneity on the fracture network. This, in turn, guided fluid flow away from the areas of highest compressive stress (near the center borehole) towards areas of lower compressive stress.

title: The delineation of low- to medium-temperature geothermal prospectivity zones in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, using GIS-based Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP)
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Emi Prasetyawati Umar, Agung Harijoko, Agung Setianto, Dikdik Risdianto, Dudi Hermawan
abstract: Geothermal potential of South Sulawesi is partly associated with old volcanic rocks aged ∼6.5–0.6 Ma but the distribution of prospective zones and geological controls of fluid circulation is insufficiently determined. Previous studies mostly depended on geological and geochemical observations with limited attention to geophysical datasets and a particular focus on magneto-telluric data which hindered reliable geothermal prospectivity mapping in old volcanic settings. Therefore, this study aimed to apply geospatial multi-criteria decision framework developed through Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) to delineate prospectivity zones for low- to medium-temperature geothermal resources. AHP weights were derived from multi-expert judgement to represent geological uncertainty and improve prospectivity classification reliability. The focus was on eight geoscientific parameters which included reservoir temperature, active manifestation type, volcanism, lineament density, lithology, gravity anomaly, hydrothermal alteration, and land surface temperature (LST). Prospectivity map reported that very low, low, and moderate classes covered 40.57%, 14.18%, and 26.77% while high and very high only had 18.05% and 0.43%, respectively. The high-to-very-high prospectivity zones recorded spatial correspondence with major structural lineaments, old volcanic units, active geothermal manifestations, thermal anomalies, hydrothermal alteration zones, and gravity anomaly patterns despite the limited coverage. The validation process conducted using receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) subsequently produced 86.8% which reflected robust predictive performance of the model. This study provided a practical framework for prioritizing prospectivity zones for further exploration and sustainable geothermal development in South Sulawesi.

title: Fracture characteristics of layered rock during supercritical carbon dioxide fracturing: an experimental and thermal–hydraulic–mechanical–damage numerical study
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Guan Rong, Qinyan Qiu, Huqi Zhang, Ruichen Luo, Zuhao Lyu
abstract: Rock heterogeneity and structural anisotropy exert significant influences on fracture propagation during reservoir stimulation. Focusing on layered sandstone, this study conducted supercritical carbon dioxide (SC-CO₂) fracturing experiments under different stress ratios and bedding angles and developed a coupled thermal–hydraulic–mechanical–damage (THMD) model incorporating the pressure- and temperature-dependent thermophysical properties of CO₂. The model parameters were constrained by laboratory measurements, and the simulated fracturing responses were evaluated against the experimentally observed breakdown pressures and dominant propagation patterns. The results indicate a pronounced interaction between the far-field stress and bedding planes in controlling damage-induced fracture propagation. In the absence of bedding planes, the borehole-connected high-damage paths propagate predominantly along the direction favored by the far-field stress state. In layered sandstone, favorably oriented weak bedding planes promote damage deflection and localization along the bedding, producing along-bedding or step-like propagation accompanied by secondary damage branches. At stress ratios below unity, bedding-guided propagation is more pronounced, whereas increasing the stress ratio above unity enhances cross-bedding matrix penetration. The onset of macroscopic unstable damage propagation is consequently delayed with increasing stress ratio, corresponding to a higher numerical breakdown pressure under the prescribed pressure-loading history. Increasing the borehole pressurization rate primarily accelerates the temporal evolution of damage and advances the onset of rapid damage growth, while its influence on the overall macroscopic propagation morphology is comparatively limited. These results elucidate the mechanisms by which far-field stress and bedding govern SC-CO₂ induced damage evolution, providing a mechanistic basis for optimizing stimulation in anisotropic layered reservoirs.

title: Origins of lithium in geothermal fluids in a continental rift setting –Insights from the Upper Rhine Graben and regional Vosgian analogues, France
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): C Lerouge, J Vidal, P Lach, C Aupart, B Sanjuan, C Dezayes, J Klee, R Millot
abstract: The Upper Rhine Graben (URG) is a continental rift where lithium-rich geothermal fluids have been exploited in Hercynian fractured crystalline basement and overlying Buntsandstein sandstones to produce heat and electricity since 2007. A combined mineralogical and geochemical study of Hercynian granites and Permian and Buntsandstein sandstones, sampled from geothermal wells and analogue outcrops was carried out to investigate lithium sources and lithium enrichment processes that lead to the present lithium concentrations in brines. Whole-rock lithium contents in sandstones (11–164 ppm) and in granites (53–398 ppm) are generally low. Micas are the dominant lithium carriers in both reservoir rocks. Magmatic biotite and muscovite in granites contain up to ∼2000 and 570 ppm Li respectively, whilst detrital muscovite in sandstones contains up to 2800 ppm Li. Petrological observations indicate that alteration of biotite and muscovite into illite is a key process controlling lithium mobilisation from crystalline and sedimentary reservoirs into geothermal fluids. Present-day URG brines are close to equilibrium with Buntsandstein sandstone reservoirs but not with crystalline basement rocks, highlighting the importance of sediment-basement transition in lithium enrichment. Lithium mobilisation likely occurred during multiple geological stages: Dismantling of Hercynian chain that originated Permian–Triassic deposits, hydrothermal activity in deep basin setting and continental rifting. Argillic hydrothermal stages in granite significantly redistributed lithium, with hydrothermal quartz acting as lithium sink. Lithium mass balance estimates confirm its mobilisation by geothermal fluids circulating through the fractured network of granitic reservoirs.

title: Lithospheric water contribution in geothermal systems of northern Sumatra: Insights from OLWC-based isotope reconstruction and Cl–B–Li geochemistry
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Rofiqul Umam
abstract: The origin and evolution of fluids in subduction zones are still poorly understood, largely because of the complex interactions between deep lithospheric fluids and meteoric water in the shallow geothermal systems. Therefore, this study aimed to estimate the contribution of lithospheric fluids to geothermal systems in northern Sumatra, Indonesia, using the Ocean-Origin Lithospheric Water Curve (OLWC). The wide range of stable isotope values (δ²H and δ¹⁸O), alongside the systematic deviation from the meteoric domain towards the OLWC and supported by hydrochemical tracers (Cl, B and Li), showed significant compositional variability. The observed nonlinear trend suggests that the lithospheric-fluid component was a product of progressive water–rock interaction, rather than mixing with seawater or magmatic fluids. Furthermore, OLWC-based reconstruction enabled the estimation of potential lithospheric endmembers and the determination of semi-quantitative lithospheric water fractions (fLW ). The results showed no systematic increase in calculated fLW was with elevating chloride concentration. Furthermore, some high-chloride waters had only a low to moderate fLW . Increased salinity was not directly associated with greater contribution of lithospheric water and cannot be considered a reliable proxy for deep fluid input. Consistent with this interpretation, B and Li geochemistry showed that fluid compositions were strongly influenced by post-source processes, including water–rock interaction, vapor separation, and near-surface modification, leading to systematic decoupling between isotopic and chemical signatures. These results suggest that geothermal fluids are dynamically evolving fluid systems rather than simple mixture of fixed endmembers. OLWC-based isotope reconstruction, integrated with Cl–B–Li geochemistry, provides an effective method for evaluating lithospheric-fluid evolution and post-source modification in subduction-related geothermal systems.

title: Overall performance analysis of a stackable thermoelectric generator for medium-low temperature geothermal resources
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Entong Xia, Heping Xie, Licheng Sun, Xiting Long, Tianyi Gao, Jun Wang, Biao Li, Shuheng Li, Jiaxi Liao, Zhengyu Mo, Min Du
abstract: To boost the realistic applicability of thermoelectric technology for harvesting geothermal energy, a stackable thermoelectric generator (STEG) is proposed, where twenty-four thermoelectric modules (TEMs) are arranged in four layers and are sandwiched between five mini-channel heat exchangers with tapered inlet /outlet. Furthermore, a one-way analytical model for the STEG is established and verified via experimental results. Meanwhile, the flow behavior and temperature field distribution within the STEG, as well as the influences of operating conditions on its output performance are analyzed comprehensively. The flow maldistribution intensity and flow resistance of the heat exchanger varies between 9.5% and 14.9%, and 1.1 ~ 16.5 kPa. The temperature field uniformity coefficient of the STEG reaches 99.4%. The power output of the STEG is proportional to the square of the heat source temperature. A linear relationship between the conversion efficiency and the heat source temperature is also observed. With higher mass flow rates, the net power output increases then decreases rapidly, and its maximum value occurs at a mass flow rate of 0.174 kg/s. Moreover, at temperature difference of 70°C, the proposed STEG generates a peak net power of 23.6 W with thermoelectric efficiency of 1.79%. Notably, the net power density reaches 35.2 kW/m3, which demonstrates its promising compactness and feasibility. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the relationship between the structural design and overall performance of STEGs.

title: Multi-depth interpretation of conventional thermal response tests for layer-specific thermal conductivities
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Mohammad Al-Tawaha, Sherif L. Abdelaziz
abstract: This study introduces a new Multi-Depth Thermal Response Test (MDTRT) data-processing framework designed to estimate layer-specific thermal conductivities in stratified ground using only standard inlet and outlet fluid temperatures. Determining how thermal properties change with depth is essential for the design of ground-coupled heat pumps and modern energy foundations. Yet, existing methods that can resolve layered conductivities depend on costly, specialized in-borehole sensors. The MDTRT framework addresses this issue through a two-stage analytical approach: it first builds a homogeneous equivalent baseline, then applies an incremental, bottom-up decoding process based on an established fluid-temperature model to separate the properties of each layer. The framework was thoroughly validated using a detailed finite element model and tested through an extensive parametric study that explored the influence of layer thickness and conductivity contrast. Results show that the MDTRT framework generally performs better than the other sensor-heavy methods. Similarly, when applied to the numerical validation case, the MDTRT framework reduced the mean error in estimated conductivity compared to other methods. Field tests using data from two separate multi-layered sites also confirmed the framework’s practical reliability, accurately matching measured fluid temperature profiles within ±0.2 °C for cases with up to eight distinct strata. By removing the need for distributed sensors while maintaining high-resolution parameter estimation, the MDTRT framework provides an accessible and precise tool for use in commercial geothermal and geotechnical engineering practice.

title: Evaluation of silica scaling potential for selected wells within Olkaria Domes geothermal field, Nakuru county, Kenya
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Anne N. Kamau, Benson G. Ongarora, Patrick K. Gevera
abstract: Geothermal energy is a reliable low-emission energy source; however, mineral scaling resulting from physicochemical changes during fluid ascent, flashing, and cooling can limit efficient heat utilisation. In Kenya’s Olkaria Domes geothermal field, amorphous silica deposition remains a major operational constraint affecting separated-brine utilisation and reinjection. This study evaluated silica scaling behaviour in four production wells (OW-921, OW-921A, OW-901A, and OW-901B) using field geochemical data integrated with WATCH and PHREEQC geochemical modelling. Reconstructed reservoir fluids remained undersaturated with respect to amorphous silica under reservoir and current separator conditions (190°C), indicating low scaling risk during existing production operations. Predicted silica saturation temperatures (SSTs) varied considerably among wells, ranging from approximately 70°C to 155°C, with values of 155°C (OW-921), 130°C (OW-921A), 100°C (OW-901A), and 70°C (OW-901B), reflecting well-specific fluid chemistry and scaling susceptibility. Mixing simulations using discharge-weighted contributions from OW-921 (3%), OW-921A (45%), OW-901A (18%), and OW-901B (34%) demonstrated that brine blending reduced silica supersaturation tendencies under representative SP921 separator station operating conditions. The combined separated brines remained undersaturated during secondary utilisation down to approximately 87°C under adiabatic boiling and 110°C under conductive cooling conditions. Reheating simulations further indicated minimum reinjection temperatures of approximately 117°C and 120°C for adiabatic and conductive pathways, respectively, to minimise silica scaling risk. Silica speciation modelling showed that CO2 degassing increased fluid pH and promoted silicic acid dissociation, thereby delaying silica saturation, while kinetic and hydrodynamic factors were identified as additional controls capable of causing deviations from equilibrium predictions. The results indicate that substantial additional heat recovery from separated brine may be feasible through downstream utilisation pathways without interfering with existing primary steam utilisation. The identified operational thresholds should be interpreted as thermodynamic estimates requiring field validation and operational monitoring. The integrated framework developed provides a transferable approach for optimising secondary heat recovery and reinjection strategies in silica-rich geothermal systems.

title: Annual performance of an earth-air heat exchanger installed beneath a university building under continental climate conditions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Asmae Boubkari, Ana Tejero-González, Sergio L. González-González, Manuel Andrés-Chicote
abstract: Earth-Air Heat Exchangers (EAHEs) are increasingly considered a promising solution for space heating and cooling using renewable energy, owing to the widespread availability and stable thermal conditions of the ground. This interest is reflected in the literature, which includes a large number of studies on these systems. However, studies involving long-term monitoring of real systems installed in operational buildings remain limited, particularly for tertiary-sector buildings. Moreover, to the authors’ knowledge, no reported case studies exist of round-duct EAHE installed beneath building foundations. The present study monitors, over one year, a straight, parallel, open-loop EAHE serving a university lecture building in the continental climate of Valladolid, Spain. The system achieved specific heating gains of 37 kWh/m² year, resulting in 22% reductions in the annual heating ventilation demand of the Air Handling Unit (AHU). Owing to the reduced summer operation of the building, cooling ventilation demand is limited, with the EAHE covering 13.7 kWh/m²·year and yielding 90% savings. In winter, the thermal effectiveness of the EAHE approached 0.4 and 0.6 under low and high operating airflow rates, respectively. In summer, effectiveness was marginally higher. The cooling and heating Coefficients of Performance (COP), calculated based on the actual electricity consumption of the fan, reached 3.3 and 3.5, respectively. These results are within the range of values reported in the literature for other EAHEs installed in tertiary buildings and may be considered marginally superior, allowing for the high peak airflow rates of up to 40,000 m3/h handled by the system.

title: Geothermal geological characteristics and resource potential assessment of hot dry rock in Saihantala Sag, Erlian Basin, China
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Jiajia Song, Zhanxiong Ma, Yuanjie Li, Qing Zhang, Zhixiu Wang, Jing Han, Weili Ge, Yanlong Li, Dongshi Qin, Xin Li
abstract: Erlian Basin features a prominent regional high-temperature background and is an area with high heat flow and active tectonics. However, current research on hot dry rock (HDR) geothermal resources in the Erlian Basin, and even in the entire Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, is still in its infancy. Based on the latest systematic steady-state temperature measurement data from HDR Well, identification results of drilling rock thin sections, and whole-core thermophysical property test data of the Saihantala Sag in the central-western Erlian Basin, combined with regional geological and tectonic settings, geophysical exploration data, and crustal layered structure of the study area, this paper comprehensively analyzes the geothermal occurrence conditions of HDR in this area, calculates the terrestrial heat flow value and lithospheric thermal structure of the HDR Well, and evaluates the resource reserves using the volumetric method. The results indicate that the Saihantala Sag has favorable geothermal and geological conditions. XGR1 HDR Well has a total depth of 4529.61 m, with a measured temperature of 152.99 °C at 4502.13 m, achieving a breakthrough in HDR exploration in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Well XGR1 mainly penetrates fine grained sandstone and mudstone caprocks of the Cretaceous, Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary, as well as low-grade metamorphic basement rocks of the Cambrian—Ordovician. The basement has an average heat production rate of 1.488 μW/m3, which means the HDR in this area is devoid of high radiogenic heat producing type. The average terrestrial heat flow (qs ) of Well XGR1 is 75.63 mW/m2, and high heat flow anomalies are mainly distributed in the shallowest buried area of the Saisihao buried hill. Lithospheric thermal structure represented by Well XGR1 show a crust-mantle heat flow ratio of 0.95, close to 1:1. The crustal heat flow (q c) and mantle heat flow (q m) are 36.75 mW/m²and 38.88 mW/m²respectively. The thermal structure is characterized by a “hot mantle”, which differs from the traditional understanding of a warm crust and warm mantle, revealing a relatively high regional thermal background, Moho surface temperature in the study area is approximately 866.18 °C. The delineated distribution area of HDR resources in the Saihantala Sag is 25.38 km2, and the amount of HDR resources within a depth of 10 km is 1.52 × 1020 J, equivalent to 52.34 × 108 tons of standard coal. This study provides a scientific basis and technical support for the evaluation, development and utilization of HDR geothermal resources in the Saihantala Sag, and lays a foundation for further subsequent development and utilization.

title: CO 2 degassing and subsequent carbonate precipitation behind the outage of geothermal water cooling infrastructure in southern Tunisia: an integrated diagnosis
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Hiba Kefi, Mohsen Henchiri, Giovanna Della Porta, Lahmadi Moumni, Mehmet Cihat Alçiçek
abstract: The geothermal water-cooling infrastructure in southern Tunisia is experiencing operational problems related to the precipitation of carbonates throughout the cooling systems, driven by CO2 degassing by flowing water. During the flow from the feeding well to collecting ponds, the decrease in water temperature is commonly associated with an increase in pH and saturation state with respect to carbonate minerals. The precipitated carbonates consist dominantly of fibrous aragonite, displaying morphologies and microfabrics resembling natural travertines. Carbonate precipitation is primarily regulated by physical factors such as inorganic CO2 degassing, decreasing from 21 to 8 mg/L, temperature cooling gradient from 67 to 25°C, pH variations (pCO2-induced) from 7.8 to 9.1, water flow hydrodynamics from riffle-flow and splashing to more laminar flow, and secondly facilitated by microbial mats dominated by filamentous cyanobacteria and green algae (diatoms, Oocardium) that colonize the diverse components of the system. The thickest carbonate precipitates were recorded in lower pools, where the water had already undergone intensive degassing. The calculated sedimentation rates of these carbonate precipitates range from 1 to 6 mm year-1 (occasionally reaching 2 cm/year), which is significantly high. The sedimentation rate is not uniform and depends on both extrinsic (wind directions, rain, intermittent cooling operations) and intrinsic physico-chemical parameters of flowing water. For the study of travertine depositional processes, the geothermal cooling towers of southern Tunisia, which can be assimilated to large-scale water softeners to make it suitable for human uses, represent reliable artificial counterparts of natural travertine-depositing systems (waterfalls, terraced slopes, and pools).

title: A segmented surrogate model for THMC responses in the near-wellbore zone of super-long gravity heat pipes
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Wanli Wang, Honglei Shi, Guiling Wang, Fangming Jiang, Wei Zhang, Linxiao Xing, Wenbo Huang, Lu Liu, Chuan Lu
abstract: The super-long gravity heat pipe, as an emerging technology for deep geothermal exploitation, has attracted considerable attention owing to its "pumpless" heat extraction feature. The heat extraction process involves complex coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical-chemical (THMC) Multiphysics processes in the near-wellbore region. Constrained by the extremely large length-to-diameter ratio of the heat pipe and the need for detailed characterization of near-wellbore fractures, conventional simulation methods face inherent trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. To address this challenge, this study proposes a segmented THMC coupled modeling strategy that captures the dynamic evolution of fracture aperture under coupled thermal, mechanical, and chemical effects. A deep neural network (DNN) surrogate model is further developed based on high-fidelity numerical simulations to accelerate calculation. The proposed method achieves high accuracy with an overall MAE of 2.786 W/m and R² of 0.998 against numerical benchmarks. The DNN surrogate reduces computation time from 847 min to 98 min, representing an 88% reduction. Field validation against the Xiong'an 4200 m gravity heat pipe test yields an average relative error of 6.11%, confirming the model's practical applicability. By synergistically integrating segmented modeling, THMC coupling with dynamic fracture aperture evolution, and DNN-based acceleration, this work provides a high-fidelity and computationally efficient solution for refined numerical simulations in deep geothermal exploitation.

title: Optimization of time-window selection in the Epidemic-Type aftershock sequence analysis for accurate estimation of fluid-related reservoir variations in geothermal development
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Naoki Aoyagi, Kyosuke Okamoto, Yusuke Mukuhira, Hiroshi Asanuma
abstract: Microseismic monitoring is one of the practical methods for indirectly tracking fluid migration within reservoirs with high temporal resolution in near real time. In geothermal fields, the background seismicity rate μ of the Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence (ETAS) model can be interpreted as fluid-induced seismicity, and its temporal variation may provide useful information for reservoir monitoring and operational management. Temporal ETAS analysis using moving time windows is therefore expected to support more accurate and timely geothermal operations and may contribute to traffic light systems based on seismic activity. However, when the number of events extracted from the catalog is limited, ETAS parameter estimates may become unstable and deviate from true values. In this study, we investigated the effects of event number and time window length on ETAS parameter estimation using synthetic catalogs based on the ETAS model of the Okuaizu geothermal field, Japan. The results show that the number of events within a time window is sufficient (e.g., ≥ 100 events) and the event occurrence rate within the time window (event density) is comparable to or lower than that of the full catalog and is not excessively low, estimates of μ remain within the confidence interval derived from the standard deviation under the 8000 event condition, which is close to the total number of events in the full catalog. These results indicate that appropriate control of the number of events within a time window and event density is essential for reliable temporal ETAS analysis using moving time windows in geothermal fields.

title: Spatiotemporal characterization of a ground heat exchanger (GHE) operating in partially saturated clay formation
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Aditya Deshmukh, Anand J. Puppala, Alireza Fakhrabadi, Puneet Bhaskar, Xinbao Yu, Hiramani Chimauriya
abstract: One of the key challenges in shallow geothermal technology is improving the thermal performance of ground heat exchangers (GHEs) while reducing operational costs. Existing enhancement techniques are typically applied uniformly along the GHE depth, despite field data showing non-uniform thermal performance. This paper presents a spatiotemporal characterization of a single u-pipe GHE, consolidating theoretical framework, laboratory characterization, and numerical modeling to identify where and when coupled heat and moisture transfer becomes significant within the GHE geometry. The coupled model is validated against a laboratory column test under ambient, and non-insulated boundary conditions and applied to characterize the three-dimensional axial and radial extent of soil drying and wetting around a GHE operating in heat rejection mode. Results reveal an asymmetric temperature and moisture distribution, with greater desaturation near the inlet leg, concentrated in the upper 40–50% of the GHE depth and extending 1.21 m - 1.52 m (4 - 5 ft) radially from the pipe. This desaturation is self-limiting, stabilizing within one to two months of operation, and corresponds to an approximately fivefold increase in matric suction near the pipe, from approximately 348 kPa (7268.13 psf) to approximately 1851 kPa (38,658.94 psf) over four months. The associated reduction in thermal conductivity and heat capacity substantially alters the heat exchange capacity of the surrounding soil. These findings establish the spatiotemporal basis for future design and operational strategies, such as targeted use of high-conductivity materials near the GHE inlet and periodic flow reversal, to improve the cost-effectiveness of shallow geothermal systems.

title: Coaxial tube heat exchangers for medium-deep geothermal utilization: numerical analysis and layout optimization
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Jianling Ye, Chicheng He, Yaowen Cao, Gang Liu, Lei Shi, Jiajun Chen, Tian Zhou
abstract: Medium-deep geothermal energy resources have been extensively researched all over the world owing to their environmental friendliness, large reserves and renewability. However, the lack of field experimental data remains a major obstacle to model validation and engineering application. Based on field measurements, a model for a single well of a medium-deep coaxial tube heat exchanger (MDCTHE) was established in this study via the application of the finite element method. The impacts of key parameters, including fluid inlet temperature, volumetric flow rate, and thermal conductivity, on thermal performance were systematically investigated. Simulation results reveal that as the inlet temperature rises from 14 °C to 44 °C, the heat transfer capacity significantly drops by 74.6% (from 603.52 kW to 153.28 kW) due to the diminished thermal driving force. Conversely, while increasing the inlet volumetric flow rate reduces fluid residence time, the enhanced convective heat transfer coefficient dominates, leading to a net increase in total heat extraction. Meanwhile, a multi-well pipe group heat transfer model was constructed using the MDCTHE simulation data, and the impact of drilling layout on system efficiency was then examined. This study establishes a theoretical and practical basis for promoting the production and use of renewable energy, and provides the empirical evidence and the theoretical framework necessary for the engineering design and the developmental research of medium-deep geothermal resources.

title: Unveiling a hidden upflow in the Nagasari Area, Dieng geothermal field, Indonesia: Fluid geochemical constraints
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Aditya Yuda Kencana, Niniek Rina Herdianita
abstract: The Dieng Geothermal Field in Central Java, Indonesia, is a high-temperature volcanic geothermal system hosted within the Quaternary Dieng Volcanic Complex. Previous conceptual models interpreted the Nagasari area as an outflow zone fed laterally from the Sileri reservoir. However, recent drilling of wells NGS-1 and NGS-2 toward Mount Nagasari encountered unexpectedly high subsurface temperatures (up to 347 °C), more characteristic of an upflow zone. This study integrates water chemistry, gas composition, stable isotopes, and pressure-temperature data from 14 wells to test the hypothesis of a previously unrecognized upflow at Nagasari and to refine the conceptual model of the Sileri-Nagasari sector. Reservoir fluids are benign, neutral-pH chloride brines with temperatures of 290–345 °C, high chloride concentrations (4000 - 15,000 mg/kg), and low total non-condensable gases (<1 wt%). Stable isotope signatures show significant δ¹⁸O enrichment (6.6–9.1‰) relative to the local meteoric water line, indicating intensive water-rock interaction at high temperature. Conservative element ratios (Cl-Li-B) confirm that fluids from Sileri, Merdada, and Nagasari share a common deep reservoir. Spatial distribution of geochemical indicators, low Na/K and CO₂/H₂, high CO₂/H₂S, gas/steam, and total NCG, delineates three distinct upflow zones beneath Mount Nagasari, Pagerkandang, and Merdada, coinciding spatially with post-caldera I eruption centers (0.46 - 0.37 Ma). Fluids ascend along these upflow zones and flow laterally toward the west, north, northeast, and the central area between them. The integration of fluid geochemistry and subsurface temperature data supports reinterpretation of the Nagasari area as an independent upflow center rather than a marginal outflow. This finding demonstrates that caldera-hosted geothermal systems with protracted post-caldera volcanism can develop multiple, coeval upflow zones corresponding to discrete eruption centers. The developed conceptual model provides a solid foundation for future drilling targeting and resource assessment in the Dieng Geothermal Field and in providing wider views of fluid circulation regimes in volcanic geothermal systems.

title: Multi-objective optimization of groundwater heat pump system integrated with thermal recharge tower in severe cold zone
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Xing Sheng, Kailiang Huang, Yu Zhao, Guohui Feng, Jiaxing Wei, Qihai Sun
abstract: Groundwater-source heat pump (GWHP) systems in severe-cold regions are vulnerable to long-term aquifer thermal imbalance, whereas existing thermal-recharge-tower (TRT) studies remain largely deterministic and component-oriented. This study developed a system-level, surrogate-assisted multi-objective optimization framework for a GWHP integrated with an air-to-water TRT. Multi-year field data defined the source-temperature input, model-validity range, and physically admissible decision-variable bounds, and a validated TRNSYS model provided high-fidelity response data. A joint PSO-MSVR surrogate, developed from 255 cases and blind-tested on an independent 90-case set, was coupled with NSGA-II, global Sobol sensitivity analysis, bootstrap-based conservative treatment of surrogate prediction uncertainty, and entropy-weighted TOPSIS. All four surrogate outputs achieved R² > 0.97 and NRMSE < 5%. The representative TOPSIS compromise, re-evaluated by the full annual TRNSYS model, yielded an annual system CO P ann of 4.28 (21.3% improvement), 3,985 MWh of thermal recharge (1.55% below the engineering benchmark), a 15-year life-cycle cost of 279.9 × 10⁴ RMB (6.2% reduction), and a load-weighted grid carbon intensity ( LWCI ) of 0.460 kg CO₂/kWh (7.6% reduction). The framework therefore combines physics-based modeling, independently validated surrogate search, sensitivity analysis, and high-fidelity engineering verification in a reproducible workflow for heating-dominated GWHP-TRT systems.

title: Chemical characteristics of the Bandaiko hyper-acidic hot spring in Kusatsu Town, Gunma prefecture, and evaluation test of scale for binary power generation
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Mio Ichino, Toshio Inoue, Yuka Kubotsu, Hideo Takizawa, Yukiko Hoshino, Daisuke Tanaka, Akira Ueda, Hideki Kuramitz
abstract: The Bandaiko hot spring, located in Kusatsu Town, Gunma Prefecture, is characterized by its hyper-acidic nature with a pH level of 1.7 and remarkable flow rate of approximately nine tons per minute. Gunma Prefecture is exploring the possibility of modifying its existing heat exchange system to establish a binary power generation facility utilizing this hyper-acidic hot spring, marking a potential first in the world. However, in the existing heat exchange facility, scale accumulation of the current facility necessitates water washing roughly once a month, but the type of scale and the rate of accumulation rate are still unknown. To address this, hot spring water was sampled and chemically analyzed, and field tests simulating scale adhesion were conducted using this water. For evaluation, quartz glass coupons and a batch-type scale sensor were utilized. The accumulated scale was identified as elemental sulfur. The use of quartz glass coupons did not enable an assessment of the scale deposition rate based on weight changes. By contrast, an 18-d immersion test with batch-type scale sensor indicated a gradual decrease in transmittance over time. The decrease in this sensor's transmittance serves as a proxy indicator for material accumulation under static immersion conditions. As it is not possible to analyze the scale adhering to the titanium heat exchanger during operation, it does not directly indicate the rate of scale deposition. Analysis of deposits on the sensor surface and scale recovered during the water washing of the heat exchanger revealed that the scale was elemental sulfur. Further analysis revealed that the elemental sulfur, derived from the chemical composition of the hot spring water, was undersaturated within the tested temperature range. The hot spring water is transported via pipeline to the heat exchange facility after gas-liquid separation at the source—located 2 km away—yet it is determined that atmospheric air enters the water at the source. This suggests that the precipitation of sulfur is caused either by the oxidation of trace amounts of H2S in the hot spring water by atmospheric oxygen or, alternatively, by bacterial activity. A subsequent bacterial analysis detected sulfur-oxidizing bacteria. These findings suggest that the formation of elemental sulfur scale likely results from the precipitation of sulfur caused by H2S oxidation—driven either by microbial activity or atmospheric oxygen—during the transport of the hot spring water. While installing sterilization equipment is an option for inhibiting bacterial activity, it entails significant costs. Given that the periodic water cleaning currently employed effectively restores heat exchange efficiency, this method remains the most appropriate approach for the time being. However, if the concentration of H2S in the hot spring water increases, reconsideration of a sterilization approach will be necessary. The novelty of this study is to connect observed sulfur scale, water chemistry, field sensor testing, equilibrium modelling, and microbial evidence in an actual utilization setting.

title: Geothermal gas geochemistry in a source-pathway-reservoir framework: review, applications, and limitations
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Sanyu Quan, Qinghai Guo
abstract: Geothermal gases serve as sensitive recorders of heat sources, fluid pathways, and reservoir conditions in geothermal systems. However, their original signals are often obscured by multi-endmember mixing, gas-water partitioning, phase separation, and sampling biases, limiting the reliability of traditional diagram-based discrimination methods. This review applies a Source-Pathway-Reservoir (SPR) evidence-chain framework to systematically evaluate sampling targets (fumaroles, hot springs, geothermal wells, and soil gases) and the interpretive boundaries of major gas components and multiple isotope systems. Noble gases, owing to their chemical inertness, offer unique advantages in source discrimination and reservoir sealing assessment, whereas reactive gases (CO2, H2S, H2, CH4, N2) are more susceptible to shallow alteration and should be interpreted with caution. The core of multi-isotope integration lies in distinguishing deep-source signals from process-induced modifications. Practical applications include reservoir temperature estimation, heat-source identification, fault-controlled fluid pathway analysis, and dynamic monitoring. Future efforts should move incrementally toward a more quantitative framework that incorporates air correction, endmember constraints, mixing modeling, and multi-indicator cross-validation, rather than relying solely on qualitative diagram-based interpretation. This review outlines the essential components of such a framework and identifies current gaps.

title: Influence of thermal treatment on the petrophysical and microstructural properties of saturated limestone
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Natalino da Silva Souza, Jéssica Nascimento Pereira, Igor Alexandre Rocha Barreto, Marcondes Lima da Costa, Daniel Nobre Nunes da Silva, Pedro Tupã Pandava Aum, Cláudio Regis dos Santos Lucas
abstract: Thermal fracturing in limestone is relevant to geothermal operations, thermal stimulation of low-permeability reservoirs, underground energy storage, and the assessment of structural integrity under elevated temperatures. However, the thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) behavior of fluid-saturated limestones under undrained conditions remains poorly understood, particularly regarding the interaction between saline pore fluids and thermally induced microstructural damage. This study systematically investigated the effects of heating from 100 to 800 °C under undrained conditions, using two NaCl concentrations (10 and 20 wt%) and deionized water, on the petrophysical properties and microstructure of Pink Desert limestone, a monomineralic limestone composed of >99.9% calcite. Saturated samples were subjected to confined heating and subsequently characterized by bulk density, effective porosity, permeability, X-ray diffraction (XRD), thermogravimetric and differential scanning calorimetry analyses (TG/DSC), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The rock exhibited high thermal stability up to approximately 625 °C, with minimal variations in density, porosity, and permeability. More pronounced changes were observed only at 800 °C, where permeability increased by up to approximately 4.2 times relative to its initial value (observed for a single specimen), whereas porosity exhibited only a modest increase (∼1.1 times). These results suggest the existence of a threshold for accelerated thermal damage development somewhere between 625 and 800 °C. The FWHM analyses confirm the preservation of calcite crystallinity throughout the thermal interval, indicating that damage occurs predominantly at the intergranular scale. Within the resolution of the analytical techniques employed and under the experimental conditions investigated, no systematic influence of salinity on the evaluated properties was detected. In summary, Pink Desert limestone exhibits high thermal resistance, with significant degradation of its transport properties occurring only as temperatures approach the initial decomposition interval of calcite. The observed permeability increase is associated with the development of a more interconnected network of thermally induced microfractures. These findings provide relevant parameters for evaluating the performance of fluid-saturated limestones in applications involving intense thermal gradients and highlight temperature as the primary controlling factor governing thermal degradation in monomineralic calcitic limestones under undrained conditions.

title: From magnetic anomaly to geothermal resource: An updated Curie depth map for the geothermal assessment of Colombia
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Sergio González-Posada, Carlos A. Vargas
abstract: The study estimates the Curie Point Depth (CPD) of the Colombian territory using magnetic anomaly data and two inversion methods, providing insights into crustal thermal structure. The availability of new magnetic information from the Geological Survey of Colombia and EMAG2V3 satellite data updates the Curie isotherm for northwestern South America. This development represents a significant asset for geothermal energy engineering. The calculation uses the centroid and fractal nonlinear curve adjustment methods, with results compared to tectonic features, ANH geothermal gradients, and element concentrations.
