title: Integrated Model for PFAS Environmental and Public Health Risk Assessment (IMPERA): A framework for multidimensional evidence integration
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Rajendra Kothavade, Sonia Marie Frias
abstract: Background Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants of growing public health concern because of their widespread occurrence, environmental persistence, complex environmental behavior, and evolving toxicological understanding. Although advances in analytical chemistry, environmental monitoring, toxicology, and regulatory guidance have strengthened PFAS assessment, interpretation remains limited because concentration- and toxicity-based metrics alone do not capture analytical completeness, PFAS composition, environmental transport, exposure context, or scientific uncertainty. Objectives This review critically evaluates current PFAS interpretation approaches and presents the Integrated Model for PFAS Environmental and Public Health Risk Assessment (IMPERA), a multidimensional evidence-integration framework designed to complement existing PFAS risk-assessment methods. Methods IMPERA was developed through a critical synthesis of evidence from PFAS analytical chemistry, environmental fate and transport, exposure science, toxicology, regulatory guidance, and decision science. Evidence was organized into five complementary domains and integrated using structured Weight-of-Evidence (WoE) principles. Results IMPERA is founded on the premise that equivalent concentration- or toxicity-based indicators do not necessarily imply equivalent environmental or public health significance. The framework integrates Analytical Coverage, PFAS Composition, Environmental Transport, System-Level Exposure, and Toxicological Interpretation through the proposed Analytical–Chemical–Environmental Coupling (ACEC) concept to generate an Integrated Evidence Profile. Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) may be applied after evidence integration when comparison among management alternatives is required. An illustrative comparison of two hypothetical drinking-water systems demonstrates how similar toxicity metrics can produce different Integrated Evidence Profiles because of differences in evidence completeness, environmental context, and uncertainty. The framework is further contextualized within a One Health perspective linking environmental, animal, and human health. Conclusions IMPERA complements existing regulatory and health-based risk-assessment approaches by providing a transparent framework for multidimensional PFAS interpretation. Although the illustrative application demonstrates its operational logic, empirical validation through case studies and reproducibility testing is required before broader implementation.

title: Transfer of arsenic in surface waters impacted by anthropogenic activities: spatio-temporal evolution, speciation and source tracking in a former mining district (Orbiel valley, France)
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Marie Heydon, Eléonore Resongles, Corinne Casiot, Eva Schreck, Rémi Freydier, Mylène Marie, Carole Causserand, Sophie Delpoux, Martin Roddaz, Alain Pages, Philippe Behra, Jérôme Viers
abstract: Past mining in the Orbiel Valley has led to long-term arsenic (As) contamination risks for ecosystems and inhabitants. Around 12 million tons of tailings produced by As and gold (Au) mines of the last century remain on site. Despite remediation efforts, including lime treatment and waste confinement, recent studies report persistent As pollution in water and sediments. Given the area complexity, a more detailed study of As sources and fate in the watershed is essential: 1) for characterizing As contamination levels in the Orbiel River and its tributaries over various hydrological periods, 2) for identifying the main As sources, and 3) for distinguishing the natural geochemical baseline from anthropogenic inputs. From 2018 to 2023, water samples (<0.22 μm) were collected from the Orbiel River and its tributaries to analyze major element and metal(loid) concentrations, alkalinity, pH, dissolved organic carbon, Sr isotope ratio and As redox state. Rock samples from regional formations were also collected to compare natural versus anthropogenic Sr isotope signature. Upstream of the mining district, median dissolved As concentration in the Orbiel River was about 2 μg·L−1 increased to 37 μg·L−1 downstream, with over 20 to 60% of dissolved As as As(III). Arsenic concentrations peaked during summer low-flow periods, suggesting groundwater contributions. The 87Sr/86Sr ratio indicated a less radiogenic, anthropogenic signal downstream, likely linked to lime-treated mine waste. However, similar isotope ratios in certain limestone areas complicated source discrimination, highlighting the need for additional tracers. Mining-impacted tributaries were identified as significant contributors to As input in the Orbiel River.

title: Mercury dynamics in open coastal-marine system: a case study of Rosignano-Solvay (Tuscany, Italy)
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Daniela Salvagio Manta, Mattia Barsanti, Maria Bonsignore, Gaspare Buffa, Ivana Delbono, Fabio Conte, Marianna Del Core, Gabriella Di Martino, Luigi Giaramita, Elvira Oliveri, Francesco Placenti, Enza Maria Quinci, Alberto Ribotti, Nadia Sabatino, Antonio Schirone, Roberto Sorgente, Giorgio Tranchida, Vincenzo Tancredi, Renato Tonielli, Anna Traina
abstract: Chlor-alkali plants have operated along the Mediterranean coastline since the 1940s, representing major point sources of mercury (Hg) to marine sediments. This study evaluates the regional-scale impact of the chlor-alkali plant at Rosignano (central Italy), advancing the “open-system paradigm” for legacy contaminants. Our multi-proxy investigation of 51 sediment cores, coupled with hydrodynamic observations and numerical simulations, reveals that circulation-driven transport facilitates the offshore dispersal of Hg-enriched particles, creating depocenters well beyond the original point source. Reworking processes maintain elevated Hg concentrations in surface sediments, sustaining potential exposure pathways for marine biota. Historical Hg inputs dominate present-day sediment contamination, with concentrations reaching up to 23× above background levels across 100 km2 of seafloor. While nearshore areas show natural attenuation via burial process of contaminated layers, offshore depocenters act as bioactive zones. Surface methylmercury data indicate ongoing biogeochemical reactivation of legacy Hg via a “benthic pump” mechanism in suboxic offshore environments. These findings point to the need for integrated global monitoring frameworks under the Minamata Convention on Mercury and complementary instruments such as the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) that account for far-field contaminant redistribution and the spatial decoupling of ecological risk in open coastal systems.

title: Rethinking heatwave analysis under climate change: A climatic-type approach across Brazil
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Leonardo Brandão do Prado, Ana Carolina Lenz de Assis, Daniel Araújo Machado da Silva, Patrick Nascimento
abstract: This study analyzes the spatial and temporal variability of heatwaves in Brazil based on Köppen climate classification, rather than administrative boundaries, over the period 1991–2020. It focuses on key heatwave characteristics, including frequency, intensity, and duration, while also examining seasonality and long-term trends across eight climate types. This approach contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how extreme heat events manifest under different atmospheric regimes. Daily maximum temperature data from the Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (INMET) were used to calculate the Warm Spell Duration Index (WSDI), with heatwaves defined as periods of at least six consecutive days exceeding the climatological 90th percentile. Data processing involved gap-filling techniques and automated workflows implemented through HEATpulse, an R package designed for heatwave detection. The results reveal 1) A consistent intensification of heat extremes, particularly after 2010. 2) A seasonal expansion of heatwaves was identified, with events extending beyond the traditional dry season in the Amazon and becoming more persistent in Equatorial Savanna climates—specifically the As (summer dry) and Aw (winter dry) types—where monthly frequencies exceeded 15 and 21 days, respectively. 3) Heatwave occurrences have also surpassed typical seasonal boundaries in other climates, including Aw regimes. 4) Statistically significant positive trends (p < 0.05) were primarily observed in tropical and semi-arid climates, indicating that extreme heat has transitioned from episodic occurrences to a structural characteristic of these regions. The findings highlight Equatorial Monsoon (Am), Equatorial Savanna (As), and Equatorial Savanna (Aw) climates as particularly vulnerable. Applying this framework, these patterns may also be relevant to analogous regions globally, including Central Africa, southern and eastern India, mainland Southeast Asia, and northern Australia, which are susceptible to heatwaves.

title: Assessing PFAS uptake in hemp and alfalfa using congener-resolved analyses and soil quality measurements
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Grace Geils, Addison Pfeil, Jenna Muenchow, Danielle Singkofer, Benjamin Opaneye, Phillip Alberti, Brian Barringer, Shelby Ellison, Ann Impullitti, Joseph E. Mondloch, Bryant Scharenbroch, Shannon C. Riha
abstract: Understanding phytoaccumulation of environmental contaminants in agricultural crops is essential for assessing contaminant cycling, ecological restoration and risk, and exposure pathways. This study assessed the uptake of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), in Cannabis sativa (CBD-hemp) and Medicago sativa (alfalfa) across two greenhouse trials. Congener-resolved-PFAS analyses were performed on soil and plant tissues to characterize uptake patterns and examine how variability in soil quality aligns with PFAS accumulation. In alfalfa, short-chain PFAS predominated in shoots and long-chain PFAS molecules in roots, while total PFAS concentrations were similar across tissues. In hemp, inflorescences carried the highest PFAS concentration and stems the lowest. For both species, translocation factors (TF; shoot/root PFAS concentration) and bioconcentration factors (BCF; plant tissue/soil PFAS concentration) decreased with increasing PFAS chain length for both perfluorosulfonic acids (PFSAs) and perfluorocarboxylic acids (PFCAs). Relationships between % soil organic matter (SOM) and PFAS uptake were species- and compound-specific, whereas soil electrical conductivity (EC) exhibited more consistent associations with PFAS concentrations in soil and plant tissues. Higher PFAS concentrations in hemp roots and lower residual soil PFAS concentrations at harvest were associated with lower EC, resulting in higher BCF values for both species. These findings suggest that soil ionic conditions may influence PFAS mobility and bioavailability and highlight the value of incorporating soil EC measurements alongside PFAS concentrations when evaluating PFAS uptake in agricultural systems.

title: Mapping potential global change impacts on biodiversity important areas of the contiguous US
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Laura A. Nunes, Talia E. Niederman, Lindsay M. Dreiss
abstract: Global trends illustrate unprecedented declines in biodiversity. The main threats driving these trends include climate change, land- and sea-use change, pollution, over-exploitation, and invasive species. Strategic allocation of conservation resources is critical to address the drivers of biodiversity loss and safeguard biodiversity and its benefits to people. However, spatial assessments quantifying the relative potential impact of these drivers on important biodiversity areas are lacking at meaningful scales for national decision making. Here, we describe the distribution and intensity of the five main threats to biodiversity loss and their spatial overlaps with areas of relatively high terrestrial and freshwater biodiversity importance in the contiguous U.S. (CONUS). Proxies for each threat are based on publicly available spatial data considering both current and future projections when possible. We assess threat intensity in relation to protected area boundaries and biodiversity important areas, and quantify deviations in threat exposure between ecoregions and national scales. Overall, 41% of CONUS are areas of high conservation concern (i.e., medium-high biodiversity value and cumulative threat risk), concentrated along eastern and western coastal regions. Combined areas of highest threat intensity (90th percentile) also cover 40% of CONUS, and almost 20% are within current protected area network, leaving a significant amount of high threat intensity areas exempt from legislative protections. We found imperiled biodiversity exposure to individual and cumulative threats varies by geographic region and taxonomic group. We propose areas of low biodiversity importance but high threat intensity as candidates for policies aimed at preserving ecosystem intactness and human health. Our threat mapping assessment provides a baseline for conservation priorities across scales and could be used to develop spatially explicit guidance for mitigating threats to imperiled biodiversity in CONUS.

title: Environmental determinants and microbial association of outdoor atmospheric antibiotic resistance genes
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Sookyung Kang, Jeounghyun Lim, Hee-Wook Ryu, Kyung-Suk Cho
abstract: Despite broad recognition of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as a major planetary health challenge, atmospheric antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) remain an overlooked pathway for global dissemination. Unlike indoor air, which poses direct exposure risks to individuals, outdoor environments serve as planetary-scale reservoirs where particulate matter (PM), gaseous pollutants, heavy metals, and meteorological dynamics collectively influence the abundance and mobility of resistance determinants. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 2015 to 2025 to assess the spatiotemporal distribution, environmental drivers, and microbial associations of atmospheric ARGs in outdoor air. Absolute concentrations of atmospheric ARGs peak in winter, coinciding with elevated PM and heating emissions, whereas relative abundances increase in spring and summer, reflecting the selective persistence of resistant taxa under seasonal stressors. Urban regions exhibit the highest ARG levels, dominated by clinically relevant genes such as the tetracycline-resistance gene (tetA) and the sulfonamide-resistance gene (sul1), while rural and livestock settings are enriched with tetA and sul1 associated with agricultural practices. Network analyses indicate frequent co-occurrence between atmospheric ARGs/MGEs and bacterial taxa, including Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter, suggesting that outdoor aerosols may provide ecological contexts for ARG persistence or potential gene exchange. As climate change, urbanization, and intensive agriculture alter air quality and atmospheric circulation, outdoor atmospheric ARGs may exacerbate inequities in the AMR burden, especially in low- and middle-income countries where monitoring remains limited. Recognizing outdoor air as a neglected domain in AMR control is therefore urgent, requiring integration of ARG surveillance into global air-quality and “One Health” frameworks.

title: Structural drivers of per - and polyfluoroalkyl substances environmental fate, bioaccumulation kinetics, and sub-cellular toxicity: A systematic review of legacy and emerging alternatives
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Cornelius Yeboah, Lyndon Nii Adjiri Sackey, Daniel Kwame Oware Asamoah, Isaac Ayew Aidoo, Mwema Felix Mwema
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) pose a critical global challenge due to extreme persistence and multi-media migration. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review synthesized data from 22 core studies to evaluate environmental fate, bioaccumulation, and sub-cellular toxicity using an adapted Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal. The findings revealed a structural division: hydrophobic long-chain compounds (PFOS, PFOA, PFNA) and chlorinated substitutes (8:2 Cl-PFESA) sequestered in solid repositories, exhibiting sediment-water partition coefficients ( log K d ) from 1.64 to 4.14 with a direct linear increase ( R 2 = 0.99 ) per carbon atom. Soluble short-chain variants (PFBA, PFBS) and ether substitutes (GenX) tracked with stormwater and translocated into edible foliage. In aquatic webs, linear PFOS showed extreme biomagnification in apex predators (Trophic Magnification Factors 3.7–9.3), accelerated by slow in-situ transformation of sediment SAmPAP precursor reservoirs. Epidemiological tracking indicated traditional water-based one-compartment toxicokinetic models systematically under-predicted real-world serum burdens (up to 116.2 μ g / L for PFOA) in high-exposure cohorts by omitting multi-media pathways like topsoil dust and local produce ingestion. At the sub-cellular scale, in silico docking verified that short-chain alternatives like PFBS possessed high competitive binding affinities for fish estrogen receptors, triggering multi-generational reproductive failure, altered endocrine signaling, and disrupted adipocyte lipogenesis. While shortening fluorocarbon chains minimizes human serum accumulation, it heightens environmental mobility and introduces sub-cellular metabolic risks. Future research must resolve baseline data deficits across the Global South and adopt multi-media toxicokinetic frameworks to establish internationally standardized reference doses.

title: Per - and Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS); environmental exposure and their related health risk assessment in different medias
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Mahsa Keshtkar, Mohammadmehdi Mehdipour, Abooalfazl Azhdarpoor
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) are emerging pollutants that pose increasing environmental and human health concerns. This article scrutinizes the pathways of human exposure to PFAS through various sources, including water, air, and food. Furthermore, the environmental persistence, bioaccumulative potential, and widespread occurrence of PFAS increase the likelihood of human exposure through multiple environmental pathways, raising concerns about their potential effects on human health. In this study, the health effects of PFAS are divided into two categories: carcinogenic and non-carcinogenic, and the available evidence on the health consequences associated with these substances is reviewed. Epidemiological studies have reported associations between PFAS exposure and a wide range of health outcomes, including cancers such as kidney, lung, prostate, testicular, and breast cancer, as well as non-carcinogenic effects such as reduced fertility, delayed fetal growth, impaired immune function, changes in cholesterol levels, thyroid disorders, and liver damage. However, for most of these outcomes, the available evidence primarily indicates associations rather than established causal relationships. Additionally, studies on the health risk assessment of PFAS are reviewed, highlighting the challenges in assessing the risks of these substances, including the lack of toxicological data, simultaneous exposure to complex mixtures of PFAS, and uncertainty in the precise definition of this family of chemical compounds. The results of this study emphasize the need for further research to better understand the risks associated with PFAS and develop effective strategies to reduce exposure and manage the risk of these substances.

title: A possible mediating role of SASP in the association between environmental air pollution and incident atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Nicholas Pellegrino, Breno S. Diniz, Ying Zhou, Richard H. Fortinsky, George A. Kuchel, Doug Brugge, Chia-Ling Kuo
abstract: Cellular senescence is a state of cell cycle arrest with the loss of capacity for replication. Senescent cells produce molecules called the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which mediate the damaging effects of senescent cells, and also signal nearby cells to become senescent. Senescence has been linked to numerous diseases, including atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Particulate matter less than 2.5 μm in aerodynamic diameter (PM2.5) has also been associated with ASCVD, as well as cellular senescence. Our aim was to evaluate whether SASP mediated the effect of PM2.5 exposure on incident ASCVD. Data were from 38,261 participants in the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP) who resided within 400 km of Greater London, including air pollution exposure measured in 2010, plasma proteomic measurements collected at baseline, and incident ASCVD ascertained through electronic health records over a mean follow-up of 13.3 years. The SASP index was derived as the first principal component of 94 SASP-related proteins selected a priori. A one–standard deviation (SD) increase in the SASP index was significantly associated with a 12.9% higher risk of incident ASCVD (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] = 1.129; 95% CI 1.096 to 1.164). PM2.5 exposure was positively associated with the SASP index (0.026 SD increase per interquartile range [IQR]; 95% CI 0.014 to 0.038) and with incident ASCVD (aHR = 1.059; 95% CI, 1.023 to 1.098 per IQR). The SASP index demonstrated a statistically significant mediation effect in the association between PM2.5 exposure and incident ASCVD (indirect effect as log(aHR) = 0.0032 mediated through the SASP index, 95% CI 0.0017 to 0.0049), accounting for 5.52% of the total association. The potential mediating role of the SASP index offers insight into a potential mechanism of how senescence may be associated with cardiovascular disease. Further research is warranted to validate our findings and inform the development of targeted public health interventions.

title: Linking micropollutant gradients and multigenerational microplastic exposure to insecticide tolerance in field populations of Anopheles gambiae s.l
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Dativa J. Shilla, Deokary Joseph Matiya, Nyanda Laini Nyamandito, Richard S. Quilliam
abstract: Urban freshwater systems increasingly serve as breeding habitats for Anopheles gambiae; however, the effects of prolonged larval exposure to complex waterborne pollutants remain insufficiently characterised. Therefore, larvae were collected from two mosquito breeding sites with pronounced spatial differences in baseline concentrations of heavy metals (Pb, Cd, Hg, As), pesticides (organochlorines/organophosphates), inorganic nutrients (NO₃−, NO₂−, NH₄+, PO₄3−), and microplastics (MPs). Principal Component Analysis demonstrated a pronounced difference in the overall pollutant profiles of the two breeding sites, with substantially greater contamination at the downstream site. The influence of repeated exposure to MPs and the insecticide deltamethrin (either on its own or with MPs) on field populations of larvae was quantified in laboratory experiments. Larval survival and development were recorded over six generations, and insecticide tolerance of adult mosquitoes derived from these larvae quantified by WHO resistance bioassay tests. Initially, MP exposure reduced larval survival and delayed development; however, after several generations, larvae exhibited increased survival, accelerated development, and enhanced adult tolerance to deltamethrin. These responses were more pronounced in mosquitoes originating from the more polluted site, suggesting potential pre-existing environmental conditioning, although differences in sibling-species composition between sites cannot be excluded as a contributing factor. Exposure to combined MPs and insecticide resulted in higher survival and shorter development times compared to insecticide exposure alone. Collectively, these findings provide evidence that repeated MP exposure, in conjunction with environmental pollution, can progressively increase phenotypic insecticide tolerance in An. gambiae. Polluted urban breeding habitats may therefore contribute to reduced insecticide susceptibility, emphasizing the need to incorporate environmental pollution considerations into vector-control and insecticide-susceptibility management strategies.

title: Meta-regression analysis of CO 2 and N 2 O emissions from agricultural soils in southern Brazil
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Elton da Silva Bicalho, Mara Regina Moitinho, Daniel De Bortoli Teixeira, Alan Rodrigo Panosso, Kurt Arnold Spokas, Diego Antonio França de Freitas, Newton La Scala Jr.
abstract: Atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases have been increasing since the beginning of the industrial age, which can be attributed to human activities related to the burning of fossil fuels and, mainly in Brazil, changes in land use and agricultural practices. This study aimed to evaluate the dynamics of soil CO2 and N2O emissions in Brazilian agricultural soils under sugarcane production systems using meta-regression models. Data were compiled from eight studies conducted in southern Brazil that investigated soil processes under sugarcane production systems. The dataset included measurements of soil CO2 and N2O emissions, information on production system types, and a range of soil chemical and physical properties. Pearson's correlation analysis was performed to identify the relationship between the variables in the dataset and soil CO2 and N2O emissions, indicating the possible candidate predictor variables for the models. Iteratively fitting models considering the random effect of the study involved testing all possible combinations of predictor variables. Akaike's information criterion was used to select the best prediction models. K-fold cross-validation was performed to evaluate the predictive ability of the selected models using Lin's concordance correlation coefficient and the root mean square prediction error. A sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate the magnitude of predictor variables in the models. The dataset was robust for the development of models to predict and understand CO2 and N2O emissions from soils under sugarcane production systems. Within this dataset, sampling depth and sugarcane production system did not contribute additional predictive power beyond that provided by soil physicochemical attributes, suggesting that the effects of depth and management on emissions are largely mediated by measurable soil properties. Moreover, air-filled pore space was the main predictor of soil CO2 emissions, whereas air-filled pore space and total pore volume were the main predictors of soil N2O emissions, underscoring the importance of soil structure in predicting soil greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Health effects of indoor environmental quality (IEQ): A systematic review of indoor environments in high-income settings
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Jet Opbroek, Sarah Koch, Gabriela P. Peralta, Elena Gimeno-Santos, Alan Domínguez, Alícia Josa-Culleré, Óscar Gonzalez, Antonis Papamanolis, Stylianos Karatzas, Lídia Murillo, Mariona Font, Theresa Pahrmann, Judith Garcia-Aymerich, Natalie Mueller
abstract: Background People spend 90% of their time indoors, yet the health impacts of indoor environmental quality (IEQ) are less understood than outdoor exposures. Understanding how indoor environmental exposures affect health is essential for healthier indoor environments. Objectives To systematically synthesize epidemiological evidence on IEQ exposures and adult health outcomes in high-income country (HIC) indoor settings. Methods Following PRISMA and Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched (March–April 2024; 7158 records). Eligible studies investigated IEQ exposures and adult health outcomes in HIC indoor settings. Reviewers systematically screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Results Data from 74 studies across residential, occupational, educational, and indoor transport environments were synthesized across direct exposures (Category A), source determinants (B), and contextual modifiers (C). Under Category A, PMs, NO2, and ultrafine particles linked to reduced lung function and airway obstruction (OR up to 8.16). Indoor cold ( 100 Bq/m3) with clinical stroke (OR 1.87), and artificial light at night (as low as 1 lx) with sleep fragmentation and metabolic disruption. For Category B, structural dampness and mould odors consistently elevated adult asthma risks (RR 1.49–1.88). For Category C, open-plan layouts compounded Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) symptoms, whereas “green” certified designs dropped PM2.5 by 57% and SBS burden by 47%. Furthermore, targeted interventions showed physiological benefits: dynamic lighting mitigated circadian disruptions, while HEPA filtration and indoor greenery mitigated cardiovascular risks. Most studies provided quantified effect estimates with low-to-moderate risk of bias; however, study designs were mainly cross-sectional. Conclusions Poor IEQ adversely affects various health outcomes, most consistently respiratory health and SBS symptoms. These findings underscore the need for longitudinal study designs, evidence-based IEQ guidelines, and better integration of exposure-response data into health impact assessment of indoor environments to support health-promoting building design and management.

title: Integrated biochar–phytoremediation–Microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP) framework for heavy metal contaminated soil remediation, carbon sequestration, and low-carbon ground stabilisation
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Vedprakash Maralapalle, Narala Gangadhara Reddy, Shiva Prashanth Kumar Kodicherla, Tammineni Gnananandarao, Jayatheja Muktinutalapati, Abdullah Ansari
abstract: Heavy-metal contamination of agricultural and industrial soils poses major environmental threaten to humanity. Conventional remediation methods such as excavation, soil washing, and cement-based solidification are costly, high carbon footprint, and often fail to restore soil biological function. Although biochar amendment, phytoremediation, and microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP) have shown promise individually, their standalone applications are limited by adsorption saturation, slow remediation rates, and microbial intolerance to high metal concentrations. This study proposes and field-validated Biochar–Phytoremediation–MICP (B–P–MICP) framework for in-situ stabilisation of heavy metals in contaminated soils. Rice husk biochar (10 t ha−1) was first applied to immobilise labile metals and improve rhizosphere conditions, followed by cultivation of Brassica juncea for phytoextraction, and subsequent MICP treatment using Sporosarcina pasteurii to enhance immobilisation. A 12-week field trial on Pb-contaminated battery-recycling soil (1840 mg kg−1 Pb) achieved a 78% reduction in CaCl2-extractable Pb and an 81% reduction in the exchangeable metal fraction, alongside improved soil organic-matter and microbial diversity. Comparative analysis showed that the integrated treatment outperformed all pairwise combinations and exceeded the Bliss independence expectation of 65.7% by 12.3 percentage points (95% CI +8.1 to +16.5, p < 0.0001), confirming that the three components act synergistically rather than independently. In addition, the framework demonstrated carbon sequestration potential and substantially lower remediation costs than conventional ex-situ methods. Overall, the proposed bio-based framework provides a rapid, cost-effective, durable, and ecologically sustainable strategy for remediation of heavy metal-contaminated soils.

title: Radon anomalies environmental radiation transfer and radiological risk assessment in a fault controlled Lake system
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Mürşide Dartay, Mücahit Yılmaz, Güllü Kırat
abstract: This study investigates the coupling between radon (222Rn) anomalies, seismic activity, hydrogeochemical transport, and radiological risk in Lake Hazar, an active fault controlled lake located along the East Anatolian Fault Zone (EAFZ), Türkiye. Soil gas and dissolved 222Rn concentrations were periodically monitored on a monthly basis from September 2024 to August 2025 using a DURRIDGE RAD7 detector coupled with RAD H2O accessories and the results were evaluated with regional seismicity within a 50 km radius. Natural radionuclide activities (40K, 238U, and 232Th) were determined using 2″ × 2″ NaI(Tl) well-type gamma spectrometry detector. 222Rn anomalies were assessed using μ + σ, μ + 2σ thresholds, the Standardized Radon Index (SRI), and the Dobrovolsky preparation radius model. Soil 222Rn ranged from 87.6 to 541.8 Bq/m3, with the highest value (SRI = 2.81) recorded in September 2024, approximately one month before the Mw 6.0 earthquake in October 2024. Although this temporal coincidence is consistent with previous observations reported for tectonically active regions, the present dataset does not allow a definitive causal interpretation. Dissolved 222Rn varied from 34.1 to 69.8 Bq/L and showed delayed but detectable responses during periods of Mw ≥ 5 seismic activity. Radiological indices calculated for fish tissues remained far below international safety thresholds: H in and H ex were < 1, Raeq values were substantially lower than the recommended limit of 370 Bq/kg, and absorbed dose rates were below the global average value of 59 nGy/h reported by UNSCEAR. In addition, annual effective dose values from fish muscle consumption remained well below the public exposure limit of 1 mSv/year recommended by ICRP, and ELCR values were within the low risk range commonly used in environmental radiological assessments. These findings indicate that active fault controlled lake systems may provide integrated environmental settings where tectonic stress, 222Rn migration, aquatic radionuclide transfer, and radiological exposure processes interact. Novelty statement This study presents an integrated environmental investigation of soil gas and dissolved water 222Rn variability, radionuclide transfer in aquatic biota, and radiological risk assessment within the tectonically active Hazar Lake system located on the East Anatolian Fault Zone (EAFZ), Türkiye. The novelty of the present study lies in the following aspects: • Simultaneous evaluation of soil and dissolved water 222Rn anomalies together with seismic activity in a fault controlled lake ecosystem. • Application of the Standardized Radon Index (SRI) approach for normalized temporal interpretation of radon anomaly behavior in both soil gas and aqueous environments. • Integration of tectonic hydrogeochemistry with environmental radioactivity and aquatic radionuclide transfer assessment. • Combined investigation of radon anomaly behavior and radionuclide accumulation in fish tissues within the same tectonically active environmental system. • Inclusion of radiological risk indices (H in , H ex , Raeq, I γ , AGED) together with internationally accepted reference values for environmental and public health interpretation. • Development of a multidisciplinary environmental monitoring framework linking lithospheric, hydrospheric, and biospheric processes in active fault controlled lake environments. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the limited studies combining 222Rn anomaly monitoring, aquatic radionuclide transfer, and radiological risk assessment within an integrated tectonic lake ecosystem framework.

title: Diflubenzuron persists and impairs behavioral and biochemical responses in the giant freshwater prawn ( Macrobrachium rosenbergii )
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Patrícia Alexandre Evangelista, Felipe Machado de Oliveira Lourenço, Thandy Junio da Silva Pinto, Diego Ferreira Gomes, Henrique Alves de Moraes, Rodrigo Floriano Pimpinato, Andressa Rubim Lopes, Ana Leticia Madeira Sanches, Valdemar Luiz Tornisielo
abstract: The intensive use of insecticides such as diflubenzuron (DFB), although effective for controlling ectoparasites in aquaculture, raises concerns regarding its environmental persistence and sublethal effects on non-target organisms. This study investigated the bioaccumulation, depletion, and sublethal effects of DFB in the freshwater prawn Macrobrachium rosenbergii, integrating kinetic, biochemical, and behavioral responses. Juveniles were exposed for seven days to two environmentally relevant concentrations of radiolabeled 14C-DFB (0.5 and 5 μg L−1), followed by seven days in clean water to evaluate depletion. Body radioactivity was monitored daily, and antioxidant defense (catalase - CAT, reduced glutathione - GSH, and glutathione reductase - GR), biotransformation (glutathione S-transferase - GST), neurotoxicity (acetylcholinesterase - AChE), and oxidative damage biomarkers (malondialdehyde - MDA) were measured at the end of each phase. Escape velocity and behavioral alterations were also assessed. Results indicated rapid bioaccumulation of DFB-derived residues and slow, incomplete elimination, with estimated biological half-life values of 72.0 and 79.3 days at 0.5 and 5 μg L−1, respectively. Mass balance (MB) analysis showed that most radioactivity remained in the water, while 22.25% and 13.30% were retained in shrimp at the lower and higher concentrations tested, respectively. Biochemical responses included increased GR activity in both treatments, increased GST activity mainly at the lower concentration, and elevated lipid peroxidation, whereas CAT and total GSH were not significantly altered. AChE activity increased during exposure and returned to control levels during depletion. Behavioral analysis showed a significant reduction in escape velocity after seven days of exposure; at day 14, this impairment persisted only at the higher concentration, while the lower-concentration treatment showed partial recovery. Abnormal behaviors, such as lethargy, erratic swimming, and early cannibalism were also observed. Overall, the results suggest that environmentally relevant concentrations of DFB can impair key physiological and behavioral functions in M. rosenbergii, with some effects persisting even after exposure cessation.

title: Quantification of host-associated fecal markers in the Seven Crater Lakes of San Pablo, Laguna, Philippines through library-independent microbial source tracking
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Mylvie Alexis M. Batican, Jonah David V. Calayo, Kherson P. Gandola, Mae Ashley G. Nacario, Laurice Beatrice Raphaelle O. dela Peña, Windell L. Rivera
abstract: Freshwater lakes in tropical regions are increasingly threatened by fecal contamination from agricultural and domestic sources, necessitating precise tools for source identification and water quality management. This study evaluated and applied three host-associated microbial source tracking (MST) markers, Pig-2-Bac (swine), Cow-Bac2 (cattle), and Ckmito1 (chicken), to assess fecal pollution in the Seven Crater Lakes of San Pablo, Laguna, Philippines. Marker performance was evaluated using fecal samples from known sources and showed high accuracy ( ≥ 0.94 ), sensitivity ( ≥ 0.85 ), and specificity ( ≥ 0.97 ). Quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis revealed widespread multisource fecal contamination, with Cow-Bac2 exhibiting the highest concentrations ( 4.38 × 10 6 gene copies/100 mL) and detection frequency ( 92.68 % ), indicating cattle as the dominant source among the evaluated livestock hosts. Marker concentrations varied significantly between seasons, with higher levels observed during the dry season ( p < 0.001 ). Although no significant differences were detected among lakes ( p = 0.792 ), within-lake variations suggested localized pollution dynamics. Significant correlations were observed between MST markers and water-quality parameters, including biological oxygen demand (BOD), total suspended solids (TSS), and fecal coliforms (FCs), underscoring the contribution of livestock waste to organic and microbial pollution. The study provides preliminary evidence supporting the application of host-associated MST approaches for identifying livestock-associated fecal contamination in tropical lake systems and establishes baseline data to support evidence-based water-quality management and regulatory monitoring in similarly hydrologically constrained environments.

title: Spatial patterns of soil organic carbon stocks in German forests at 10 m resolution
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Marius Möller, Nikolai Knapp, Marc Scherstjanoi, Viktoria Dietrich, Nicole Wellbrock, Friederike Lang
abstract: Forest soils are highly heterogeneous and global maps often fail to capture the forest floor and subsoil, making depth-resolved mapping of forest soil organic carbon (SOC) quantities particularly challenging. SOC stock estimation involves two stages, calculating stock values from measured data and their subsequent spatial regionalization. Here, we tested different regionalization approaches using National Forest Soil Inventory (NFSI) data for German forests: A direct Calculate-Then-Model (CTM) approach, an indirect Model-Then-Calculate (MTC) approach, and an extended Model-Then-Model (MTM) approach based on random forest and residual kriging. The study is based on data from 1796 sampling locations from all over Germany, and the study aimed to (1) produce SOC stock maps for forest floor, topsoil, and subsoil at 10-m resolution, (2) compare direct and indirect approaches across depth intervals, and (3) evaluate the plausibility of predicted SOC distributions against measured inventory data. Total SOC stocks across forest floors, topsoil, and subsoil to 1 m ranged from 51 to 202 tC ha−1, with pronounced regional contrasts across Germany. The Model-then-Model (MTM) approach performed best, achieving the highest predictive accuracy and the lowest errors in terms of calibration, goodness-of-fit, and systematic over- and underestimation along the SOC stock gradient. Cross-validated R2 values reached 0.69 for forest floor, 0.66 for topsoil, and 0.42 for subsoil, outperforming the other approaches. The strongest predictors differed by depth, with humus-related and vegetation variables dominating forest floor SOC stocks, whereas topsoil and subsoil SOC stocks were mainly controlled by soil properties, especially predicted SOC concentration, coarse fragments, and bulk density. These results show that forest SOC stocks are depth-specific and require modeling approaches that reflect distinct ecological and pedological controls. The Model-Then-Model (MTM) framework improved predictive performance and map quality, making it a promising tool for forest-specific carbon accounting and climate-relevant SOC assessments for greenhouse-gas reporting.

title: Machine learning-enhanced game theory composite drought index for reliable drought monitoring and forecasting in cold Mediterranean mountain climates
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Mozhgan Yarahmadi, Ali Haghizadeh, Leila Ghasemi
abstract: A reliable composite drought index is essential for effective drought monitoring. This study used game theory to develop a spatially variable weighted drought index (GTDI) that combines the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) and the Standardized Soil Moisture Index (SSMI). Precipitation, temperature, and soil moisture data came from ERA5-Land for Lorestan Province (1969–2020). We calculated SPEI and SSMI on a 3-month timescale and obtained the GTDI by solving a system of linear equations. The GTDI was near-normally distributed (mean −0.038, SD 0.962). Its correlation with SPEI (0.97, p < 0.001) was stronger than with SSMI (0.83, p < 0.001), which points to meteorological drivers as the main influence. Average drought intensity in dry months was 1.57, and the longest drought lasted three months. Seasonally, the most severe droughts occurred in autumn (−0.90) and summer (−0.80). K-means clustering identified four patterns: severe summer drought (32.3%), moderate winter drought (32.2%), mild autumn drought (18.0%), and spring non-drought conditions (17.2%). The Mann–Kendall test showed no significant annual trend (Z = −0.885, p = 0.374), though 10-year moving windows suggested drying trends in the mid-1980s and early 2000s. A Random Forest forecast for 2021–2025 gave high accuracy (R2 = 0.9114, RMSE = 0.2876, MAE = 0.2008). Feature importance analysis ranked the 12-month lagged GTDI as the top predictor (74.1%). The forecast pointed to a mean GTDI of about −0.208, with severe drought in 12 months. The GTDI appears useful for monitoring and predicting drought in semi-arid regions with cold Mediterranean mountain climates. But these results are specific to Lorestan Province; more cross-regional work is needed to test broader applicability. Independent validation against ground-based measurements and drought impact data also remains a priority for future research.

title: The atmospheric-surface Nexus in a hyper-arid coastal metropolis: Compound heat and pollution risk across Doha's urban morphologies (2018–2025)
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Shikha Patel, Ammar Abulibdeh
abstract: Rapid urbanization in hyper-arid coastal cities can generate compound environmental risks through interacting surface heat, biometeorological stress, and atmospheric pollution. This study characterizes the Atmospheric–Surface Nexus in Doha, Qatar, by integrating seven satellite-derived environmental variables across six morphologically distinct urban zones in 2018 and 2025. Land Surface Temperature (LST), Approximate Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (AWBGT; used as an uncalibrated biometeorological proxy), tropospheric NO₂, SO₂ and CO, Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) were evaluated using a multi-tier statistical framework incorporating non-parametric tests, correlation analysis, and multivariate regression with multicollinearity and residual spatial-dependence diagnostics. Results show that thermal change was strongly season-dependent rather than uniformly increasing, with the largest upward shift occurring during March–May. This shift was particularly evident in rapidly developing peri-urban areas, indicating an encroachment of elevated heat conditions into the climatologically mild part of the year. Multivariate models identified urban morphology and NO₂ among the strongest statistical predictors of AWBGT, while the NO₂–LST Spearman correlation increased from ρ = +0.103 in 2018 to +0.493 in 2025, suggesting stronger statistical coupling between atmospheric pollution and surface thermal conditions. The analysis also reveals a Green–Blue Paradox. Vegetation and water features can reduce LST while their association with moisture may limit corresponding reductions in humidity-sensitive AWBGT under coastal conditions. Although the absence of in-situ meteorological calibration limits interpretation of absolute biometeorological risk, the findings identify morphology-specific and seasonally shifting patterns of compound heat exposure and provide a transferable framework for urban heat-risk assessment in rapidly urbanizing hyper-arid coastal cities.

title: Ecotoxicological assessment of cement leachates from low-carbon cements in marine conditions
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Océane Thibault, Vanessa Sonois-Mazars, Fanny Clergeaud, Maud Schiettekatte, Maeva Giraudo, Deeksha-Arya Margapuram, Lucas Leroy, Gennaro Candela, Carole Veckerlé, Laurent Intertaglia, Marie Salgues, Alexandra Bertron, Benjamin Erable, Raphaël Lami
abstract: Developing low-carbon cementitious materials is essential for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the construction sector, particularly for marine infrastructure dedicated to renewable marine energies. However, their potential ecotoxicological effects remain poorly documented. This study evaluated the chemical and biological effects of leachates from three cement types (CEM I, CEM III, and CEM V) under controlled saline conditions simulating seawater exposure. Leachates were chemically characterized using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES), and their ecotoxicity was assessed using a multi-species approach that included sea urchin fertilization (Paracentrotus lividus), microalgal growth (Phaeodactylum tricornutum), bacterial bioluminescence (Aliivibrio fischeri), and microbial functional responses (growth, biofilm formation, and quorum sensing). A Toxicological Priority Index-based approach was used to integrate toxicity across biological endpoints. Targeted trace elements were not quantified under the analytical conditions used, whereas concentrations of major elements, including Ca, Al, Si, and K, varied with binder composition. However, the sensitivity of ICP-OES in the saline matrix did not allow the presence of trace elements at lower concentrations to be excluded. Despite these relatively moderate dissolved concentrations, all leachates induced measurable biological effects. CEM I exhibited the highest overall toxicity, strongly inhibiting sea urchin fertilization, microalgal growth, and bacterial activity. In contrast, CEM III and CEM V showed lower overall toxicity but more pronounced effects on specific microbial functions. These results indicate that toxicity cannot be directly inferred from trace-element concentrations and likely reflects a combination of physicochemical changes associated with cement dissolution, including pH, alkalinity, ionic composition, and potentially other dissolved constituents. Therefore, although low-carbon cements reduce CO2 emissions, their distinct compositions can alter ecotoxicological profiles and, consequently, biological responses in marine environments. These findings highlight the importance of integrating ecotoxicological criteria into the evaluation of cementitious materials to support the development of more sustainable marine infrastructure.

title: Characteristics and trend of the wildfire activity in the Southern Hemisphere (2003–2022)
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Niels Groenen, Michaël Sicard, Pierre Nabat
abstract: Global wildfire activity has a major impact on regional climates because of the large amount of particulate matter injected into the atmosphere during and after the biomass burning. If its evolution has been extensively studied in specific regions of the globe, very few studies have been presented for the Southern Hemisphere, at a continental scale. This study aims to evaluate wildfire activity across three continents: Southern Africa (SAF), South America (SAM), and Oceania (OCE), and quantify its trend over the last two decades (2004–2024), using Active Fire MODIS satellite data. The first key outcome of this work is the heterogeneity of the wildfire seasonality among the three continents. The Oceanian continent, in particular, showed no clear seasonality during the studied time period, suggesting that different fire regimes co-exist in this area. The SAF and SAM continents exhibited clear seasonal patterns with a 20-week fire activity duration from May to October, characterised by low inter-annual variability for SAF, and a 14-week duration from July to October, marked by high inter-annual variability for SAM. Trend-changing points were determined using the robust Piecewise Linear Functions method, leading to different time slicing for each continent’s trends. In terms of fire number (and summed FRP) tendencies, the results show a decrease of −13 (−21)% per decade for SAF (2010–2022), and an increase of +22 (+42)% per decade for SAM (2013–2022). The number (and summed FRP) of the most severe fires follows a slightly stronger decreasing trend for SAF, while their trend triples (almost doubles) for SAM compared to all fires. This may be attributed to an increase in fire activity driven by the sensitivity of wildfires in the SAM region to climatic conditions and their recent changes, as well as to regional land-use practices and fire management strategies.

title: Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) analysis and 16S rRNA gene sequencing of indoor air pollutants in a 3000-capacity religious auditorium
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): M.E. Emetere, B.O. Atobatele, O.T. Olapade, J.O. Popoola, F.O. Akinluyi, A.A. Owoseni, B.A. Irewolede, K.A. Aderibigbe
abstract: A thorough molecular and environmental evaluation of microbial isolates and indoor air quality (IAQ) at a place of worship is presented in this work. The study used a dual-methodological approach, including systematic environmental monitoring to assess occupant health concerns and 16S rRNA gene sequencing for taxonomic identification. Four different bacterial isolates were successfully identified by molecular analysis using BLAST and phylogenetic reconstruction: Bacillus tropicus (A11), Leclercia adecarboxylata (A12), Acinetobacter sp. (A13), and Escherichia coli (A14). The evolutionary position of isolate A13 indicated possible horizontal gene transfer, underscoring the existence of flexible, opportunistic pathogens within the indoor environment, whereas isolates A11 and A14 demonstrated significant genetic stability. Concurrently, six sessions of air quality monitoring showed a thermally demanding environment, with humidity (56.00–70.51%) and temperatures (29.21–33.79 °C) continuously surpassing ASHRAE guidelines. The average pollutant concentrations are within WHO and USEPA safety criteria, however, there were outliers that may suggest sporadic pollutant penetration (outdoor) or resuspension of dust. The results demonstrate a clear relationship between increased chemical pollutants (TVOCs) and reduced thermal comfort. To reduce the congregation's acute respiratory and cardiovascular risks, optimal ventilation systems and source-control measures are urgently needed, as evidenced by the presence of clinically relevant microorganisms combined with dangerous pollution levels.

title: Weather overrides fuel memory: Seasonal dynamics of fire hazard and the limits of the fire return interval
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Vicente Paulo Santana Neto, José Marinaldo Gleriani, Fillipe Tamiozzo Pereira Torres, Adelia de Jesus Nobre Nunes, Igor Sanches Marini
abstract: Wildfire regimes in Mediterranean hotspots like Portugal are driven by anthropogenic factors and fuel build-up, causing severe socio-economic impacts. This study hypothesizes: 1) that seasonally-disaggregated models outperform an overall annual model by revealing shifts between weather- and fuel-driven regimes; and 2) that incorporating fuel memory, via the Fire Return Interval (FRI), enhances predictive accuracy across all weather conditions. Three fire seasons (High: Aug-Sep; Medium: Jul; Low: Oct-Jun) were statistically defined. Hazard maps were generated using a data-driven Spatial Multi-Criteria Evaluation (SMCE) and Simple Additive Weighting (SAW) approach. The FRI was calculated as the 10th percentile (P10) of re-burn intervals (1990–2024) per land cover class and geoclimatic zone; a temporal mask based on this threshold was applied to assign zero hazard to recently burned areas. All models were validated against independent 2019–2024 fire perimeters using the Area Under the Curve (AUC) method. The first hypothesis was partially validated: the seasonal High (AUC = 0.77) and Low (AUC = 0.81) models outperformed the Overall (AUC = 0.73). We found dominant hazard drivers shifted seasonally: the July model (AUC = 0.58) was linked to drought (low number of days per year with precipitation >10 mm, hereafter NDP10), whereas the High, Low, and Overall models were driven by topography, highly flammable land cover (shrublands) and high fuel load (proxied by high NDP10). However, the second hypothesis was refuted for the critical period, as the FRI mask decreased predictive performance in the High-season model. The findings indicate that while seasonality is essential for differentiating hazard drivers, this “fuel memory” is overridden by extreme weather conditions. Management strategies based solely on historical burn patterns are, therefore, insufficient to mitigate hazard in extreme events.

title: Hydro-morphometric Stage-Area-Volume thresholds controlling atmospheric moisture feedbacks and environmental water requirements in desiccating saline lakes
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Saleh Nasiri, Mohammad Zare, Ezzat Raeisi, Zargham Mohammadi, Fereidoun Rezanezhad
abstract: In endorheic basins with arid or semi-arid climates, lakebed geometry fundamentally controls water retention and regional atmospheric moisture feedbacks. However, quantifying these hydro-morphometric interactions to define environmental flow requirements remains challenging due to ambiguities in Stage-Area-Volume (S-A-V) relationships caused by spectral confusion between shallow brines and evaporite crusts. We propose a geometry-driven framework that resolves these limitations by integrating high-resolution bathymetric reconstructions with regional atmospheric moisture dynamics. Multi-decadal Landsat imagery (1972–2024) coupled with targeted RTK-GNSS surveys introduced a novel Temporal Stability Ratio (TSR) metric that substantially reduced saline-induced spectral biases. Analysis of the volume-area sensitivity coefficient (β) in a desiccating terminal saline lake delineated hydro-morphological functional zones, identifying key transition thresholds at 268.7 and 411.5 km2 that separate evaporation-dominated from volume-dominated regimes. Time-series analysis revealed a post-2001 surface-dominated state with severely reduced hydrological memory. Variance decomposition of meteorological records demonstrated that each 100-km2 increase in lake surface area elevates regional relative humidity by 1.35 percentage points, an effect that holds across monthly lags at the seasonal scale. The gradual loss of this microclimatic moderation exposes adjacent globally recognized agricultural heritage systems to extreme moisture deficits. These coupled hydro-climatic thresholds support phased filling strategies to reduce evaporative losses, increase storage reliability, and protect regional biodiversity alongside transnational regional economic security. The approach links physical lakebed geometry to atmospheric feedbacks and provides a transferable model for environmental water allocation in complex saline lake systems worldwide.

title: Remote sensing and artificial intelligence integration for seabed seagrass distribution and probabilistic seagrass biomass carbon potential
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1052 Author(s): Gandhi Napitupulu, Han Soo Lee, Vinayak Nitin Bhanage, Jae-Soon Jeong, Yuji Sakuno
abstract: The Seto Inland Sea (SIS), Japan's largest semi-enclosed coastal sea, hosts seagrass meadows that form an important and quantifiable reservoir of biomass-based carbon. Reliable mapping of these meadows is therefore essential for ecosystem assessment and coastal management. This study integrates a multiband depth-invariant bottom index (BI) derived from Sentinel-2 imagery with machine learning and deep learning classifiers to map seabed seagrass distribution and estimate the probabilistic seagrass biomass carbon potential of the inner SIS between 2019 and 2025. Sentinel-2 imagery was processed in Google Earth Engine, and Bands 2 (blue), 3 (green), and 4 (red) were combined into three BI configurations ( B I 2 − 3 , B I 3 − 4 , and B I 2 − 4 ). Of nine classifiers tested, Random Forest (RF) performed best, reaching 92.31% accuracy and κ = 0.81 under a single stratified split. More conservative validation across 50 repeated random splits gave 87.4 ± 9.5% accuracy and κ = 0.686 ± 0.225, while spatial leave-one-site-out (LOSO) validation gave 77.4% accuracy and κ = 0.50, indicating reduced transferability to unsurveyed sites. Among the three band-pair configurations, B I 2 − 3 was the dominant predictor (variable importance = 0.93). Building on this classification, seagrass biomass carbon potential was estimated by combining satellite-derived seagrass probabilities with field-based biomass distributions through Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation. The resulting estimate reflects standing seagrass biomass carbon only, excluding sediment organic carbon, burial, decomposition, and lateral carbon export, and should be read as a biomass carbon potential rather than a total blue carbon stock. Monthly carbon potential followed a clear seasonal cycle, rising from winter into spring and peaking in May–June. Together, these results show that combining a multiband BI with artificial intelligence (AI)-based classification enables site-specific seagrass mapping and biomass-based carbon assessment in optically complex coastal waters, while underscoring the need for spatially independent validation before extrapolating beyond surveyed sites.

title: Modeling Eucalyptus growth and nitrogen uptake under rainfed and irrigated conditions: A comparison of two crop simulation models
description: Publication date: Available online 22 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment Author(s): Ramon Amaro de Sales, Júlio Cesar Lima Neves, Elvis Felipe Elli, Hélio Garcia Leite, Evandro Chaves de Oliveira, Samuel Cordeiro Vitor Martins
abstract: To support management decisions and climate adaptation, process-based growth models such as 3-PG and APSIM have become increasingly important tools for simulating forest productivity under diverse environmental conditions. Comparative evaluations of these models are essential for understanding their capacity to represent Eucalyptus growth across contrasting climates, soils, genotypes, and management regimes. This study compared the performance of APSIM Next Generation and 3-PG in simulating Eucalyptus growth and related processes following calibration and validation with field data collected under contrasting water and nutrient supply conditions. In the validation of stand volume, APSIM achieved NSE = 0.76, R2 = 0.83, and RMSD = 44.6 m3 ha−1, whereas 3-PG produced NSE = 0.66, R2 = 0.77, and RMSD = 37.3 m3 ha−1. Consistent with their structural characteristics, both models were responsive to variations in water availability and nitrogen management. Variable-specific differences were observed: both models performed well for stand volume and mean annual increment; APSIM provided a more detailed representation of biomass partitioning and nitrogen dynamics; whereas 3-PG showed advantages for structural variables requiring parsimonious parameterization, depending on site and genotype. Local deviations were reduced at harvest age. Overall, APSIM and 3-PG proved to be effective tools for simulating Eucalyptus growth across contrasting edaphoclimatic conditions, demonstrating strong predictive performance for stand volume. These results support their application as decision-support tools for site-specific genotype selection, evaluation of water and nutrient management strategies, and assessment of climate-change impacts on forest productivity.

title: Abiotic degradation of methylmercury mediated by hydroxyl radicals generated during ferrous oxidation in rice paddy soils
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 432 Author(s): Jiang Liu, Han Li, Chunmei Li, Meng Qi, Sihua Zhu, Rong Huang, Guangdeng Chen, Bo Meng, Xinbin Feng
abstract: Rice consumption is a primary exposure pathway for neurotoxic methylmercury (MeHg), with paddy soils acting as critical hotspots for net MeHg accumulation. Although microbial and photolytic demethylation are well-documented, dark abiotic demethylation mechanisms within light-impenetrable soil matrices remain poorly understood. This study investigated the dark abiotic MeHg degradation driven by hydroxyl radicals (·OH) generated during the oxygenation of different ferrous species: surface adsorbed Fe(II) on ferric oxides (≡Fe3O4-Fe(II)), ferrous sulfide (FeS), and ferrous disulfide (FeS2). Upon air exposure, substantial ·OH accumulation occurred during the oxidation of ≡Fe3O4-Fe(II) (428.4 ± 5.82 μM) and FeS (561.9 ± 26.0 μM) systems over 72 h, whereas low-spin FeS2 remained inert under our experimental conditions. In autoclaved paddy soil microcosms under oxic conditions, this oxidation cascade led to a significant dark demethylation of 35.45% (≡Fe3O4-Fe(II)) and 27.22% (FeS) of spiked MeHg over 48 h, while anoxic controls remained stable. Mechanistic analyses revealed divergent interfacial electron transfer pathways: surface passivation by amorphous Fe(III) limited the long-term reactivity of ≡Fe3O4-Fe(II), whereas the destruction of the FeS lattice and potential generated core–shell structure sustained internal electron pumping and prolonged MeHg demethylation (maximum MeHg demethylation rate constant of 0.192 h−1). These findings elucidate a previously overlooked dark abiotic MeHg sink in redox-fluctuating rice paddy soils, demonstrating that Fe(II)-mediated Fenton-like reactions under alternating redox conditions can mitigate MeHg accumulation, a process that has not been accounted for in current Hg transport models.

title: Ca-Sr isotope constraints on riverine Ca cycling under anthropogenic perturbations: insights from a tributary of Lower Mekong
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 432 Author(s): Shitong Zhang, Guilin Han, Xi Gao
abstract: Understanding how natural processes and anthropogenic perturbations jointly regulate riverine Ca cycling is essential for elucidating isotope dynamics and elemental fluxes in human-impacted watersheds. Ca isotopes provide a promising tool for investigating complex bedrock weathering, in-stream processes, and external inputs within river systems. This work investigated dissolved Ca and δ 44/40Ca data from a typical agricultural river in Thailand, and explored Ca-Sr isotope systematics for identifying potential constraints on riverine Ca cycling. The δ 44/40Ca values of river water ranged from 0.49‰ to 1.09‰ with an average of 0.79‰, while agricultural wastewater, urban sewage and groundwater exhibited relatively higher δ 44/40Ca (0.88‰∼1.22‰). The ternary mixing of bedrock endmembers explains only part of the observed δ 44/40Ca variations, and model calculations yield sample-specific theoretical initial δ 44/40Ca values of 0.60‰∼0.65‰, lower than most of the corresponding δ 44/40Ca measurements. Distinct correlations among δ 44/40Ca, saturation index, and Sr/Ca indicate different constraints on Ca transport along the river continuum, and fractionation calculations further suggest that tributaries may experience substantially greater Ca removal through secondary precipitation. By jointly evaluating Ca-Sr isotopes, the results show that riverine Ca cycling is governed by the combined effects of lithological weathering, secondary fractionation, hydrological mixing, and localized anthropogenic inputs. The human-related signals are most evident in several tributaries but become progressively weakened along the river continuum due to enhanced hydrological mixing and signal integration. Together, these results demonstrated that the combined Ca-Sr isotopes, when evaluated alongside major-ion chemistry, saturation constraints, and catchment characteristics, provide a useful framework for identifying departures from lithological expectations and assessing the geochemical plausibility of secondary processes and localized anthropogenic overprints on riverine Ca cycling.

title: Nanoscale chemistry of magnetite framboids in the tarda meteorite: a proxy for fluid chemistry
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 432 Author(s): B.J.K. Wilson, G.A. Arcuri, T. Casagrande, C.M. Andrei, B. Langelier, K.T. Tait, M.G. Daly
abstract: Tarda is a C2-ungrouped carbonaceous chondrite that preserves a record of low-temperature aqueous alteration on its parent asteroid. While the original fluid has disappeared, constraining its composition is essential for understanding the chemical environment that influenced both secondary mineral formation and prebiotic organic chemistry. Magnetite framboids are an abundant aqueous alteration product in Tarda and likely recorded some of the chemical species from its mother solution, entrained within the framboidal magnetite grain boundaries. To investigate this, we conducted a nanoscale study on five magnetite framboids using transmission electron microscopy, energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy, and atom probe tomography. Magnetite framboids in Tarda exhibit a wide range of textures, crystallite sizes, and packing arrangements, reflecting a progressive sequence of discrete nucleation and growth events likely occurring in isolated water droplets. Energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy analysis of four interacting framboids reveals trace element enrichments of mostly Ti and Si along ∼5 nm thick grain boundaries, with the strongest enrichments observed in the framboids with smaller crystallites, which likely precipitated at the beginning and end of the local precipitation sequence. Using atom probe tomography, we captured a ∼5 nm thick planar feature enriched in trace abundances of Na, Mg, Ca, Mn, and Si, likely corresponding to a magnetite boundary. These findings suggest that magnetite framboids in Tarda formed from a generally alkaline fluid that contained a diverse suite of cations and evolved as water–rock interaction progressed. While the fluid composition inferred here resembles alkaline, metal-containing fluids known to promote organic synthesis on Earth, experimental work is needed to determine how such conditions could influence complex organic synthesis in asteroid environments.

title: Resolving edge-site specificity of Zn sorption on montmorillonite and pyrophyllite: insights from Zn isotope fractionation
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 432 Author(s): Yiren Duan, Hongtao He, Shichao An, Wei Li, Xiancai Lu
abstract: Clay minerals are major reservoirs of zinc (Zn) at Earth’s surface and exert strong control on Zn geochemical cycling through sorption reactions. However, distinguishing among structurally distinct Zn sorption environments remains challenging at heterogeneous mineral surfaces. This challenge is particularly relevant to 2:1 phyllosilicates, where permanent-charge sites, interlayer domains, and chemically heterogeneous edge sites can contribute simultaneously to Zn sorption. Here, we combine Zn isotope measurements with X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectroscopy and ab initio density functional theory calculations to constrain Zn sorption structures on montmorillonite and pyrophyllite. Zn isotope fractionation varies systematically with pH and ionic strength, consistent with shifts in the dominant sorption environment. Sorption at cation-exchange sites produces negligible isotope fractionation (Δ66Znsorbed-aqueous ≈ 0‰), whereas edge-site sorption yields large positive fractionation (Δ66Znsorbed-aqueous = +0.43‰ to +0.48‰). XAFS links this shift to a transition from aqueous-like outer-sphere Zn to inner-sphere Zn with shorter Zn–O bonds and tetrahedral-like coordination at clay edges, but cannot uniquely identify the responsible edge functionality. Density functional theory calculations predict distinct isotope fractionations among candidate complexes: −0.20‰ for terminal ≡SiO-bound octahedral Zn, +0.06‰ to +0.08‰ for octahedral Al-associated configurations, and large positive values for tetrahedral Zn associated with aluminol (+0.89‰) and Al–O–Si bridging sites (+0.90‰). Combined with XAFS, these results constrain the plausible edge structures to tetrahedral Zn in Al-associated environments, although the relative contributions of aluminol- and Al–O–Si bridging-associated complexes cannot be uniquely resolved. These results indicate that Zn isotope fractionation, integrated with XAFS and atomistic calculations, provides a complementary means of discriminating among plausible metal complexes at heterogeneous mineral surfaces.

title: Corrigendum to “Experimental characterization of multi-pathway diffusion of lithium in feldspar” [Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 421 (2026) 252–268]
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Brendan Garvey, Megan Holycross, Gabriel Larouche

title: Disrupted magmatic evolution controls Nb and REE co-enrichment in alkaline-carbonatite systems
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Chunwan Wei, Cheng Xu, John Mavrogenes, Jindrich Kynicky, Wenlei Song, Yuhan Ma
abstract: Alkaline-carbonatite complexes host major Nb and rare earth element (REE) resources, but the two are rarely concentrated in the same lithological unit. Thus, the processes that allow their co-concentration despite their contrasting geochemical behavior remain unclear. Here we investigate the Khotgor complex, Mongolia, where Nb and REE mineralization is concentrated in calcite-rich syenite, whereas associated feldspar-dominated syenites and carbonatites are non-mineralized. Calcite and REE-bearing minerals from the mineralized syenite and carbonatites have uniform 87Sr/86Sr(i) (∼0.70373) and εNd(i) (∼+1.5), indicating a common mantle-sourced magmatic system. Pyrochlore records progressive Nb sequestration during evolution from silicate-dominated magmas to carbonate-rich liquid. Sparse, zoned Ta-Ti-Zr-rich grains associated with phenocrysts were followed by more abundant, unzoned Nb-dominant pyrochlore aggregate intergrowths of calcite and synchysite. Later hydrothermal modification produced Ba-Sr-rich domains while largely retaining Nb. Calcite grains in the mineralized unit record a shift from magmatic crystallization to REE precipitation, as shown by the decrease in La/YbCN from ∼19 in phenocryst cores to ∼6 in synchysite-bearing matrix calcite. Strong negative Ce anomalies (Ce*∼0.03) in matrix calcites and complementary positive anomalies (Ce*∼2.5) in phenocryst rims record subsequent oxidation. Low δ18O values (∼2.74 ‰) of fluid-related patchy apatite record involvement of an isotopically light meteoric fluid, whereas the increase in calcite δ18O from ∼8 ‰ in phenocryst cores to 10–25 ‰ in rims and matrix reflects calcite-fluid fractionation during cooling. Non-mineralized carbonatites (La/YbCN ∼ 0.06) represent carbonate-rich fractions formed after REE sequestration. We infer that magmatic differentiation co-concentrated Nb and REE in a carbonate-rich liquid, in which Nb precipitated as pyrochlore, while meteoric ingress triggered in situ REE precipitation without substantial Nb remobilization, thereby trapping both metals within the same mineralized unit.

title: Nickel and magnesium isotopic evidence for rapid melt-mantle interactions in supra-subduction zone settings
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Zhuang Ma, Shui-Jiong Wang, Fahui Xiong, Wenzhong Wang, Kun-Feng Qiu, Long Zhang, Zhenyu Chen, Hanjie Wen, Li-Guang Wu
abstract: Supra-subduction zone (SSZ) settings are characterized by extensive melt-mantle interactions that contribute substantially to the enrichment of economically critical metals. However, the rates and durations of these interactions are not well understood. In this study, we integrate nickel (Ni) and magnesium (Mg) isotopic analyses, first-principles calculations, and chromium-aluminum (Cr-Al) diffusion chronometry of chromite from SSZ-type ophiolites to elucidate the processes and timescales of melt-mantle interaction during chromite formation. Chromite and coexisting olivine from the Luobusa and Yushigou ophiolites exhibit systematically heavy Ni-Mg isotopic compositions (δ 60/58Ni = 0.63‰ to 0.96‰ for chromite and 0.09‰ to 0.36‰ for olivine; δ 26/24Mg = 0.16‰ to 0.61‰ for chromite and −0.26‰ to −0.13‰ for olivine) compared to mantle values, with significant inter-mineral isotope disequilibrium. These features cannot be attributed to subsolidus elemental exchange, but instead indicate that kinetic isotope fractionation during melt-mantle interaction was the dominant process. Diffusion modeling of both Ni-Mg isotopes and Cr-Al zoning in chromite yields consistently short timescales: Ni-Mg isotope diffusion constrains the duration to centennial scales, while Cr-Al diffusion modeling gives a median of decades to centuries (80% < several thousand years). Our findings demonstrate that melt-mantle interactions in SSZ settings are transient but highly efficient, providing a temporal framework to constrain the rapid formation of podiform chromitites.

title: Mg and Ca isotopes of phreatic groundwater on a carbonate island: implications for meteoric diagenesis of carbonates
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Huiwen Huang, Gang Li, Yun Luo, Weihai Xu, Wen Yan
abstract: Meteoric diagenesis can significantly overprint primary geochemical signatures of marine carbonates. Constraining the associated geochemical differentiation is therefore essential for distinguishing primary signals from alteration, but remains difficult based on altered-carbonate geochemistry alone. We investigated major ion concentrations and Ca–Mg isotopic compositions (δ 44/40Ca and δ26Mg) of groundwater from Yongshu Island (southern South China Sea), a site marked by extensive freshwater–seawater mixing within its subsurface aquifers.
