By using Cl− as a conservative seawater tracer in a binary mixing model, the freshwater δ26Mg value of −2.1 ‰ was obtained, whereas the freshwater δ 44/40Ca value (∼0 ‰) was assumed to equal that of seawater, as it showed no correlation with Ca2+ concentration. The inferred δ26Mg and δ 44/40Ca values of freshwater are markedly higher than those expected from carbonate dissolution. Together with box modeling of meteoric diagenetic water–rock reactions, these elevated isotopic values are inferred to arise from fluid isotopic evolution under sediment-buffered conditions within the vadose zone. The newly obtained δ26Mg and δ 44/40Ca compositions of freshwater were used to model meteoric phreatic diagenesis of carbonate rocks. The modeled results can well reproduce the coupled Ca–Mg isotopic evolution observed in young meteoric water-altered carbonates from coral islands in the South China Sea and the Great Barrier Reef, Australia. These results are interpreted to reflect predominantly fluid-buffered meteoric diagenesis within the meteoric phreatic zone. Differentiating the sediment-buffered vadose zone from the fluid-buffered phreatic zone allows for a coherent interpretation of the Ca–Mg isotopic compositions in both meteoric limestones and reef-island freshwater. Elucidating Mg and Ca isotopic behavior in the vadose and phreatic zones during meteoric diagenesis will provide a robust framework for interpreting paleoenvironmental signals preserved in freshwater-altered carbonates.

title: Erosion-driven changes in soil cation exchange capacity quantified using barium isotopes
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Luke Bridgestock, Emily Stevenson, J.Jotautas Baronas, Alasdair Knight, Harold J. Bradbury, Alexandra V. Turchyn, Edward T. Tipper
abstract: Human activities have perturbed the balance between soil erosion and formation rates, driving declines in soil quality. Quantifying these soil imbalances remains challenging, especially at large scales. Here we present a novel isotope mass balance approach to quantify river catchment wide rates of change in cation exchange capacity (CEC), a key soil quality metric, in response to erosional perturbations. The approach uses differences in Ba isotope composition between river export fluxes and chemical weathering inputs to solve for rates of change of Ba storage within upstream soil exchange pools. Data for river water and suspended particulate material (SPM) samples from the Irrawaddy and Salween river demonstrate the utility of the approach. River dissolved loads and exchange pools of co-existing SPM loads feature a Ba isotope fractionation of Δ138/134Ba diss-sp = 0.23 ± 0.14 ‰. Variations in the Ba isotope composition of the sum of these two Ba pools in river outputs (δ 138/134Baout) are predominantly controlled by SPM concentration. At low SPM concentrations δ 138/134Baout are offset to higher values relative to average rocks. This is interpreted to reflect the accumulation of isotopically light Ba in upstream soil exchange pools due to CEC increases. Using a mass balance framework, catchment wide changes in CEC are quantified from the Ba isotopic data. During peak discharge conditions the Salween River basin is balanced within uncertainty of the data for its catchment wide CEC budget, while the Irrawaddy River basin features net CEC accumulation of at least 35 ± 5 meq/m2/year. Net CEC accumulation in the Irrawaddy River basin is interpreted to reflect SPM deposition in floodplains, while the CEC balance observed in the Salween River basin likely reflects the limited floodplain area of this catchment. These results demonstrate the utility of this approach to quantify river catchment wide soil quality (CEC) changes driven by human perturbations to terrestrial sediment transport.

title: Structure-informed prediction of organic matter thermodynamics from quantum chemistry and machine learning
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Thomas P. Sibille, Klaus-Holger Knorr, Oliver J. Lechtenfeld, Maximilian P. Lau
abstract: Thermodynamic constraints shape the degradation and persistence of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in aquatic environments. Predicting the Gibbs energy of the oxidation half reaction per mole of carbon (ΔG° ( Cox )) is therefore central to assessing the thermodynamic potential of organic matter degradation. A widely used approach is the linear relationship between nominal oxidation state of carbon (NOSC) and ΔG° ( Cox ), introduced by LaRowe and Van Cappellen, which provides a convenient and versatile single-proxy estimate. However, NOSC is a stoichiometric descriptor and assigns identical ΔG° ( Cox ) values to formulae that reflect structures differing by more than 90 kJ molC-1. This underlying diversity of structures can be isomeric, but can also reflect variation in molecular size, heteroatom composition, hydrogen abundance, and level of unsaturation. Here we present a structure-informed Random Forest model for ΔG° ( Cox ) trained on a curated set of over 3,500 quantum-chemically calculated DOM-relevant molecules spanning diverse elemental compositions and structures. The model was trained using formula-derived descriptors, including elemental ratios, molecular mass (Mr), double bond equivalence (DBE), heteroatom content, NOSC and others. Predictions are made at the molecular level and represent an average across potential isomers of a formula. It relies on ΔG° ( Cox ) data derived with the Becke three-parameter Lee-Yang-Parr density functional (B3LYP) and captures thermodynamic variability that the NOSC-based linear relationship systematically misses. As proof of concept, the model was applied to ultra-high resolution mass spectrometry (UHR-MS) data for four benchmark DOM reference materials, yielding ΔG° ( Cox ) distributions that are broader and multimodal compared to the NOSC-based estimates. These results demonstrate that machine learning models grounded in quantum chemical data provide a more differentiated thermodynamic representation of DOM formula space and support improved prediction of organic matter oxidation potential.

title: Redox overprinting and anthropogenic source shifts recorded by mercury isotope systematics in Eastern Mediterranean deep-sea sediments
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Xiaowei Chen, Daniel Cossa, Jiawang Wu, Lars-Eric Heimbürger-Boavida, Songjing Li, Zhao Wang, Stéphane Guédron, Wang Zheng, Yi Liu, Jiubin Chen, Ruoyu Sun
abstract: Deep-sea sediments constitute long-term archives of mercury (Hg) burial, yet the chronological record can be biased by post-depositional diagenetic processes, particularly in areas with high organic matter export and redox variations. We present Hg stable isotope data from Holocene deep-sea sediment cores of the Ionian Sea (Eastern Mediterranean) to quantify how depositional redox conditions, early diagenesis, and anthropogenic forcing shape sedimentary Hg systematics. The distinct organic-rich sapropel S1 developed during the early Holocene provides a natural redox perturbation experiment. During sapropel formation, Hg concentrations and accumulation rates increased markedly in concert with organic carbon burial, reflecting efficient scavenging of dissolved seawater Hg under enhanced productivity and stratified water-column conditions with reduced deep-water ventilation. Hg isotope signatures remained invariant and indistinguishable from background sediments, implying minimal isotopic fractionation during primary deposition and preservation of contemporaneous seawater isotope signatures. In contrast, post-depositional oxidation (“burn-down”) of the sapropel induced substantial Hg remobilization and redistribution across redox fronts, generating pronounced negative excursions in δ202Hg (up to ∼1.6‰, relative to background) coincident with manganese and molybdenum enrichments. These shifts suggest that early diagenesis imposed strong mass-dependent fractionation (MDF), most likely during oxidative mobilization and subsequent re-immobilization of Hg into authigenic phases. Throughout sapropel deposition and oxidation, mass-independent fractionation (MIF, Δ199Hg and Δ200Hg) remained largely unaffected, indicating that Hg MIF signatures appear insensitive to these post-depositional processes and may preserve surface-derived signatures. The upper oxic sediments in the late Holocene show little impact of redox-driven diagenesis on Hg and record two isotopically distinct anthropogenic phases. A modest Hg enrichment during the late Iron Age–Roman period is characterized by elevated δ202Hg and near-zero Δ199Hg values, consistent with lateral transport of local metallurgical residues. In contrast, Industrial Era sediments display sharply increased Hg enrichment accompanied by lower δ202Hg and slightly positive Δ199Hg values, suggesting dominant inputs from industrial Hg emissions at a broader scale. Together, these results suggest that sedimentary Hg isotopes preserve both depositional and diagenetic information. When interpreted within a stratigraphically constrained redox framework, paired MDF–MIF systematics provide a robust approach for disentangling redox overprinting from source variability, thereby strengthening the reliability of marine sediments as archives of past Hg cycling and environmental change.

title: Clumped isotope evidence for methane cycling in coastal aquatic system
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Xinchu Wang, Xu Zhang, Wei Guo, Hu Ding, Jiarui Liu, Rob M. Ellam, Si-Liang Li, Cong-Qiang Liu
abstract: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that plays an important role in Earth’s climate change. The aquatic methane emissions are dynamic hotspots, while the cause of high variability of methane fluxes is uncertain given the complexity of multiple, overlapping microbial processes in methane cycling. Here, we investigated methane cycling across a salinity gradient in a coastal aquatic system (CAS) by integrating the relative abundances of doubly substituted “clumped” methane isotopologues (13CH3D and 12CH2D2) with field surveys, bulk isotopes and metagenomic sequencing. We found that methane production involved mixed methanogenic pathways, while spatially variable methane oxidation overprinted these primary signals. Two contrasting clumped isotope patterns were observed: (1) In saline zones, methane has high Δ13CH3D but low Δ12CH2D2 values, consistent with strong kinetic and/or combinatorial isotope effects. (2) In freshwater zones, clumped isotope signatures shift from depleted toward more enriched value. Yet, despite Δ13CH3D and Δ12CH2D2 moving partly toward thermodynamic equilibrium, kinetic isotope effects remain expressed. Taken together, the observed clumped isotope patterns reflect a combination of mixing, kinetic effects, and partial isotope exchange. Metagenomic and functional gene data further supported the coexistence of methane production and oxidation potential across the CAS, providing independent biological evidence for the processes inferred from the isotope systematics. We interpret the partial isotope exchange as low reaction reversibility linked to rate-limiting enzyme, methyl coenzyme M reductase (MCR) complex, which catalyzes the last step of methanogenesis and the first step of methanotrophy. Thus, clumped isotope data improve our understanding of methane biogeochemical cycling and hence provide new insights into methane estimation in Earth system models.

title: Multicomponent diffusion in basaltic to andesitic melts: Toward a temperature- and composition-independent eigenvector matrix
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Bobo Bai, Youxue Zhang
abstract: Multicomponent diffusion in natural silicate melts controls many igneous processes such as magma mixing and crystal growth. In N -component silicate melts, multicomponent diffusion is characterized by an N - 1 × N - 1 diffusion matrix [ D ] , whose eigenvectors define N - 1 eigen-components that diffuse independently. Each eigenvalue is the diffusion coefficient for the corresponding eigen-component. Previous studies demonstrated that diffusion eigenvectors in 8-component SiO2-TiO2-Al2O3-FeO-MgO-CaO-Na2O-K2O basaltic melts are roughly invariant with temperature. In this work, we extend this investigation to andesitic compositions to test the temperature independence of diffusion eigenvectors in more evolved melts. Thirteen diffusion couple experiments were carried out at 1250, 1350, and 1500 °C: twelve andesite-andesite couples and one basalt-andesite couple. Diffusion profiles from the twelve andesite-andesite diffusion couple experiments can be fit simultaneously with a single eigenvector matrix, supporting the hypothesis that the eigenvectors are temperature invariant in andesitic melts. The eigenvector matrix obtained from the andesitic melt is similar to that in basalt, indicating possible compositional invariance across the basaltic–andesitic range. To test compositional independence, we simultaneously fit andesitic diffusion couple profiles in this study and basaltic diffusion couple profiles from previous investigations using a single eigenvector matrix. All diffusion profiles can be well reproduced using a single eigenvector matrix, supporting the hypothesis that a common eigenvector/eigensubspace structure can characterize multicomponent diffusion in basaltic to andesitic melts over the investigated temperature and compositional range. The fitted eigenvector matrix was further tested using diffusion profiles from olivine dissolution experiments. The model reproduces the major features of the fitted profiles and can predict diffusion profiles at higher pressures that were not used in fitting. The results provide additional support for the broader applicability of the proposed multicomponent diffusion model. The extracted eigenvector matrix and eigenvalues are incorporated in an updated open-access diffusion calculator to compute multicomponent diffusion profiles in basaltic to andesitic melts.

title: Platinum occurs as α-PtO 2 nanoparticles in deep-sea ferromanganese deposits
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Jianlin Liao, Yan Li, Julien Léger, Andrea Koschinsky, Catherine Dejoie, Anne-Claire Gaillot, Irina Snigireva, Andrea Giacomelli, Stephan N. Steinmann, Olivier Mathon, Alain Manceau
abstract: Understanding how critical metals such as platinum (Pt) are enriched in marine environments is essential for advancing knowledge of their geochemical cycles and the formation of oceanic mineral resources. Pt occurs in seawater at picomolar concentrations, yet deep-sea ferromanganese (FeMn) deposits contain up to eight orders of magnitude more Pt. The mechanism behind this enrichment remains unresolved. Although FeMn deposits exhibit high Pt partitioning, their low Pt levels and the co-occurrence of multiple elements pose challenges to investigating Pt oxidation state and uptake processes using traditional spectroscopic methods. In this study, high-energy-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was used to elucidate how Pt is sequestered at the atomic scale in FeMn crusts and nodules from the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian oceans. Pt is present in the tetravalent form, resulting from the oxidation of dissolved divalent Pt in seawater upon interaction with Mn oxides. Tetravalent Pt is precipitated as α-PtO2 nanoparticles with longer Pt-Pt distances than in well-crystallized α-PtO2. Density functional theory calculations indicate that the local structure of Pt is best described by α-PtO2 layers topotactically stacked on vernadite phyllomanganates, similar to (Co,Ni)-asbolane. The Pt content depth profiles are constant during spot analyses by laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry, suggesting that the Pt nanoparticles are uniformly dispersed within the ablated volume, rather than occurring as discrete metallic nuggets. These findings reveal a new pathway for Pt immobilization in marine environments and suggest that thermodynamically stable α-PtO2 serves as a long-term sink for oceanic Pt. The advanced capabilities of high-energy-resolution XAS offer new opportunities to deepen understanding of how trace metals are sequestered in structurally disordered and chemically complex natural materials, with potential applications in georesource exploration.

title: Geochemical data links Late Quaternary-age concretion formation to North Atlantic cold climate episodes
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Angel Mojarro, Adam B. Jost, Benjamin T. Uveges, Kristin D. Bergmann, Tyler Mackey, Diana Dumit, Mark L. Roberts, Jakob Vinther, Kristian Svennevig, Lisbeth L. Pedersen, Lis Allaart, Ole Bennike, Roger E. Summons
abstract: Concretions are lithified bodies found in sedimentary rocks often formed as a result of microbial decay of an organic carbon source thereby promoting carbonate authigenesis. Prior studies have demonstrated that this process can enhance the preservation of biological and geochemical signals relative to the unconsolidated host sediment. What remains uncertain is why certain locations or geologic time periods appear to be particularly conducive toward concretion formation. Here we present an integrated radiocarbon, carbonate clumped isotope, and stable carbon isotope analysis of concretions from three Late Quaternary-age deposits across West Greenland and Canada which have encapsulated fish remains. These concretions contain capelin, Mallotus villosus, a small forage fish whose spawning leads to mass mortalities of males. Microbial decay of the resultant carrion generates alkalinity that can stimulate concretion formation. However, despite the periodic nature of the capelin lifecycle, concretion assemblages do not occur after every post-spawning mortality event. Carbon isotope values (–19.8 to –14.0‰) indicate that alkalinity was derived from capelin carrion via bacterial sulfate reduction rather than methanogenesis. Radiocarbon ages of concretion carbonate date the fish-derived carbon and variable contributions of 14C-depleted (old) carbon from the marine reservoir and therefore provide maximum age constraints on formation timing. After applying appropriate site-specific marine reservoir corrections, ages subsequently converge with independent stratigraphic chronologies at each location. Clumped isotope analysis and reconstructed precipitation temperatures from West Greenland reflect regional oxygen isotope and temperature trends associated with cooling, increasing aridity/evaporation, and glacier stillstands during the 8.2-kyr climate anomaly. Results from Canada reveal a record of glacial freshening and retreat of the Champlain Sea coinciding with a ∼60 m decrease in sea level together with anomalously cool and arid periods. We propose a two-factor model in which cryogenic and/or evaporative concentration of dissolved inorganic carbon during cold-climate intervals, coupled with transient microbial alkalinity pulses from capelin mass mortalities, mediated rapid syn-sedimentary concretion formation. Our work further suggests that geochemical records preserved within carbonate concretions may be utilized to supplement and possibly reconstruct past climate events.

title: Sulfur diffusion in lunar melts and its implications for lunar mantle sulfur abundance
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Kang Liu, Li Zhang, Hesan Wu, Wan-Cai Li, Huaiwei Ni
abstract: Lunar volcanic glass beads preserve records of sulfur evolution in primitive lunar magmas and provide important constraints on the sulfur inventory of the lunar interior. Reconstruction of their pre-eruptive sulfur contents requires sulfur diffusivity data for lunar melts, which have remained largely unavailable. Here we experimentally determined sulfur diffusivities in three synthetic lunar basaltic melts, spanning compositions from Apollo green (low TiO2, 0.52 wt%) and orange (intermediate TiO2, 8.58 wt%) to red (high TiO2, 13.93 wt%), with SiO2 decreasing from 45.35 to 35.92 wt% and MgO from 16.00 to 11.00 wt%, using diffusion-couple experiments at 0.5 GPa and 1674–1876 K in a piston cylinder apparatus. Sulfur diffusivity increases systematically from green to orange to red glass compositions, with NBO/T rising from 1.76 to 2.49 to 2.82, respectively. At 1673 K, sulfur diffusivity in lunar melts is 6–13 times higher than that in terrestrial basaltic melts (NBO/T = 0.61–0.79), primarily owing to the more depolymerized structure of lunar melts. Combining these results with published experimental data, we develop a general parameterization for sulfur diffusivity in anhydrous lunar and terrestrial silicate melts under reduced conditions as a function of temperature (T) and melt composition (X Si+Al, expressed by the combined mole fraction of Si + Al), which reproduces nearly all available experimental data within a factor of 2. Applying our new sulfur diffusivity data to Apollo green and orange glass beads yields revised pre-eruptive sulfur concentrations of 282–311 and 331 μg/g, corresponding to mantle source sulfur abundances of 9–28 and 27–63 μg/g, respectively. These estimates differ substantially from values previously inferred for Apollo and Chang’e mare basalts, indicating significant sulfur heterogeneity within the lunar interior, likely inherited from lunar magma ocean differentiation and subsequent mantle overturn.

title: Rapid prediction of CO 2 solubility in brines using segmented depressurization-steady-state experiments and physics-constrained time-series learning
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Danqun Wang, Zhiping Li, Jingtao Lai, Yan Zhang, Jianping Guo, Qian Zhang
abstract: CO2-brine solubility controls CO2 partitioning and solubility trapping in saline subsurface systems. Mixed-ion composition, high salinity, and pressures around the critical pressure of pure CO2 increase thermodynamic nonlinearity and make equilibrium prediction more difficult. The objective of this study is to enable rapid and physically consistent early prediction of equilibrium CO2 solubility from partial experimental observations. Stepwise depressurization-to-equilibrium experiments were conducted for NaCl brines and mixed chloride brines prepared from NaCl, CaCl2, and MgCl2 at an approximate anhydrous salt mass ratio of 3:1:1, over 30/50/70 °C, 2–20 MPa, and 30/50/70 g L−1. CO2 solubility increased with pressure and decreased with temperature and salinity. At the same mass salinity, mixed brines showed lower solubility than NaCl brines. The first-order Setschenow relation adequately described the data (R2 ≈ 0.90–0.99), providing quantitative salting-out parameters and a salinity-dependent reference for the subsequent prediction framework. We then developed a two-stage time-series framework for dynamic tracking and early prediction of equilibrium solubility. The framework combines a feasible-domain constraint based on the thermodynamic upper bound C*(T, P, S) with a first-order relaxation residual used as a practical regularization term. These constraints helped reduce extrapolation drift and physically infeasible predictions in the tested cases, with complementary effects on prediction feasibility and trajectory stability. Overall, the experimental dataset and Setschenow-based salting-out analysis provide the data and physical basis for thermodynamically constrained early prediction of CO2 equilibrium solubility within the tested NaCl and mixed NaCl-CaCl2-MgCl2 brine systems. At this stage, the framework should be viewed primarily as a laboratory-scale tool for experimental acceleration and condition screening within the investigated range.

title: Biogeochemical controls on dissolved micronutrient (Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd) distributions in the Equatorial Pacific Ocean
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Naman D. Singh, Zvi Steiner, Rena Czeschel, Peter Brandt, Yuping Guo, Xue-Gang Chen, Jana Blanke, Angèle Nicolas, Jinqiang Guo, Kathleen J. Gosnell, Edel M. O’Sullivan, Dominik Jasinski, André Mutzberg, Tim Steffens, Eric P. Achterberg
abstract: The Equatorial Pacific Ocean (EPO) is one of the most productive regions in the ocean with upwelling of nutrient-rich subsurface waters and strong outgassing of CO2, and thereby playing a prominent role in the global carbon cycle. We report distributions of dissolved (d) and particulate (p) trace metals (TM) including nickel (dNi), copper (dCu), zinc (dZn) and cadmium (dCd), along the GEOTRACES transect, GP11, in the EPO during a developing El Niño phase, associated with anomalous surface winds and currents. Using estimates of surface dTM fluxes and water mass mixing in deeper waters, we assessed biogeochemical controls on dTM distributions in the water column. Surface waters (depths 200 m), water mass mixing and organic matter (OM) remineralization largely governed the dCd distribution. The dNi, dCu and dZn distributions and their relationships with macronutrients were determined by particle scavenging of remineralized Ni, Cu and Zn and/or their retention (slower remineralization) to particles. Strong enrichments in dNi and dCu were observed in deep waters (depths > 2500 m) of the eastern and central EPO, which could not be explained by water mass mixing and OM remineralization. Particulate data indicated a limited influence of reversible scavenging and deep-water remineralization, with the supply from sediments likely supporting the dNi and dCu increases in deep waters. Our results underscore the need to better quantify benthic trace metal fluxes across Pacific abyssal sediments, as sedimentary inputs may substantially influence deep ocean micronutrient reservoirs and their eventual redistribution to the upper ocean.

title: Textures of Chassignite meteorites: Clues to cumulate formation and early deformation processes on Mars
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): N. Meunier-Mili, M.-A. Kaczmarek, M. Bystricky
abstract: Chassignite meteorites are martian achondrites that display a magmatic cumulate texture and are mainly composed of olivine with a small amount of poikilitic pyroxene. This study presents a detailed petrological and microstructural analysis using electron backscatter diffraction of all chassignite meteorites documented up to now, Chassigny, NWA 2737 and NWA 8694, in order to decipher early magmatic, deformation and shock processes. The new results reveal that olivine crystals in chassignite meteorites initially formed through synneusis, a magmatic process where individual crystals accumulate and aggregate together in specific orientations in the earlier stages of consolidation. Many olivine crystals stick together along (100) crystalline faces as evidenced by the significant concentration of misorientation [100] axes at grain boundaries for all three samples. Synneusis was probably interrupted and progressively replaced by crystal settling until complete crystallisation was achieved. Olivine crystallographic preferred orientations indicate slip on [100](010) and olivine subgrain boundaries reveal high densities of geometrically necessary dislocations of the [100](010) type. The [100](010) slip system is active at high temperatures and low stresses in the Earth’s upper mantle and is often observed in plastically deformed peridotites, though it is not necessarily dominant in terrestrial olivine cumulative rocks. Furthermore, pyroxene crystallographic preferred orientations are consistent with those of olivine ([100] olivine axes parallel to pyroxene [001] axes), supporting the hypothesis of minor plastic deformation of olivine and pyroxene at high temperatures and low stresses. These observations are consistent with possible crystallization and emplacement of the chassignite-type magma in the shallow martian crust. Finally the strong shock events recorded by these meteorites are supported by significant internal deformation of olivine grains, concentration of misorientation axes along their [100] axes, and the activation of the [001](010) slip system leading to formation of olivine subgrain boundaries. Altogether these results are good indicators to decipher primary planetary processes.

title: Non-monotonic rare earth element redistribution under intense subtropical weathering
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Ruifei Yu, Lidong Zhu, Ziyi Zhang, Jiabin Wu, Fengquan Li, Tianyang Wang, Wei Ye, Licheng Guo, Philip A.E. Pogge von Strandmann, Xiao Zhang, Ying Huang
abstract: Rare earth elements (REEs) are widely used as tracers of chemical weathering, yet their redistribution in intensely weathered subtropical systems remains poorly constrained. We investigate REE redistribution in loess-like Quaternary Red Clay (QRC) from mid-subtropical China using geochemical, statistical, and clay mineralogical approaches. Across intensely weathered conditions (CIA > 80), segmented regression and generalized additive models (GAMs) reveal a reproducible non-monotonic ΣREE trajectory with statistically supported breakpoints near CIA ≈ 86 and ≈ 89. Rather than following a simple monotonic depletion trend expected from progressive leaching alone, ΣREE shows a relative stabilization or slight recovery within the CIA 86–89 interval, followed by pronounced depletion under more extreme weathering conditions. Clay mineralogical observations indicate progressive shifts in mineral assemblages, including decreasing proportions of primary minerals and increasing abundance of secondary minerals, providing a plausible context for observed REE fractionation. The reproducibility of this non-monotonic pattern across multiple sections suggests that progressive weathering dominates, whereas variations in sediment input modulate its local expression. These findings demonstrate that REE redistribution in deeply weathered subtropical systems reflects coupled geochemical, mineralogical, and open-system sedimentary controls.

title: Magnitude of stable iron isotope fractionation limited by multiple stages of terrestrial core formation
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Gabriel Nathan, Seth A. Jacobson
abstract: One proposed mechanism for generating iron isotopic differences between planetary mantles and chondrites is metal-silicate equilibration during terrestrial core formation. Prior studies of this isotopic fractionation effect employ single-stage core formation models that are inconsistent with reproducing the siderophile element budget of the Earth’s mantle. Here, we model iron isotopic evolution of the Earth’s mantle in a multistage core formation scenario that is consistent with dynamic models of planet formation and reproduces the geochemistry of the bulk silicate Earth, specifically the refractory moderately siderophile elements. We find that multiple stages of core formation rebalance the fractionating effect of metal-silicate equilibration for the iron isotopic system, comparable to or smaller than typical analytical uncertainties in mantle rocks. Ultimately, this rebalancing effect — coupled with stochastic accretion and differentiation histories which further complicate planetary formation processes — makes it unlikely that isotopic fractionation during metal-silicate equilibration is the primary mechanism responsible for the iron isotopic composition of the Earth’s mantle.

title: The solubility and speciation of REE phosphate endmembers (CePO 4 and YPO 4 ) in Cl-rich aqueous fluids from 350 to 450 °C and implications for natural systems
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Charles T. Kershaw, Nicole C. Hurtig, Alexander P. Gysi, Artas A. Migdisov, Laura E. Waters, Daniel Harlov
abstract: The rare earth elements (REE) are important metals used increasingly in advanced technologies. Within the crust, the elements Ce and Y are commonly more abundant compared to other lanthanides (La-Lu) and comprise important end-member constituents of REE-bearing minerals. Specifically, Ce is part of the light (L) REE which have larger ionic radii than the heavy (H) REE, which are grouped together with Y. These differences in ionic radius can lead to important physiochemical trends within the lanthanide group. Despite a recent increase in experimental and thermodynamic data for the REE at high temperature and pressure, there is still a significant lack of these data at supercritical conditions. In this study we conducted batch-type experiments to measure the solubility of REE phosphates (CePO4 and YPO4) at varying starting pH (1.5–10), and salinity (0.01–1.4 mol/kg NaCl) at 350 and P sat, and from 400 to 450 °C at 700 bar. Results show that the solubility of Ce (0.14 ± 0.01–33.0 ± 1.6 ppb) is generally higher than Y (0.16 ± 0.01–13.8 ± 0.7 ppb) and that Ce complexes more strongly with both chloride and hydroxyl ligands compared to Y. The solubilities of both REE phosphates are highly pH-dependent and, to a lesser extent, depend on salinity at the studied conditions. The solubility data from this study were implemented into the GEMSFITS program to optimize the thermodynamic properties of Ce and Y hydroxyl and chloride species. The updated standard partial molal Gibbs energies of formation (Δ f G0 T,P ) are used within the experimental temperature and pressure range to accurately predict the CePO4 and YPO4 solubility and Ce and Y speciation behavior. Based on the updated thermodynamic properties we also provide formation constants (log β n Cl,OH) for Ce and Y hydroxyl and chloride species. Updated thermodynamic properties are applied to model REE-apatite dissolution and REE mobility based on the Pea Ridge iron oxide apatite deposit in Missouri, USA. The apatite dissolution model replicates natural observations including the replacement of monazite and xenotime after apatite and is an example of the utility of the application of new thermodynamic constants to supercritical crustal fluids. The findings of this study advance the predictive capabilities of geochemical models, our understanding of the behavior of individual REE, and permit modeling the overarching fractionation trends between LREE and HREE in supercritical crustal fluids.

title: Experimental constraints on lithium isotope systematics in Porites corals: robustness of Li/Mg and δ 7 Li paleoceanographic proxies
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Toshihiro Yoshimura, Wenshuai Li, Xiao-Ming Liu
abstract: Coral skeletons have been increasingly utilized as geochemical archives for reconstructing past seawater temperature. The Li isotope composition of coral skeletons is a promising proxy, as it reflects both environmental conditions and physiological processes. In this study, we analyzed the Li isotope composition of massive Porites australiensis coral skeletons cultured under temperature-controlled conditions to evaluate the influence of seawater temperature and the vital effect. Our results show that Li isotope composition remains uniform, mostly ranging from 15 to 19‰ with a mean value of ∼ 17‰, and is similar to inorganic aragonite for samples with Li/Mg of > 1.5 mmol/mol. Conversely, the samples exhibiting higher growth rates both at 27 and 29°C show 7Li enrichment probably influenced by cellular processes. These results demonstrate that coral skeletal δ7Li is influenced by biologically mediated fractionation, which likely modifies equilibrium exchange with seawater especially at higher growth rates. The pronounced variability observed under controlled conditions highlights the important role of temperature-dependent cellular processes in regulating Li transport and incorporation during coral biomineralization.

title: FTIR constraints on Martian mantle water from clinopyroxene in nakhlite and shergottite meteorites
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Ioana-Bogdana Radu, Cécile Deligny, Henrik Skogby, Roland Stalder, Jeremy J. Bellucci, Martin J. Whitehouse
abstract: Water on Mars has traditionally been estimated from hydrogen contents in melt inclusions and apatite, yet these may not account for magma degassing or post-crystallization dehydration. Pyroxenes offer an alternative approach, as they incorporate trace amounts of water during crystallisation via charge-balancing structural defects, that are retained after dehydration enabling experimentally reversing water loss and constraining magmatic water contents. Here we report the first hydrothermal rehydration experiments on pyroxene from both nakhlites and shergottites. The treated nakhlite augites contain 140‒185 ppm H2O, consistent with previous values for Nakhla (130 ± 26 ppm) and within the range of terrestrial basaltic pyroxene. Using clinopyroxene-melt partition coefficients, this corresponds to 1.59 ± 0.03‒1.83 ± 0.10 wt% average H2O in the nakhlite magma, slightly higher than previous estimates (0.69‒1.42 wt% H2O). The complex hydrothermal history of nakhlites, including evidence for magmatic degassing and interaction with H2O-poor, Cl-rich fluids, suggests these estimates may represent minimum values of the nakhlite magmatic water content. Assuming a low degree of partial melting, the nakhlite mantle source is expected to contain 80‒91 ppm H2O, overlapping previous estimates (59‒184 ppm), and comparable to Earth’s MORB mantle (54‒330 ppm). This is consistent with a common magmatic source for all nakhlites, and broadly consistent with water estimates for the chassignite mantle source (39‒252 ppm), suggesting that any exogenous fluid assimilation had a negligible effect on the net water budget. In contrast, shergottite pigeonites show no detectable water by Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy, consistent with expected water contents of ∼ 2‒11 ppm H2O derived from published source compositions for depleted and enriched shergottites. Together, these results refine our understanding of martian magmatic water content, consistent with a common, more water-rich mantle source for nakhlites, distinct from the more heterogeneous and generally drier shergottite mantle reservoirs.

title: Synergistic interfacial and multi-omics regulation of La 3+ /Gd 3+ biomineralization by Micromonospora auratinigra
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Lili Wang, Chenyu Yin, Xinyu Chen, Chengliang Cao, Xiuming Liu, Wenping He, Rongpeng Li, Jihong Jiang, Jinjuan Liu
abstract: Microorganisms play pivotal roles in the formation of weathering crust-type rare earth elements (REEs) deposits, yet the mechanisms underlying microbial-mediated REEs immobilization and secondary mineral formation remain insufficiently understood. This study systematically explores the synergistic biosorption and biomineralization mechanisms of La3+ and Gd3+ by the highly tolerant actinobacterium Micromonospora auratinigra. Under optimized conditions (biomass 1.5 g/L, pH 5, La/Gd ratio 2:1), the strain exhibited a preferential affinity for Gd3+ (135.9 mg/g) over La3+ (110.1 mg/g), with further enhanced uptake in mixed systems (143.1 mg/g). Kinetic and isotherm modeling indicated monolayer chemisorption behavior following pseudo-second-order kinetics and Langmuir adsorption patterns. Functional group masking experiments, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses revealed that carboxyl, phosphate, and amino groups on the cell surface were key contributors to REEs binding, with carboxyl groups playing the dominant role. Electron microscopy confirmed the formation of LaPO4 and GdPO4 nanocrystals on the bacterial surface, while HRTEM and SAED analyses revealed the formation of distinct monazite-type mineral phases. Multi-omics analysis demonstrated that the biosorption and mineralization processes were regulated by peptidoglycan functional groups, heavy metal resistance genes, oxidative stress response systems, and phosphate metabolism pathways. Notably, upregulation of phosphate transport and regulatory genes (pstSCAB, phoR/phoU) promoted phosphate acquisition and REEs-phosphate precipitation, while downregulation of organic acid biosynthesis genes prevented mineral dissolution. This work elucidates the molecular and interfacial mechanisms by which M. auratinigra immobilizes REEs, offering new insights into microbial mediation of REEs geochemical cycling. These findings provide a theoretical basis for the development of environmentally friendly technologies for REEs recovery and sustainable resource utilization.

title: Heavy Rb isotope composition of subduction zone fluids resulting from fluid-rock interaction in continental subduction zones
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Anxia Chen, Yi-Xiang Chen, Dingsheng Jiang, Hans-Peter Schertl, Shouzhen Yang, Fang Huang
abstract: Subduction zone fluids are key agents for the transport of rubidium (Rb), yet the Rb isotope compositions of these fluids and the associated fractionation during fluid-rock interaction remain poorly constrained. This hinders the application of Rb isotopes as a powerful tracer for fluid-mediated mass transfer in subduction zones. To address this problem, we present a systematic Rb isotope study of ultrahigh-pressure whiteschists and their metagranite protoliths from the Western Alps. The whiteschists formed through intense Mg-rich fluid infiltration during deep continental subduction, whereas the metagranites underwent ultrahigh-pressure metamorphism with negligible fluid-rock interaction. The whiteschists show significantly lower and more variable δ87Rb (−1.06‰ to 0.04‰) than the metagranites (−0.15‰ to 0.06‰). The δ87Rb values of the whiteschists correlate negatively with MgO and fluid-mobile element concentrations, indicating significant Rb isotope fractionation during fluid-rock interaction. Under extreme fluid-rock interaction conditions, modeling yields a first-order apparent integrated isotope effect (Δ87Rbrock-fluid) of −1.53‰ to −1.07‰, corresponding to a calculated fluid composition (δ87Rbfluid) of ∼0.47‰. Although this represents an end-member condition under high fluid-rock ratios, the result demonstrates that subduction zone fluids preferentially extract the heavy Rb isotope (87Rb), leaving the residual rocks enriched in the light one (85Rb). Our findings establish Rb isotopes as a sensitive tracer of fluid-rock interaction processes and provide key constraints for understanding Rb isotope variations in arc magmas and mantle heterogeneity.

title: Complexity of baddeleyite microstructure and Pb-Pb age in lunar gabbroic breccias: implications for the NWA 773 Clan chronology
description: Publication date: 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 431 Author(s): Liying Huang, Lee Francis White, Xuchao Zhao, Mahesh Anand, Muhammad Zeeshan Mughal, Yuchen Xu, Yang Liu, Yongliao Zou
abstract: Baddeleyite (monoclinic-ZrO2) is a key accessory mineral for dating mafic rocks and tracing magmatic and impact processes. Although its crystal structure is highly sensitive to pressure–temperature (P-T) conditions, integrated studies linking microstructural response of lunar baddeleyite to P-T histories and Pb-Pb ages remain limited. Here we integrate in-situ Pb-Pb dating with high-resolution electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis of baddeleyite grains in two lunar gabbroic breccia meteorites, Northwest Africa 773 and 3333. Based on crystallographic and petrographic characteristics, baddeleyite grains are classified into five groups, reflecting diverse P-T histories. A notable finding is widespread preservation of cubic heritage baddeleyite, despite relatively lower-T records recorded by coexisting silicates. This feature is attributed to elevated shock pressures that depress stability fields of high-T ZrO2 polymorphs, modification of phase stability by impurities (e.g., Ti and Fe), and grains experienced high-T conditions prior to incorporation into their present host rocks. Clast-hosted baddeleyite yields a coherent weighted mean Pb-Pb age of 3100 ± 8.5 Ma (n = 9), interpreted as the primary magmatic crystallization age, whereas matrix-hosted grains show a broader age distribution around ∼3.1 Ga. Two matrix-hosted grains associated with impact melt veins yield a younger age of 2941 ± 20 Ma, consistent with later ∼2.9 Ga impact modification. The absence of a systematic relationship between Pb-Pb age and microstructural type suggests that ZrO2 phase transformations alone do not exert a first-order control on Pb mobility. Instead, heterogeneous propagation of pressure and temperature during shock metamorphism, together with the intensity and duration of thermal events, appears to govern isotopic disturbance. These results highlight the importance of integrated microstructural and geochronological approaches for reconstructing complex lunar thermal histories.

title: Porewater nitrate isotope dynamics in selected benthic habitats: Modulation by sediment reactivity and process coupling via nitrite
description: Publication date: Available online 3 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Alessandra Mazzoli, Peter Reichert, Cameron M. Callbeck, Claudia Frey, Paul M. Magyar, Tim J. Paulus, Donald E. Canfield, Sergei Katsev, Jakob Zopfi, Moritz F. Lehmann
abstract: Denitrification is the primary pathway for fixed nitrogen (N) removal from aquatic systems. Its occurrence in sediments is promoted by suboxic conditions, high organic matter reactivity, sharp redox transitions, and the co-occurrence of multiple N-transformation processes. Benthic denitrification can be investigated through natural abundance nitrate N and oxygen (O) isotope ratio measurements to trace nitrate reduction and related N transformation processes within the sediment. Yet, while the biological and apparent (i.e., in the overlying water) isotope effects for nitrate reduction, εDen, have been widely investigated, the controls on their expression at the sediment porewater level remain underexplored, particularly in lacustrine systems. Additionally, it is unclear how simultaneously occurring N-cycle processes may modify the resulting nitrate isotope signatures. Since apparent εDen values are commonly used to estimate benthic denitrification, it is also crucial to identify how these processes affect their expression. Here, we measured nitrate isotope ratios in sediment porewaters from multiple lacustrine and marine settings and quantified denitrification, dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium, and anammox rates using 15N-tracer incubations. We further employed a novel diagenetic N isotope model to estimate εDen under different sedimentary reactivity and redox conditions. In most investigated environments, Rayleigh-derived N and O isotope effects are strongly reduced (mostly < 4‰) in porewaters compared to reported biological isotope effects, whereas model-based estimates provide intermediate fractionations. We attribute the generally low isotope fractionation to high sediment reactivity and insufficient nitrate diffusion to the nitrate-reducing zone, leading to near-complete nitrate consumption at the microbial level (i.e., before the cellular level effect is expressed at the porewater level). Consistent with this interpretation, environments characterized by higher organic matter reactivity exhibited the lowest isotope fractionation. The N and O isotope values in nitrate exhibited partial decoupling, resulting in both negative and positive Δδ18O:Δδ15N deviations from 1:1. Negative deviations may reflect an enhanced contribution of the periplasmatic nitrate reductase, particularly in lacustrine environments with fluctuating O2 concentrations. Positive deviations likely indicate nitrate (re)generation via nitrification or anammox, and tight nitrate-nitrite redox cycling (i.e., nitrate reduction coupled to nitrite oxidation). The spatial overlap of N transformations in our model results (e.g., nitrification–denitrification) increased the coupling of processes through nitrite, which strongly influences nitrate isotope dynamics. Model simulations indicate that nitrite-reducing processes generate 15N-enriched nitrite due to N isotopic fractionation; subsequent nitrite oxidation, associated with an inverse kinetic isotope effect, produces highly 15N-enriched nitrate. Such 15N enrichment of nitrate should therefore not be interpreted as evidence for nitrate reduction and fixed-N loss. Our findings demonstrate that explicit consideration of nitrite dynamics is essential for correctly interpreting nitrate isotope data in sediment porewaters and for avoiding inaccurate estimation of benthic N transformation pathways and N-loss rates.

title: Sulfur isotope fractionation during metal–silicate equilibration and implications for Earth’s mantle
description: Publication date: Available online 3 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Lucas Calvo, Jabrane Labidi, Anat Shahar, Edith Kubik, Julien Siebert
abstract: Sulfur (S), a moderately siderophile and volatile element, may have been delivered to Earth during the planet’s main stage of accretion. Alternatively, it may have been supplied by the late veneer, after the core was fully segregated from the mantle. Mid-ocean ridge basalts present a systematic depletion in the heavier S isotope, 34S, relative to chondrites. This has been suggested to reflect isotopic fractionation during core–mantle differentiation or during evaporative loss from Earth’s magma ocean. Two studies have estimated the metal–silicate S isotope fractionation but yielded conflicting results. Laboratory experiments suggest that equilibrium fractionation favors the heavy 34S in metal during metal–silicate equilibria. However, the magnitude of the 34S/32S fractionation between metal and silicate appears too small to explain the composition of mid-ocean ridge basalts. In contrast, ab-initio calculations predict fractionation in the opposite direction, with a much smaller magnitude. Here, we present a series of experiments conducted with the triple-isotope technique. This approach allows for a robust determination of sulfur isotope fractionation between metal and silicate. We also report a set of conventional time-series experiments with variable starting isotopic compositions, and compare the results from both approaches. The reported results confirm that metal–silicate equilibration produces significant 34S-depletion in silicates, with a magnitude of 0.65 ± 0.28‰ at 1673 K, in agreement with previous experimental work. This fractionation is parametrized as a function of temperature to account for Earth’s mantle composition following 1000 ∗ ln α M e t . - S i l . ≈ a / T 2 = 1.819 ± 0.784 × 10 6 K - 2 . This fractionation can explain most depleted mantle estimates; however, additional processes such as the effect of high-pressure equilibrium, sulfide–melt equilibria, or long-term mantle recycling may contribute to the observed Earth’s mantle regional variations.

title: Recycling of terrestrial mercury in modern subduction zones: constraints from Hg-Sr-Nd-B isotope systematics
description: Publication date: Available online 2 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Dian-Bing Wang, Ping-Ping Liu, Runsheng Yin
abstract: Mercury (Hg) isotopes, particularly mass-independent fractionation (MIF; expressed as Δ199Hg), serve as a powerful tracer for tracking the recycling of surficial materials into Earth’s deep interior. However, the contribution of terrestrial Hg to modern subduction zones remains poorly understood. Here we present new Hg–B–Sr–Nd isotopic data for volcanic rocks from eight stratovolcanoes and the Toba super-sized volcanic system, all located along the Sumatra segment of the Sunda arc. Sumatra volcanic rocks have negative Δ199Hg values (from −0.19 to −0.02‰), indicating an input of terrestrial Hg. Their mass-dependent fractionation (MDF; expressed as δ202Hg) ranges from −2.08 to −1.07‰, lower than that of the Mesozoic basement on Sumatra (−0.05‰). Together with Sr-Nd isotope constraints indicating minor crustal contamination, these observations rule out a crustal origin for the negative Δ199Hg anomalies and instead reflect a mantle source modified by recycled terrestrial Hg. The near-zero Δ199Hg values of the Nicobar Fan sediments (−0.01 to 0.03‰) indicate that the recycled terrestrial Hg in the mantle source is unlikely to originate from the Nicobar Fan but more likely reflects locally derived Sumatran terrigenous sediments. Three-endmember mixing models coupling Δ199Hg with Sr–Nd isotopes further indicate that the subducted sediment contribution was dominated by Nicobar Fan sediments but included a smaller proportion of Sumatra terrigenous component carrying the negative Hg-MIF signature, with total sediment additions of <5 wt% beneath the Sumatra stratovolcanoes and ∼5–10 wt% beneath the Toba volcanic system. Boron isotopes indicate slab-derived fluid additions of ∼0.01–1.0 wt% and ∼0.01–0.05 wt% beneath Sumatra stratovolcanoes and Toba volcanic systems, respectively. Mass-balance calculations show that fluids containing ∼20 ppb to 3.3 ppm Hg could reproduce the average Δ199Hg value of the Sumatra volcanic rocks, indicating that slab-derived dehydration fluids are potential carriers transferring terrestrial Hg into the mantle wedge. Near the slab tear zone, sediment melts generated during the diapiric ascent and partial melting of subducted sediments result in the enriched Sr-Nd isotopic compositions of the Toba volcanic rocks. Our results demonstrate that Hg isotopes, when integrated with Sr-Nd-B isotope systematics, serve as a sensitive tracer for distinguishing recycling of various components in subduction zones.

title: The effect of pressure and temperature on the fluid/melt partitioning of porphyry ore metals
description: Publication date: Available online 2 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Ivano Gennaro, Alexandra Tsay, Zoltán Zajacz
abstract: A major fraction of the total Cu, Mo, and Au mined worldwide is derived from porphyry ore deposits, with Ag representing an abundant by-product from the exploitation of these deposits. The relative endowment of these metals is linked to deposit depth, with Au-rich deposits forming in the shallowest levels of the crust while Mo-rich deposits form deeper. These deposits are fed by magmatic-hydrothermal fluids derived from magma chambers which likely sit 5–15 km below the surface, but attainment of fluid saturation at greater depths has also been proposed. These deposits display a general depth-dependent metal endowment. To determine the effect of pressure (P) and temperature (T) on the ability of the fluid phase to extract these metals from the melt, experiments were conducted in cold-seal pressure vessels and a piston cylinder apparatus covering a range of P (150–700 MPa) and T (760–950 °C) conditions at which fluid exsolution is most likely to occur in crustal magma reservoir systems. Experimental capsules were composed of a Au-Ag-Cu alloy as the source of metals and contained a synthetic rhyolite glass, fluid of 1 or 12 mol Cl/kg H2O, and natural quartz chip for the entrapment of synthetic fluid inclusions. Metal solubilities in the melt and fluid phases increase roughly linearly with increasing T; Cl concentration only affects the solubility of metals in the fluid phase. Fluid/melt partition coefficients of Cu, Ag, and Au decrease monotonically with increasing T and are generally unaffected by P at a fixed fluid salinity. Chlorine and Mo partitioning into the fluid increase by a factor of 4 with P increasing from 150 to 500 MPa at low fluid salinities but decrease slightly at high fluid salinities. Empirical functions were fit which describe the solubility, fluid/melt partitioning, and metal/Na exchange of Cl, Cu, Ag, Au, and Mo as functions of T and P. A simplified magma degassing model based on these equations reveals that ore metal extraction from magmas is the most effective at upper crustal emplacement depths and relatively high initial water concentrations.

title: Qualitative assessment of high–temperature disequilibrium sulfur isotope fractionation in the gas–silicate melt–sulfide liquid system from experiments
description: Publication date: Available online 1 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Shashank Prabha Mohan, Kenneth T. Koga
abstract: Experiments using a dynamic 1–atm gas–mixing furnace simulatedoxidation and reduction processes, as observed during volcanic degassing, by manipulating the oxygen (log fO2) and sulfurfugacities(log fS2). The experiments weredesignedto identify the rate–limiting processes in sulfur isotope fractionation and determine the mechanisms of exchange between silicate melt and a sulfide liquid under dynamic conditions. Six series of experiments were conducted using high–Mg olivine crystals as capsules andbasalt andFepowder as the charges.The experimental approach involved equilibrating samples at initial conditions for eight hoursat 1300 °C, followed by continuous atmospheric changes within the furnace ata constantrateuntilthefinal conditionswere attained, after which samples were quenched. The imposed dynamicity varied from 15 min to 120 min,with rate of fugacity changesbetween –8.4 and 10.4 log unit hr–1 for fO2 and –4 to 4.4 log unit hr–1 for fS2.S isotope fractionation between the silicate melt and sulfide liquid was verified to be at disequilibrium using the existing equilibrium model, with the silicate melt being isotopically lighter than would be expected at equilibrium conditions. Despitesulfur’stransfer within the basaltic melt through diffusion, diffusive isotopic fractionation was not observed in any samples. This provides us a β value of 0 for sulfur isotopic diffusionat hightemperatures, where β quantifies the mass (m) dependence of the diffusion coefficient (D) of the isotopes 1,2 as ( D 1 / D 2 ) = ( m 2 / m 1 ) β , while also showing a lack of an effect of pressure on sulfur isotope diffusion. The observed disequilibrium fractionation is hypothesized to be due to isotope fractionation at the interface between the phase boundaries.

title: Oxygen isotope exchange unravels million-year long hydrogeochemical evolution of a deep carbonate aquifer in the Swiss Molasse Basin
description: Publication date: Available online 30 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Christoph Wanner, Lukas Aschwanden, Mirjam Kiczka, H. Niklaus Waber, Michael Heidinger, Emiliano Stopelli, Daniel Traber
abstract: The stable isotope composition of groundwaters is essential to characterize their origin and processes of their hydrogeochemical evolution. In carbonate aquifers, the interaction between groundwater and carbonates enriched in 18O may shift groundwater δ18O values to the right of the global meteoric water line. Although experimental studies showed that the exchange of oxygen isotopes between groundwater and carbonates may proceed rapidly under ambient conditions, there is little information regarding the kinetics of the exchange under geological conditions. To better quantify the relevance of carbonate-groundwater interaction on oxygen isotope signatures of both groundwater and carbonates, we present an extensive hydrogeochemical characterization of deep groundwaters collected during a deep drilling campaign in the Swiss Molasse Basin. Combining information from chemical and isotopic analyses, groundwater residence time tracers, the geological evolution of the area, as well as geochemical modelling we quantitatively demonstrate that the exchange of oxygen isotopes is mainly relevant for carbonate-dominated aquifers consisting of fractured rock with a low porosity and a large solid to liquid ratio. For such conditions, isotopic equilibrium is reached in more than a few hundred thousand but less than 20 Mio years at temperatures below 70 °C. It follows that the equilibration of groundwater δ18O values may serve as independent proxy for the residence time of very old groundwaters. Moreover, our study shows that for rock buffered systems the oxygen isotope exchange has only minor effects on the oxygen isotope composition of rock-forming calcite. Accordingly, it does not affect the use of the δ18O signature of calcite as environmental proxy.

title: Authigenic apatite formation mediated by sulfate-reducing bacteria using cyanobacterial biomass as the sole carbon and phosphorus sources
description: Publication date: Available online 29 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Juntong Pan, Xiaolei Liu, Geng Wu, Huan Liu, Donglei Zhang, Hailiang Dong
abstract: Sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) and phytoplankton are hypothesized to be intimately linked to phosphogenesis over geological timescales, as evidenced by the occurrence of cyanobacteria-like microfossils and authigenic pyrite (commonly framboidal, with sulfide sourced primarily from microbial sulfate reduction in low-temperature sedimentary settings) in ancient phosphorite deposits. The prevailing model driven by sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (SOB) primarily accounts for phosphogenesis at redox interfaces, and is therefore difficult to apply to the phosphorite deposits formed in pervasively anoxic, organic-rich environments. In such geological records, SRB were demonstrably active; however, the direct pathways by which SRB induces authigenic apatite formation from complex organic matter (e.g., cyanobacterial biomass) have not yet been investigated in detail under controlled laboratory conditions. Here, we demonstrate that Desulfovibrio desulfuricans, a representative SRB strain, can utilize cyanobacterial biomass (structurally complex and refractory, yet common organic substates in environments) as its sole carbon, electron, and phosphorus source to induce authigenic apatite formation under anoxic conditions. Specifically, D. desulfuricans growth was coupled to sulfate reduction and accompanied by upregulation of alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, facilitating the liberation of inorganic phosphate from cyanobacterial biomass-associated phosphorus. Amendment with lactate further increased phosphorus release, suggesting that the presence of labile substrate can prime the degradation of refractory cyanobacterial biomass. During this process, proteinaceous and carbohydrate components were preferentially degraded, while the residual organic matter became progressively sulfurized, thereby linking phosphogenesis directly to organic matter preservation. In the presence of calcium ions (Ca2+), this microbial activity facilitates the precipitation of phosphate minerals such as hydroxyapatite and calcium hydrogen phosphate, demonstrating morphologies (e.g., botryoidal) distinct from the rosettes-like brushite formed in the abiotic control. These results provide plausible explanations for phosphorite formation in organic-rich, sulfidic environments, highlighting the important role of SRB in linking the biogeochemical cycles of carbon, sulfur, and phosphorus

title: Two-stage Mg isotope behavior during silicate weathering and its implication for tracing continental weathering intensity
description: Publication date: Available online 29 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Long Ma, Yuanqiang Guo, Kang-Jun Huang
abstract: Magnesium isotope (δ26Mg) provides a promising tool for tracing continental silicate weathering, yet its application to geological records is limited due to an incomplete understanding of Mg isotope behavior during weathering processes. Here, we present a systematic mineralogical, geochemical, and Mg isotopic investigation on two granitic weathering profiles (Lushan and Zhuhai) and one basaltic profile (Haikou). Our results demonstrated that under low-to-moderate weathering conditions, external inputs exert limited influence, and variations in δ26Mg bulk are mainly governed by coupled primary mineral dissolution and clay formation. Because structurally bound Mg in clays is hosted in relatively short and stiff Mg-O bonds compared to aqueous Mg2+, 26Mg is preferentially retained in the solid phase, leading to progressively heavier δ26Mg bulk values as clay abundance increases with increasing weathering intensity. Meanwhile, due to the competing influences of primary minerals, the net increase in δ26Mg bulk remains modest, 0.06 to 0.20‰ in this study. In contrast, under highly weathered conditions, structurally bound Mg gradually decreases and exchangeable Mg increasingly controls δ26Mg bulk . Because exchangeable Mg is hosted in weakly bound and distorted coordination environments with relatively long Mg-O bonds to aqueous Mg2+, it preferentially incorporates 24Mg. As a result, δ26Mg bulk values decrease with increasing weathering intensity, which is further lowered by external inputs. Compilation of our data with published studies imply that δ26Mg bulk during silicate weathering exhibits a generalized two-stage behavior. Stage I is characterized by MgO/Al2O3 > 0.04, CIA (Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O) × 100%) ∼90, or scatter Δ26Mg values, resulting from the increasingly dominated exchangeable Mg that has potential influence from external inputs. This framework establishes clear constraints on when δ26Mg bulk can reliably trace weathering intensity and provides a robust basis for interpreting riverine Mg isotope signatures and their implications for continental weathering and Earth-surface processes.

title: Time-resolved Mo isotopes track source evolution from recycled slab components to a coherent OIB-type mantle source
description: Publication date: Available online 25 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Dongjing Xu, Xiu-Zheng Zhang, Yue Qi, Jie Li, Bing Chen, Pei-Na Guo, Tao Du, Qiang Wang
abstract: Subduction returns surface lithologies to the mantle and helps generate enriched domains sampled by ocean-island basalts (OIB). Many studies identify recycled components in OIB sources, but few resolve how these components mature into coherent, melt-fertile mantle domains. We examine this transition using Miocene and late Middle Pleistocene alkaline lavas that record temporally distinct sampling of a regional slab-modified asthenosphere above stagnant Tethyan slab material in southeastern Yunnan. New major- and trace-element, Sr–Nd–Pb and Mo isotope data for ca. 0.25–0.22 Ma Pingbian basanites are compared with published ca. 13–11 Ma Maguan basalts. The Pingbian lavas form a compact, silica-undersaturated, high-Nb suite. Relative to Maguan, Pingbian has narrower ranges of source-sensitive trace-element ratios and Sr–Nd–Pb isotope compositions and a clearer enriched mantle 1 (EM1)-like signature, characterized by low 206Pb/204Pb and 143Nd/144Nd and intermediate 87Sr/86Sr. These features define a more focused melt-producing domain, whereas δ 98/95Mo spans −0.41‰ to +0.04‰. Integrated δ 98/95Mo–Ce/Mo, trace-element and Sr–Nd–Pb relationships are consistent with similar recycled component classes in both suites but different effective weighting, with weaker expression of eclogitized oceanic crust and sediment-derived material and stronger expression of hydrated slab mantle in Pingbian. The resolved Mo isotope excursions indicate that component-scale heterogeneity persisted within this focused source. We define OIB-source maturation as source focusing and component reweighting within an inherited recycled slab inventory, rather than replacement by a new reservoir. More broadly, this paired record suggests that EM1-like OIB-type sources above stagnant slabs can develop through such reorganization, while Mo isotopes may retain component-level memory despite the narrowing of trace-element and Sr–Nd–Pb signatures.

title: Small sulfur isotope fractionations by environmentally relevant sulfur oxidizers under oligotrophic conditions
description: Publication date: Available online 25 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Daniela Osorio-Rodriguez, Thomas E. Hanson, Douglas E. LaRowe, Victoria J. Orphan, Alex L. Sessions, Jess F. Adkins
abstract: Isotopic fractionation associated with microbial sulfur oxidation (MSO) provides critical constraints on the sulfur cycle. Sulfur isotope fractionations associated with MSO have been reported to range between −5 to 4‰ for a variety of microbial sulfur oxidizers. This finding led to the assumption that, unlike microbial sulfate reduction, which can have fractionations in the range between −66 to 5‰ in culture experiments, and up to about −70‰ based on in-situ measurements and theoretical considerations, fractionations during MSO are negligible. However, the reported fractionation factors for MSO may not be environmentally relevant, as most studies were conducted under nutrient-replete conditions and rapid microbial growth. Furthermore, the discovery of a 13‰ fractionation during the oxidation of sulfur by the Thermodesulfobacteriota Desulfurivibrio alkaliphilus suggests that specific metabolisms or growth conditions that have not yet been explored could produce larger isotopic fractionations during MSO. The fact that D. alkaliphilus only grows at alkaline pH and utilizes an uncommon pathway for sulfur oxidation motivated us to explore the causes of the unusually large isotope fractionation observed in this organism. In this study, we measured sulfur isotope fractionations by D. alkaliphilus, Chlorobaculum tepidum, and Candidatus Thioglobus autotrophicus (representative of different environments and metabolic pathways for sulfur oxidation), aiming to identify a S isotope proxy for MSO under the nutrient-limited, slow-growth conditions that characterize natural environments. We found small fractionations for C. tepidum and Ca. T. autotrophicus (−0.4 to 2.3‰), similar to the ones reported under abundant nutrients and fast growth rates. In contrast, D. alkaliphilus produced large fractionations during the oxidation of sulfide (11.6 to 18.6‰) under a range of nutrient concentrations. However, small growth rates and cell-specific sulfur oxidation rates generated negligible fractionations during the intermediate-to-sulfate oxidation step (0.1 to 1.5‰) by this microbe. Our results suggest that small sulfur isotope fractionations by MSO should be the norm under natural, oligotrophic conditions, which limits the utility of stable sulfur isotopes as a proxy for oxidative processes in the S geologic record.

title: Secular evolution of marine carbonate δ 66 Zn and its implications for nutrient cycling through time
description: Publication date: Available online 25 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Francis Albarède, Janne Blichert-Toft, Kurt O. Konhauser, Andrew H. Knoll, Marine Pinto, Aline Lamboux, Harilaos Tsikos, Gilles Dromart
abstract: The Zn isotope composition of marine carbonates provides a window into major reorganizations of the Earth surface system. Here, we present 185 new δ 66 Zn measurements from 176 carbonate samples spanning the Early Archean (3.48 Ga) to the Paleogene, integrated with 220 published analyses of carbonates, banded iron formations (BIF), sulfides, organic-rich sediments, and Fe–Mn crusts. The composite record reveals four first-order transitions: (1) a Late Archean decline in carbonate δ 66 Zn culminating near the Great Oxidation Event (GOE); (2) a reversal of the carbonate–BIF Zn isotope offset across the GOE; (3) relative Zn isotope stability during the mid-Proterozoic; and (4) a progressive rise in δ 66 Zn and amplification of isotopic variability from the Neoproterozoic onward.We argue that these secular trends reflect shifts in Zn partitioning among Fe-rich phases, carbonates, phosphates, and organic matter in response to evolving ocean chemistry and ecosystem structure, including the rise of eukaryotic algae. A single-reservoir Zn isotope mass-balance model, including sedimentary removal and exchange with diagenetic and hydrothermal fluids, is used to evaluate how changes in these fluxes and their isotope fractionations are expressed in the δ 66 Zn values of sedimentary rocks. Because the marine Zn cycle has a short residence time relative to the geological timescales considered here, the model supports interpretation of carbonate δ 66 Zn as a tracer of changes in Zn sources, sinks, and their coupling to continental weathering, phosphorus cycling, redox transitions, and biological innovation through Earth history.

title: Mercury isotopes in coral skeletons as proxies for marine Hg cycling: assessing fidelity and fractionation during biomineralization
description: Publication date: Available online 23 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Fei Cao, Yongquan Zhang, Ruoyu Sun, Larissa Schneider, Songjing Li, Rui Zhang, Pengfei Li, Wang Zheng, Jiubin Chen, Yi Liu
abstract: Stable mercury (Hg) isotopes provide powerful tools for tracing marine Hg sources and transformations. However, suitable geological archives that record long-term changes in seawater Hg isotopes remain scarce, limiting reconstructions of past marine Hg cycling. Here, we evaluate the potential of coral skeletons as archives of seawater Hg isotope compositions and assess the mechanisms controlling Hg incorporation during coral calcification. We systematically investigate the effectiveness and isotopic impacts of chemical cleaning protocols designed to isolate aragonite-bound Hg in coral skeletons. Sequential leaching and oxidative soaking experiments demonstrate that a substantial fraction of Hg in untreated coral skeletons is associated with non-aragonitic phases, primarily organic matter, and can be efficiently removed by optimized oxidative cleaning. These treatments result in large decreases in Hg concentrations and systematic changes in mass-dependent fractionation (MDF; δ202Hg), while mass-independent fractionation (MIF; Δ199Hg and Δ200Hg) signatures remain invariant. This indicates that cleaning selectively affects MDF without altering source-diagnostic MIF signals. Applying the optimized cleaning protocol, we analyze Hg concentrations and isotope compositions in coral skeletons collected from nearshore and offshore environments in the South China Sea. Coral skeletons preserve distinct regional differences in Hg MIF, which are consistent with published regional seawater values, reflecting contrasting contributions from atmospheric and terrestrial Hg sources. In contrast, δ202Hg values are consistently more negative than seawater by approximately 1 ‰, indicating systematic MDF during skeletal incorporation, likely driven by biologically mediated kinetic effects associated with calcification. Our results suggest that coral skeletons generally preserve seawater Hg MIF signatures while exhibiting predictable MDF during biomineralization. These findings establish coral skeletons as promising archives for reconstructing long-term changes in marine Hg cycling in response to natural variability and anthropogenic perturbations.

title: Diagenetic fluid overprinting of micrite stable isotopes: implications for paleo-elevation reconstruction
description: Publication date: Available online 23 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Keran Li, Anlin Ma, Xiumian Hu, Chaojin Lu, Yoseph Datu Adiatma, Lin Li, Ardiansyah Koeshidayatullah, He Zhang, Di Yang, Zhiwu Li
abstract: Lacustrine carbonate micrite is commonly treated as a reliable archive of surface-water oxygen isotopes and is widely used for paleo-elevation reconstruction in orogenic belts. However, recent evidence for shallow-burial dolomitization in lacustrine micrites raises concern that bulk sample may not preserve a single primary signal. Here we evaluate the fidelity of geochemical signals preserved in the micritic carbonates of the Eocene Gerze Basin in central Tibet. The geochemical compositions of calcite and dolomite fractions in bulk samples were isolated using sequential acetic-acid leaching and show one primary or least altered calcite end-member (Calcite EM) and two diagenetic dolomite end-members (Dolomite EM1 and EM2). Numerical simulation suggests that the higher and more variable δ 44/40Ca values in Dolomite EM2 formed under fluid-buffered conditions. In contrast, Dolomite EM1, with moderately positive δ 44/40Ca values, is a product of sediment-buffered dolomitization. Accounting for this diagenetic alteration, each 10 % increase in the proportion of Dolomite EM2 in bulk carbonates would increase the reconstructed paleo-elevation by 0.5–0.8 km. These results show that Gerze Basin micrite is not a homogeneous recorder of lake-water δ18O and that unrecognized dolomitization can substantially bias paleo-elevation reconstructions.

title: Temperature-dependent Fe(II) thresholds for magnetite formation during Fe(II)-catalyzed ferrihydrite transformation
description: Publication date: Available online 21 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Jiahao Chen, Anhuai Lu, Yuefei Ding, Qishun Sun, Liao Chang, Anxu Sheng, Yurong Deng, Shan Huang, Yongheng Jiang, Yoshio Takahashi, Xinglan Cui, Liuqin Huang, Juan Liu
abstract: Fe(II)-catalyzed ferrihydrite (Fh) transformation is a critical process controlling secondary Fe mineral formation, Fe redox reactivity, and the cycling of associated nutrients and trace elements in anoxic and suboxic environments. Although aqueous Fe(II) (Fe(II)aq) availability is known to regulate Fh transformation pathways, the critical Fe(II)aq concentration required for magnetite (Mt) formation at different temperatures remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated Fe(II)-catalyzed Fh transformation at 25, 45, and 65 °C under anoxic, circumneutral pH conditions across a range of initial Fe(II)aq concentrations. Time-resolved analyses of mineral phases, Fe(II) speciation, particle morphology, and magnetic properties were combined with thermodynamic calculations to determine how temperature regulates transformation kinetics, pathway selection, and Mt formation. Increasing temperature significantly reduced the apparent Fe(II)aq threshold for Mt formation, from > 10.0 mM at 25 °C to 0.6–0.8 mM at 45 °C and 0.3–0.4 mM at 65 °C. Mineralogical evolution followed a two-stage pathway: rapid Fh dissolution and accumulation of lepidocrocite (Lp) and goethite (Gt) during Stage I, followed by Lp consumption and competitive partitioning between Gt growth and Mt formation during Stage II. Elevated temperature shifted the dominant Stage II pathway from template-directed Gt growth toward Lp-to-Mt conversion, changing the overall pathway from Fh → Lp/Gt → Gt to Fh → Lp/Gt → Mt/Gt.
