Study focus This study developed a daily-scale copula framework to characterize compound drought–fire weather conditions associated with five large-scale wildfires in Japan in 2025. Drought was represented by the 3-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI3) and soil moisture (SM), and fire weather by effective humidity (EH) and wind speed. The analysis evaluated dependence and compound severity for drought–fire weather variable pairs, quantified pre-fire changes in EH and SM using seven-day rolling slopes, and mapped compound severity at representative locations across all prefectures on key wildfire dates. New hydrological insights for the region Drought–fire weather pairs generally showed weak daily-scale dependence. Several combinations reached severe or extreme levels during both Ofunato wildfires and the Otsuki wildfire, reflecting moisture deficits coinciding with low EH or strong winds. Okayama and Imabari showed compound anomalies of varying severity and rapid prefire declines in EH and SM. On 26 February, severe compound conditions occurred at many representative locations along the Pacific side, indicating that geographically separated wildfires occurred within a broader regional background of concurrent moisture deficits and adverse fire weather conditions. Severe compound conditions during wildfire periods and rapid pre-fire drying may represent complementary aspects of the hydrometeorological conditions associated with large-scale wildfires in Japan.

title: Catchment-dependent runoff-partitioning uncertainty in the near-optimal parameter space: Insights from 62 catchments in Southeastern China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yi Nan, Yan Li, Fuqiang Tian, Jingan Lin, Yao Zhuang, Diego Avesani
abstract: Study region This study was conducted in 62 small- to medium-sized catchments in southeastern China. Study focus Parameter equifinality can be especially problematic when hydrological models are used not only to reproduce streamflow, but also to infer internal runoff-generation processes. We used the semi-distributed THREW model and 10,000 Latin-hypercube parameter sets per catchment to examine how equifinality affects surface-subsurface runoff partitioning. The contribution of subsurface runoff to total runoff was evaluated within the near-optimal parameter space defined by performance rank and by an absolute Kling-Gupta efficiency threshold, and the resulting uncertainty was compared across catchments and related to a parsimonious set of catchment descriptors. The analysis therefore quantifies parameter-conditioned uncertainty in THREW-estimated runoff partitioning under the fixed model structure, input data, and streamflow-evaluation framework. New hydrological insights for the region Near-optimal parameter sets that reproduce streamflow similarly can imply markedly different surface-subsurface runoff partitioning, and the magnitude of this uncertainty varies systematically among catchments in southeastern China. Among the selected first-order catchment descriptors examined, runoff ratio showed the most consistent association with this variability. Higher-QR catchments exhibited a narrower spread in subsurface runoff contribution among the highest-ranked parameter sets, but broader parameter support and greater partitioning variability under a fixed KGE tolerance. Thus, runoff-partitioning equifinality has a catchment-dependent regional structure, and its apparent magnitude depends on how the near-optimal parameter space is defined. These findings identify runoff ratio as a regional signature of where runoff-partitioning inference from streamflow alone is more or less constrained.

title: Quantification of flood-occurrence risks in the middle reaches of the Yellow River under climate and land-use changes
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qianling Ci, Wenjing Wang, Chuyu Wu, Ying Han, Yuwei Wang, Xingda Chen, Yida Lu, Dan Li, Shuisen Chen, Jinxia Fu
abstract: Study region The study area is the Middle Reaches of the Yellow River (MRYR), China. Study focus Flood-occurrence risk under concurrent hydroclimatic and land-use change remains poorly quantified in the MRYR. We developed an AHP–FCE–GIS framework integrating 19 climatic, hydrological, topographic, and land-use indicators to reconstruct risk evolution during 1990–2020 and project 2050 conditions under SSP1–1.9, SSP2–4.5, and SSP5–8.5. The framework was evaluated using historical flood/non-flood reference locations, ROC–AUC, and spatial-block cross-validation. New hydrological insights for the region Historical FORI showed an overall increase, but the 1990–2000 reconstruction was weakly constrained. Between the better-validated 2001–2010 and 2011–2020 periods, mean FORI increased from 0.494 to 0.578 and the high-risk area from 26.7% to 46.6%. This shift coincided with a 20.2% increase in annual precipitation and a 111.09% expansion of urban land during 2000–2020. Future mean FORI reached 0.520, 0.551, and 0.603 under SSP119, SSP245, and SSP585, respectively. Under SSP585, 59.14% of the basin was classified as high or very high risk, compared with 28.57% under SSP119 and 28.30% under SSP245. Despite the largest annual precipitation increase under SSP119, its overall risk remained lowest, indicating that annual precipitation alone cannot explain future risk. The Yiluo and Wei basins remained persistent hotspots, while SSP585 extended severe risk toward the Fen River Basin and Yellow River mainstream. These findings support spatially differentiated, climate-adaptive basin management.

title: From deterministic to stochastic: A hybrid framework coupling machine learning with Bluecat for probabilistic satellite-based precipitation estimation over Greece
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Nikos Tepetidis, Theano Iliopoulou, Panayiotis Dimitriadis, Ioannis Benekos, Alberto Montanari, Demetris Koutsoyiannis
abstract: Study region: This study focuses on Greece, characterized by complex topography and strong spatial and temporal variability in precipitation variability, which challenge accurate rainfall estimation and hydrological applications. Reliable precipitation data are essential for hydrological modeling, water resource management and rainfall extremes assessment, while satellite products provide extensive spatial coverage but are subject to systematic biases relative to ground observations. Study focus: We develop a hybrid machine learning-stochastic framework for post-processing satellite-derived precipitation using ground-based observations. Daily gauge and Integrated Multi-Satellite Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG) data for the period 2000–2021 are used to evaluate independent machine learning algorithms and the proposed framework. The stochastic component provides uncertainty estimation, achieving 88.7% coverage at a 90% confidence level. We introduce a method for estimating the output distribution to generate intensity-time scale-return period (ombrian) curves using annual maximum daily rainfall from a denser station network. New hydrological insights for the region: The proposed framework substantially improves satellite precipitation estimates over Greece. The estimated output distribution achieves Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) values of 0.99 and 0.96, respectively, compared with 0.78 and 0.65 for the original satellite product. The framework provides accurate precipitation estimates and reliable uncertainty quantification, supporting hydrological modeling, flood frequency analysis and robust Ombrian curve development in regions with complex terrain. By integrating post-processing techniques within the learning pipeline, the proposed method improves accuracy over conventional merging approaches.

title: A water-balance-guided hybrid machine-learning framework for quantifying recharge to assess groundwater depletion in the Southeastern USA
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fatemeh Saedi, Mukesh Kumar, T. Prabhakar Clement
abstract: Study region Southeastern United States Study focus Groundwater recharge is an important hydrological flux; however, recharge estimation methods used in the literature estimate different types of recharge fluxes. The focus of the current study is to elucidate the distinction between two common recharge estimates, namely water-balance (WB) recharge, which represents water leaking below the root zone, and water-table fluctuation (WTF) recharge, which represents the net amount of recharge reaching the groundwater table. We developed a water-balance-guided hybrid machine-learning framework that first estimates WB recharge and uses it as a predictor to constrain net recharge predictions. Several machine-learning models were evaluated, and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) was selected to be the best-performing model. The new ML-model-derived data are mapped at the HUC12 scale across the Southeastern US. The modeled recharge was then used to quantify groundwater depletion (GWD) levels as the imbalance between recharge and total fresh groundwater withdrawals. New hydrological insights Results show that the net recharge for the region generally ranges from about 10–15% of average annual local rainfall for most of the catchments. Furthermore, estimated GWD levels exhibited noticeable spatiotemporal variability, with cumulative depletion reaching approximately 31 km³ during 2008–2020 with an average annual depletion rate of about 2.5 km³ /year. This study highlights the importance of distinguishing different types of recharge estimates and also demonstrates the need for using net recharge in GWD assessments.

title: A novel hybrid Elk-Eel and grouper optimizer coupled with machine learning for integrated irrigation water quality index prediction and Pareto-optimal monitoring cost reduction
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Mahmoud E. Abd-Elmaboud, Youssef M. Youssef, Mohamed Abdellatief, Mohamed Elkollaly, Mohsen Sherif, Ahmed El-Shafie, Ahmed M. Saqr
abstract: Study region Eastern Nile Delta aquifer, Egypt Study focus Groundwater quality across the Eastern Nile Delta is deteriorating under seawater intrusion and upward Miocene leakage. Irrigation sustainability is at risk. Comprehensive hydrochemical monitoring, however, remains prohibitively costly for many water authorities in the region. This study asks whether machine learning can improve prediction of the Integrated Irrigation Water Quality Index (IIWQI), and whether its input parameters can be safely reduced without loss of accuracy. A novel Hybrid Elk-Eel and Grouper Optimizer (HEEGO) tunes ten machine learning algorithms across 501 wells spanning three aquifer subsystems. A dependency-aware Cost-Weighted Feature Importance (CWFI) framework then ranks parameters for removal, accounting explicitly for those shared across several derived water-quality indices. New hydrological insights for the region IIWQI assessment reveals that 58.3% of sampled wells are unsuitable for irrigation, concentrated where Na⁺-Cl⁻ facies dominate the northern coastal zone. HEEGO improves prediction accuracy by a mean 12.9% in RMSE across the ten algorithms. The central contribution, however, is economic. The CWFI framework identifies a four-parameter monitoring subset, EC, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, and Mg²⁺, that preserves the full eighteen-parameter protocol's accuracy, R²= 0.9851 against 0.9853, with no loss in classification reliability. Per-sample analytical cost falls by 79.5%, saving an estimated $48,597 a year, or $485,970 over ten years, across the 501-well network. Substantial monitoring-cost reductions are therefore achievable without compromising water-quality assessment. For resource-constrained authorities in similarly salinity-affected agricultural aquifers, this offers a practical route toward more frequent and sustainable groundwater surveillance.

title: Stepwise-clustered downscaling of spatiotemporal variations in compound drought-heatwave extremes over the Yangtze River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zhirui Yang, Ya Zhou, Guohe Huang, Yongping Li, Xiong Zhou, Jiayan Ren, Feng Wang, Yiting Wei, Xinyue Ren
abstract: Global warming is intensifying compound drought-heatwave events (CDHWs), yet coarse-resolution climate models cannot adequately resolve local variations across the complex terrain and monsoon climate of the Yangtze River Basin (YRB). This study developed a Stepwise Clustering Drought-Heatwave Downscaling (SCDHD) framework to downscale daily maximum temperature, precipitation, and potential evapotranspiration at the station scale and project CDHW variations across the YRB and its five climatic regions under SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5. Historical evaluation showed that the framework reasonably reproduced the main climate variables and key drought and heatwave characteristics. Under SSP2–4.5, CDHW frequency increased by 0.116 events per decade, with increases of 129.73% and 96.23% in the Semi-Arid Plateau and Semi-Humid Basin, respectively, during 2061–2090 relative to 2031–2060. Under SSP5–8.5, frequency increased initially but declined overall by 0.167 events per decade during 2032–2089, mainly reflecting changes in the Humid Delta, Semi-Humid Plain, and Semi-Humid Hill. In contrast, maximum duration, mean duration, and mean event intensity increased significantly under both scenarios, at rates of 0.978–1.406 days decade⁻¹ , 0.707–1.268 days event⁻¹ decade⁻¹ , and 1.481–4.667 °C·day event⁻¹ decade⁻¹ , respectively, with larger increases under SSP5–8.5. The contrasting changes in frequency, duration, and intensity demonstrate the need for multiple complementary indicators when characterizing future CDHW hazards.

title: SWAT-based analysis of LULC change impacts on hydrology of the Subarnarekha River Basin, India
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Farhin Tabassum, Akhouri Pramod Krishna, Virendra Singh Rathore, C. Jeganathan
abstract: Study region Subarnarekha River Basin (SRB) is a predominantly rainfed, river basin of Eastern India, spanning parts of Jharkhand, West Bengal, and Odisha. Study focus This study examined the impacts of historical and future land use and land cover (LULC) changes on the hydrology of the SRB. LULC maps for the year 2012, 2017, and 2022 were generated from 5.8 m IRS LISS-IV imagery using support vector machine (SVM) classifier. Future scenarios for 2030, 2040, and 2050 were simulated using a multi-layer perceptron-Markov chain (MLP-MC) model. These LULC datasets were integrated into the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) to evaluate hydrological responses. Model calibration and validation using streamflow observations from four gauging stations showed strong performance, with Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency values ranging from 0.72 to 0.90. New hydrological insights for the region Between 2012 and 2022, built-up land, barren land, and agricultural land increased by 79.39%, 14.81%, and 0.89%, respectively, while forest cover and water bodies declined by 5.54% and 17.45%. These changes increased surface runoff (2.56%) and water yield (1.07%) while reducing groundwater flow (1.29%), lateral flow (5.87%), and evapotranspiration (0.77%). Similar hydrological responses are projected under future LULC scenarios, with impacts becoming increasingly pronounced at the sub-watershed scale. These findings support sustainable watershed management in the SRB and provide a framework for assessing hydrological impacts of land-use change in similar monsoon-dominated river basins.

title: Rainfall structure controls soil water transport and recharge along a humid hillslope revealed by stable isotopes
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Haowen Liu, Junliang Jin, Li Guo, Aiming Huang, Ailin Zhan, Yufei Ma, Cuishan Liu, Guoqing Wang
abstract: Study region This study was conducted on a forested hillslope in a humid hilly catchment at the Chuzhou Hydrological Experimental Station, eastern China, where frequent rainfall, seasonal precipitation variability, and complex soil water redistribution occur. Study focus Rainfall temporal structure may influence hillslope soil water transport, mixing, and storage, but remains insufficiently quantified in humid hilly catchments. Event-scale stable isotope observations (δ²H and δ¹⁸O) and high-resolution soil moisture monitoring were combined to investigate soil water dynamics across upslope, midslope, and downslope positions under Uniform, Extreme, and Uneven rainfall patterns. Soil water response, event-water contribution, and active exchange depth were evaluated to clarify rainfall- and hillslope-position controls on infiltration and redistribution. New hydrological insights The active soil water exchange zone was mainly confined to 0–20 cm at the upslope and midslope, but extended to approximately 40 cm at the downslope. Uniform rainfall favored gradual infiltration and longer event-water retention, whereas uneven rainfall promoted rapid event-water transmission but limited storage. The two observed extreme events suggested activation of a larger soil profile and shorter response lags. Their contrasting responses further pointed to a possible influence of intra-event rainfall distribution on event-water retention under high rainfall input. The upslope was characterized by vertical infiltration, the midslope showed possible lateral redistribution, and the downslope exhibited responses consistent with convergence and earlier fill-and-spill behavior. These findings highlight rainfall-structure controls on hillslope soil water partitioning under variable precipitation regimes.

title: Future projections of cryosphere degradation and its hydrological impacts in the upper Bulgan River basin, Altai Mountains
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zehua Chang, Leilei Yong, Yahui Wang, Kang Wang, Batsuren Dorjsuren, Otgonbayar Demberel, Hongkai Gao
abstract: Study region The nested Baitag and Duchinjil catchments in the upper Bulgan River basin, Altai Mountains, western Mongolia, have small glacier coverage and widespread permafrost. Study focus FLEX-Cryo model was used to assess future cryosphere and runoff changes. The model was evaluated using runoff and cryospheric data. Bias corrected projections from 13 CMIP6 models were used separately to drive the model under SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5. New hydrological insights for the region Ensemble mean annual runoff shows no significant trend during 2024–2100. Winter runoff increases, summer runoff decreases, and runoff timing advances in both catchments. Under SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5 scenario, glaciers persist as remnants in Baitag at the end of the century but disappear in Duchinjil around 2060. At the Duchinjil station, annual maximum snow depth increases while snow cover duration decreases under both scenarios. Permafrost area decreases in Baitag under both scenarios. Mean active layer thickness increases from approximately 2.25 m to 2.95 m under SSP2–4.5 and 3.42 m under SSP5–8.5 by 2099. Summer runoff decreases approximately twice as fast in upstream Duchinjil as in Baitag. Under SSP5–8.5, peak runoff advances by 18 days in Baitag and 38 days in Duchinjil between 2030–2034 and 2090–2094. Hydrological assessments in similar cold and arid mountain catchments should emphasize seasonal runoff changes and runoff timing.

title: Multi-time scale analysis of loess landform evolution for Dongzhi tableland, southwestern Loess Plateau, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shuang Yuan, Qiang Xu, Wei Liu, Siming He, Kuanyao Zhao, Xuan Wang, Pinglang Kou, Qi Zhou
abstract: Study region Dongzhi tableland, southwestern Loess Plateau, eastern Gansu Province, China. Study focus The loess tableland has shrunk greatly over the past thousand years, and this trend is expected to continue. Predictions of loess tableland evolution can support the design and implementation of adequate mitigation measures. To address the limitations of generic Landscape Evolution Models (LEMs) in loess regions, this paper establishes a modified LEM tailored for loess landforms. The model incorporates water as an actual flowing medium in real-time computations, capturing the effects of soil creep, soil detachment, sediment transportation, and sedimentation on loess landscape evolution in a relatively simple and practical manner. Field observations validated that the stream incision law could be modified by adjusting the erosion incision index to make it more suitable for loess regions. The evolution processes of two watersheds with different scales were calculated and analyzed with the established loess geomorphic evolution model. New hydrological insights for the region The numerical results show that the loess geomorphic evolution model can effectively describe the process of erosion and expansion of loess gullies. In local areas, the model can also describe the evolution process from loess tableland to loess ridge to loess hill. When the erosion incision index m is less than 0.3, the model can better balance the proportions of lateral erosion and downcutting erosion in loess regions. The parameters that control the rate of erosion in the model were verified using archaeological evidence and data on similar landforms presented in the scientific literature. When the selected gully advance rate is 0.26 m/year, the time accuracy of the model can reach 95.4%. This model may be extended to other loess areas to assess the extent of landform evolution.

title: Deciphering regional hydro-climatic drivers across diverse climatic zones using a causal explainable ensemble with interaction-aware stable framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Abdol Rassoul Zarei
abstract: Study region This study spans 40 diverse synoptic stations across Iran, covering a multi-decadal period from 1967 to 2024. The selected domain encompasses a wide range of topographical and climatological conditions, including hyper-arid central deserts, humid coastal plains, and alpine environments. Study focus The research addresses the limitations of conventional correlational methods in attributing hydro-climatic drivers of actual evapotranspiration (AET). We introduce the Interaction-aware Stable Causal Importance Index (I-SCII) framework, which integrates computational modeling (XGBoost), diagnostic interpretability (SHAP), and causal inference (Generalized Causal Forests). The framework is designed to disentangle mechanistic influences from statistical associations while accounting for non-linear interactions and temporal non-stationarity. New hydrological insights for the region The results reveal a systematic divergence between correlational and causally-informed attribution. Conventional models consistently overestimate the role of precipitation as a direct driver, whereas the proposed framework successfully mitigates the inflated importance of reactive variables and identifies maximum temperature and wind speed as the dominant forcing mechanisms across 26 and 8 strategic stations, respectively. These findings align with the Budyko framework and sensible heat advection theories, providing a more robust, physically consistent foundation for regional water resource management in semi-arid and arid environments.

title: Variability and drivers of litter water-holding parameters in subtropical China based on field experiments and meta-analysis
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Wei Li, Denghua Yan, Yicheng Wang, Tianling Qin, Xizhi Lv, Cheng Zhang, Guoqiang Dong
abstract: Study region This study examined litter water-holding characteristics at local and regional scales in subtropical China. Field experiments were conducted in the upper Pi River basin, while regional patterns were assessed using published data across subtropical China. Study focus This study quantified variation in litter water-holding characteristics and identified their controlling factors. Field experiments measured the maximum water-holding rate (MWHR) of different forest types and litter components. The effects of litter properties and decomposition on MWHR were evaluated. A meta-analysis assessed regional variation in natural water-holding rate (NWHR), MWHR, and effective water-retention rate (EWRR), and their responses to environmental gradients. New hydrological insights for the region MWHR reached 249.24% in deciduous broadleaf forests and 223.56% in bamboo forests. It differed among litter components in the order leaves > roots > stems > fruits. Litter chemical and optical properties explained 54%–88% of MWHR variation, with total carbon, lignin content, and color tone coefficient as key predictors. MWHR initially increased and then decreased during decomposition. Across subtropical China, mean NWHR, MWHR, and EWRR were 40.7%, 232.2%, and 146.5%, respectively. NWHR and MWHR decreased with increasing temperature but increased with elevation (p < 0.001). These results show that litter water retention is controlled by litter traits, decomposition, and environmental gradients. The quantified parameters can improve the representation of litter water storage in forest hydrological models.

title: Potential groundwater recharge estimates in the Yucatan Peninsula using gridded data products & parsimonious water balance models
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ana C. Siles-Zarate, J. Agustín Breña-Naranjo
abstract: Study region The Yucatan Peninsula (YP) and its unconfined aquifer, covering a surface of almost 150,000 km2 and being the only terrestrial freshwater source for human activities and ecosystems. Study focus This research work aims at characterizing potential groundwater recharge rates at the Yucatan Peninsula (Mexico), one of the world's largest karstic aquifer systems by means of reanalysis, satellite and data assimilation products. Gridded precipitation, evapotranspiration and spaceborne-derived gravimetry water storage variation products were applied whereas ground climatological data and previous recharge estimates were used for validation. These 10 datasets were tested over 21 different input combinations and 4 water balance methods (Budyko dimensionless & functional equations, simple water and gravimetry-based balance). New hydrological insights for the region Results suggest that the long-term annual potential recharge across the Yucatan Peninsula varied between 169 and 222 mm/year according to the first, third and fourth methods whereas the second method provided higher recharge rates. The precipitation and evapotranspiration data products that better mimicked the long-term recharge rates were CHIRPS & GLDAS/TerraClimate, respectively. We conclude that (1) five out of twenty-one gridded input combinations were reliable estimators of mean annual groundwater recharge (2) simple water balance models are useful groundwater balance studies in this karstic region largely dominated by subsurface storage (3) Interannual variability of recharge from cyclonic precipitation events are well represented according to our models’ behavior.

title: Short-, medium-, and long-term reference evapotranspiration forecasting based on intelligent temperature forecast correction and regional calibration of the Hargreaves model
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zhongxin Ma, Xin Han, Baozhong Zhang, Xin Wang, Qian Huang, Zhigong Peng, Kai Zhang, Xin Li
abstract: Study Area Yellow River Irrigation Area is a key agricultural irrigation region in Shandong Province, China. Study focus This study evaluates the spatiotemporal characteristics of maximum (T′max) and minimum (T′min) temperature forecast errors over 1–40-day lead times using data from 2019 to 2023. Four temperature forecast correction methods—the decaying-average method based on autocorrelation function (ACF-DAM), stepwise regression (SR), genetic algorithm (GA)-optimized long short-term memory (GA-LSTM), and GA-optimized random forest (GA-RF)—were compared, and the optimal correction method was selected for each lead time. Corrected temperatures were input into a calibrated Hargreaves model to estimate reference evapotranspiration (ETo) at short- (1–3 days), medium- (4–15 days), and long- (16–40 days) lead times. The Penman–Monteith method was used as a reference benchmark for evaluating regional applicability. New hydrological insight This study compared multiple temperature forecast correction methods across different lead times, thereby addressing the limited application of lead-time-specific temperature forecast error correction in regional ETo forecasting. Across the five representative lead times, the optimal correction schemes reduced the mean station-wise RMSE of corrected T′max and T′min by 11.2096%–40.0618% and 2.2416%–21.3531%, respectively, relative to the raw forecasts. The 3-day lead time yielded the best ETo forecasting performance, with a cross-station mean RMSE of 0.8917 mm d−1, a b value of 0.9608, and an r value of 0.8930. Spatially, the Yellow River Delta and northern plains exhibit notably lower ETo prediction errors than the central region, indicating a clear spatial heterogeneity in forecast reliability. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of integrating forecast error characterization into regional-scale evapotranspiration modeling, offering an operational pathway to optimize irrigation water allocation and strengthen drought resilience in semi-arid agricultural basins where water resources are under increasing pressure.

title: Bias correction of satellite precipitation products in the Levant
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fakhry Jayousi, Fiachra O’Loughlin
abstract: Study Region: This study focuses on the Levant, a climatically diverse and semi-arid Eastern Mediterranean region with strong rainfall gradients, complex topography, and uneven rain-gauge coverage complicating precipitation observation and hydrological assessment. Study Focus: Reliable precipitation estimation remains a fundamental challenge for regional hydrology. This study evaluates ten bias-correction methods, including seven statistical approaches and three machine-learning approaches, applied to four widely used satellite precipitation products: CCS-CDR, CMORPH, PDIR and IMERG. Daily observations from 361 rain gauges for 2004–2016 are used to assess two adjustment-validation strategies: a local station-specific Leave-One-Year-Out (LOYO) framework and a regional Leave-One-Station-Out (LOSO) framework. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Conventional statistical methods provide limited improvements, whereas machine-learning approaches substantially improve performance, increasing R 2 by up to 0.40 and reducing RMSE by up to 35%. IMERG demonstrates the strongest baseline skill and the most consistent response to correction. Regional models consistently outperform local approaches, with regional LGBM producing the most accurate and spatially coherent correction. Additional rainfall-regime diagnostics show that while ML correction improves daily agreement, it modifies the occurrence of light intensity rainfall and upper-tail behaviour. These findings show that regional machine-learning adjustment can improve the reliability and transferability of satellite precipitation estimates, while distributional diagnostics remain necessary for hydrological applications sensitive to rainfall-regime structure.

title: Surface-cover controls on reference-to-actual evaporation in silty pyroclastic soils of Campania region, Italy: evidence from an 12-year lysimeter experiment
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): L. Coppola, A. Reder, G. Rianna, A. Tarantino, L. Pagano
abstract: Study region pyroclastic soils investigated in this study are widespread on natural slopes, not only in Italy (particularly in the Campania region), but also in numerous volcanic regions worldwide. Their intrinsic and state-dependent properties make them highly sensitive to soil–atmosphere interactions, which strongly influence both rainfall infiltration and water losses through evaporation. Study focus estimating potential and actual evaporation under different land-cover conditions is essential for several hydrological applications. This study derives empirical functions for the FAO single-crop approach, namely the crop coefficient (kc) and the water-content reduction function (kr(θ)), for a non-plastic silty volcanic soil. The analysis is based on a 12-year lysimeter experiment performed under three surface conditions: bare soil, grass-covered soil, and bare soil covered by a wooden ember cover (WEC). A procedure based on cumulative evaporation fluxes was adopted to reduce short-term measurement scatter and identify the water-content thresholds separating energy-limited and water-limited regimes. New hydrological insights for the region results highlight substantial differences in potential evaporation among the investigated surface conditions and distinct forms of kr(θ), including a bilinear decay for the WEC associated with its capillary-barrier effect. Vegetation maintains higher evaporative efficiency under dry conditions, whereas the WEC markedly reduces actual evaporation despite its high radiative absorption. The calibrated parameters were used to develop predictive abaci for estimating monthly evaporation from atmospheric variables alone, providing practical tools for hydrological modelling, agricultural applications, and weather-induced landslide hazard assessment.

title: Spatiotemporal characteristics of extreme precipitation indices and their associations with large-scale climate teleconnections in the Yellow River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yuhong Guo, Yunkun Song, Xiaodong Yan
abstract: Study region The Yellow River Basin (YRB), China, is a climate-sensitive region characterized by limited water resources and high vulnerability to extreme precipitation events, which strongly influence the regional hydrological cycle and increase the risk of floods and related disasters. Study focus This study investigates the spatiotemporal characteristics of nine extreme precipitation indices (EPIs) in the YRB using the CN05.1 dataset and explores their relationships with large-scale climate circulation factors. Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD) is applied to identify the scale-dependent influences of major teleconnection patterns on extreme precipitation variability. New hydrological insights for the region: CDD and CWD showed significant decreasing trends, while most other precipitation indices exhibited increasing trends, suggesting enhanced precipitation intensity and more frequent extreme precipitation events across the YRB, despite shorter dry and wet spells. Extreme precipitation variability was characterized by pronounced multiscale climatic influences, with ENSO and EASM contributing mainly at interannual timescales, and IOD-related variability and other large-scale atmospheric circulation anomalies exerting influences at longer timescales. At longer timescales, including decadal to multidecadal variability, PDO, AMO, and long-term ocean–atmosphere interactions become increasingly important. These findings improve the understanding of the multiscale climatic mechanisms governing extreme precipitation and provide a scientific basis for regional water resource management, flood risk mitigation, and climate adaptation.

title: An Earth observation framework for reservoir water level estimation in a data-scarce transboundary basin for flood preparedness
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Muhammad Rizwan Akram, Arshad Ali, Naeem Aftab
abstract: Study region The Pong Dam on the Beas River in Himachal, India, regulates a 12,561 km² catchment with a storage capacity of 8.57 billion m³ . Its flood releases influence downstream flow along the transboundary Sutlej River in Pakistan, yet real-time water level data are not routinely shared, limiting flood preparedness. Study focus This study develops an Observation framework using Sentinel-1 SAR imagery in Google Earth Engine to estimate Pong Dam water levels from reservoir extents. An adaptive Otsu threshold on VV–VH backscatter, refined by DEM-constrained terrain masking, generates a reservoir area time series (2018–2025), paired with historical water levels to train and validate polynomial regression and Support Vector Regression models. New hydrological insights The refined DEM-constrained backscatter substantially outperformed single-polarization (R² = 0.97 vs 0.47), confirming its reliability as a water level proxy for Pong Dam. Among the predictive models tested, Support Vector Regression and polynomial regression achieved RMSE ≈ 3.3–3.8 ft (1.0–1.2 m) on an independent, chronological test set. Seasonal Otsu thresholds, peaking during July–September monsoon, reveal flood-critical hydrological transitions coinciding with the dam’s peak outflows. The framework provides an operationally validated, ground-data-independent approach to reservoir monitoring, supporting flood early warning in downstream Pakistan. Water levels, RMSE, and MAE are reported in feet (ft), matching the gauge records, with SI equivalents in parentheses throughout (1 ft = 0.3048 m).

title: Vegetation-mediated hydrological controls on landslide susceptibility: Evidence from watershed-scale and site-specific analyses
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Songtang He, Zhenhong Shen, Zongji Yang, Jiangang Chen, Daojie Wang, Yong Li, Xudong Hu, Yongming Lin, Cheng Li, Jun Zhang
abstract: Study region Jinkouhe District, located in southwestern Sichuan Province, China, is a mountainous region characterized by dense vegetation, complex terrain, frequent rainfall, and intensive human activities. Despite high vegetation coverage, landslides remain frequent, providing an ideal case for exploring the interactions among vegetation, hydrological processes, and slope instability. Study focus This study investigates how vegetation interacts with rainfall, lithology, wind speed, and slope gradient to regulate landslide susceptibility. A multi-scale framework integrating watershed-scale susceptibility assessment and site-scale slope stability analysis was developed. Geographic detector and structural equation modeling were used to identify dominant environmental controls and their interactions, while slope stability calculations quantified the effects of vegetation-related loading and artificial waste loading under different hydrological conditions. New hydrological insights for the region Results reveal that vegetation does not always enhance slope stability in humid mountainous regions. The combined effects of vegetation, rainfall, and wind speed increased landslide susceptibility, expanding high-risk zones by over 20%. Factor interactions showed stronger explanatory power than individual factors, with slope–rainfall interaction being the most influential. Under saturated conditions, vegetation-related effects reduced slope stability due to increased gravitational loading and enhanced infiltration. These findings demonstrate that vegetation acts as a dynamic component of hillslope hydrological systems, and its influence on landslide susceptibility depends on rainfall conditions and multi-factor interactions.

title: Seasonal agreement of GLDAS and FLDAS soil-moisture products with precipitation in the Lake Urmia Basin, northwestern Iran
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Alireza Daneshi, Tahereh Mohammadi, Soraya Yaghobi, Gholamreza Khosravi, Iman Islami, Hassan Fathizad, Hossein Omrani, Lichang Yin, Zhenlei Yang, Weili Duan, Hossein Azadi
abstract: Study Region The Lake Urmia Basin is a semi-arid endorheic watershed in northwestern Iran affected by lake shrinkage, intensive water use, drought and strong hydroclimatic gradients. Basin-wide long-term in-situ soil-moisture observations were unavailable. Study Focus We examined seasonal agreement between GLDAS-Noah and FLDAS-Noah near-surface soil moisture and GPCC precipitation during 2000–2020. Monthly fields were spatially harmonized on a common basin overlay, and January, April, July and October represented winter, spring, summer and autumn. After screening an initial 25-station precipitation pool, GPCC was compared with 24 retained meteorological stations; one missing station-month value was excluded, yielding 6047 valid paired observations. Correlations, error metrics and spatial maps were used as an indirect hydroclimatic consistency assessment, not direct validation of soil-moisture accuracy. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Agreement varied by month and location. The station comparison showed small mean GPCC bias in January and July, positive bias in April and October, and modest point-grid correlations, indicating that GPCC better represents basin-scale precipitation magnitude than local station variability. GLDAS showed strongest precipitation correspondence in January, FLDAS in April, and the two soil-moisture products agreed more closely in July and October after correction of a July/October label issue. The products can support regional drought screening, but use should remain conditional on season, physiography and independent soil-moisture validation needs.

title: Meteorological-to-agricultural drought propagation in Southwest China: Spatiotemporal characteristics and driving mechanisms from a three-dimensional perspective
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Lei Liu, Zhiling Zhou, Dong Wang, Shu Chen
abstract: Study region Southwest China is a climatically and topographically complex region frequently affected by drought, posing substantial risks to agriculture, water security, and ecosystems. Study focus This study develops a three-dimensional event-based framework to investigate meteorological-to-agricultural drought (MD-to-AD) propagation in Southwest China during 1961–2021. MD and AD were characterized at the monthly scale using standardized drought indices with a 3-month accumulation period. Drought events were identified through connected-component labeling and linked using spatiotemporal matching. Trajectory clustering and atmospheric diagnostics were then used to distinguish dominant propagation patterns and associated atmospheric mechanisms. New hydrological insights for the region A total of 220 MD and 105 AD events were identified, with severe events becoming more persistent and intense after 2000. MD exhibited greater spatial mobility, whereas AD showed stronger persistence and memory. 30 propagation relationships were detected, comprising 24 one-to-one and six one-to-many types. One-to-one propagation had a shorter mean response time but a longer mean distance, whereas one-to-many propagation showed a longer lag, a shorter distance, and weaker individual AD responses. Two distinct patterns emerged: slower, longer-distance, predominantly southward propagation in western–central Southwest China and faster, shorter-distance, mainly eastward and southeastward propagation in central-eastern and southeastern regions. These patterns were associated with distinct atmospheric circulation configurations and may be jointly modulated by large-scale circulation anomalies, Tibetan Plateau effects, land–atmosphere feedbacks, and land-surface heterogeneity.

title: Mechanism identification and engineering translation of urban green-space stormwater regulation from interpretable machine learning to CEC-based compensatory diagnosis: Evidence from 208 plots in cold-region Shenyang
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xi Wang, Yao FU, Tiemao Shi, Xiaoyan Cao
abstract: Study region and problem background This study examines 208 urban green-space plots in central Shenyang, a cold-region old industrial city in Northeast China, where intensified short-duration rainfall, impervious surfaces, heterogeneous infiltration, ageing drainage networks and freeze-thaw disturbance jointly shape pluvial-flood responses in constrained built-up areas. Methods and main results XGBoost models were built for 1-, 3-, 10-, 30- and 50-year design-rainfall scenarios and compared with RF and MLR. XGBoost achieved test-set R2 of 0.825–0.892 and 10-fold CV R2 of 0.804–0.874; Additional gradient-boosting models such as LightGBM and CatBoost were reserved for future benchmarking under the same multi-return-period framework to maintain consistency of the XGBoost-TreeSHAP-PDP-CEC interpretation chain in the present study. Inundation statistics, feature importance, PDP response ranges and CEC pathways jointly indicated an approximately 10-year mechanism-transition zone. Below this zone, regulation was mainly controlled by infiltration capacity, vegetation cover and vertical structure; above it, imperviousness, catchment organization and drainage support became dominant. Mechanism translation and validation CEC identified six compensatory pathways linking ecological area, retention facilities, drainage support, vertical structure, patch aggregation and vegetation connectivity to specific hydrological deficits. SWMM checking showed that CEC-guided integrated regulation (S3) reduced inundation more consistently than single-factor regulation (S2); under the 50-year scenario, area-wide mean depth decreased by 54.3% and 27.2%, respectively and public records from the July 2024 storm showed directional overlap with SWMM high-risk zones. The framework provides a front-end diagnostic route for screening plot-level adaptive renewal, while engineering implementation still requires causal hydrological verification, field feasibility, detailed design and cost assessment.

title: An integrated framework for evidence-based climate adaptation planning in water-related disaster management in Malwathu Oya Basin, Sri Lanka
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ranapura Dewage Thilini Kaushalya, Mohamed Rasmy, Katsunori Tamakawa, Toshio Koike
abstract: Study region The Malwathu Oya basin, located in the dry zone of Sri Lanka, is highly vulnerable to hydroclimatic variability, experiencing recurrent floods during monsoon periods and water scarcity during dry periods. Study focus This study develops an integrated framework for risk-informed adaptation planning by linking multi-model climate projections, hydrological simulations, and socio-economic impact assessment. Climate projections characterize changes in rainfall variability and extremes and are incorporated into a seamless hydrological model to simulate basin-scale flow dynamics. Model outputs are coupled with depth–damage functions to estimate economic losses and population exposure under current and future conditions, and to evaluate adaptation strategies. New hydrological insights for the region Climate projections (2050–2075) indicate an overall increase in annual rainfall. This increase is characterized by greater temporal concentration and variability, leading to reduced discharges during dry months. Flood hazards are projected to intensify, with depths exceeding two meters and 30–40% expansion of inundation extent. Flood damages are expected to increase by 3–4 times for buildings, twofold for agriculture, with rural communities most vulnerable. Adaptation analysis shows that coordinated reservoir operations and crop diversification can effectively reduce multi-hazard risks. These findings highlight the importance of integrating climate, hydrological, and socio-economic processes to better represent basin-scale risks by providing a transferable framework for evidence-based adaptation planning and strengthening integrated water resources management (IWRM) in climate-vulnerable basins.

title: Impacts of climate and land use changes on water retention in the transboundary Yuanjiang-Red River Basin: Historical attribution and future projections
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yi Zou, Roberto Ranzi, Xuan Ji, Paolo Colosio, Nguyen Hao Quang, Xuan Luo, Fan Zhou, Jianxing Li, Yungang Li
abstract: Study region the Yuanjiang–Red River Basin (YRRB), Southeast Asia. Study focus Water retention (WR) capacity in the transboundary YRRB has been increasingly affected by combined climate and land-use changes. However, limited quantitative attribution of historical drivers and uncertain future projections hinder the development of effective cross-border adaptation strategies. This study integrated the Variable Infiltration Capacity model, a fixed-varying scenario design, and variable-specific Bayesian model averaging of bias-corrected, downscaled Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 climate projections to attribute historical WR changes during 1973–2015 and project WR changes during 2016–2050 under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathway scenarios. New hydrological insights for the region Historical WR averaged 572 mm and showed a nonsignificant decline of 18 mm decade⁻¹ , primarily attributable to climate change. Local buffering effects associated with land-use change were insufficient to offset this basin-wide decline. Future WR is projected to decline by 29.6%–33.5%. Empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis indicated a shift toward greater spatial heterogeneity. Relative to SSP126, EOF1 decreased from 79% to 64%–68%, whereas EOF2 increased from 7% to 12%–17% under SSP245 and SSP585. This overall shift was associated with the combined effects of declining precipitation and increasing evapotranspiration. These findings inform coordinated cross-border ecological restoration and spatially targeted water management between China and Vietnam.

title: Revealing water supply-demand responses to varying inflow frequencies in inter-basin water diversion projects using a non-iterative deterministic sampling algorithm
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Haomiao Cheng, Xiaoman Sun, Zuping Xu, Zhiming Qi, Matthew Tom Harrison, Matthew W. Sima, Yi Gong, Liang Wang, Jilin Cheng
abstract: Study region The Eastern Route of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project (ER-SNWDP), China, the world's largest cascade pumping station system. Study focus Inter-basin water diversion projects (IWDPs) are key engineering measures for alleviating regional water scarcity, but their water supply scheduling involves a high-dimensional nonlinear optimization problem under reservoir operation constraints. This study developed a universal framework to minimize the water supply-demand gap (WSG) in IWDPs by optimizing multi-reservoir water supply scheduling. A non-iterative deterministic sampling algorithm, the Orthogonal Latin Neighborhood Algorithm (OLNA), was proposed to efficiently determine optimal scheduling strategies. This methodology was applied to the ER-SNWDP and the water supply-demand responses to varying inflow frequencies were also revealed. New hydrological insights for the region The universality and efficiency of OLNA were verified to be superior to mainstream heuristic algorithms in solving multi-year multi-reservoir scheduling problems under varying hydrological conditions. It was found that the WSG of the ER-SNWDP has the potential to be reduced by 1.28 × 1010 m3 under 75% inflow frequency. Escalating water demand during high inflow frequency (hydrological droughts) exacerbates supply-demand imbalances despite optimized strategies. A Limit Equilibrium Point (LEP), the transition from sufficient water supply to water shortage (i.e., WSG=0), was found to decrease as the inflow frequency increased but to increase with higher initial reservoir storage. These findings provide guidance for water regulation and drought-risk mitigation in IWDPs.

title: Soil moisture and evapotranspiration in four temperate agricultural catchments of Southern Sweden under future climatic conditions
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Louise Gadkari Malmquist, Magdalena Bieroza, Fernando Jaramillo, Jennie Barron
abstract: Study region We modelled four agriculturally dominated catchments that represent key agro-climatic production zones in southern Sweden: Tidan (58.37 N, 13.92E), Enköpingsån-Örsundaån (59.83 N, 17.0E), Saxån-Braån (55.96 N, 13.14E) and Gamlebyån-Loftaån (57.96 N, 16.30). These catchments were chosen to represent the typical production systems, land cover and soil conditions, influenced by distinct weather regimes Study focus Our objective was to assess how current and future extreme weather impacts soil moisture availability and evapotranspiration in agricultural catchments. We applied the Soil and Water Assessment Tool to four agriculturally dominated catchments in southern Sweden that represent main crop production regions. A reference period (1991–2023) was simulated and compared with future climate scenarios (CMIP6 SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5, periods 2024–2040 and 2041–2060), generated using the weather generator LARS-WG. The scenarios showed significant temperature increase but non-significant precipitation change. Soil moisture dynamics were evaluated weekly, using the soil moisture deficiency index (SMDI) for topsoil and subsoil, and the evapotranspiration deficiency index (ETDI) in relation to temperature (TX90p) and precipitation (SPI) indices. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Results showed significant drying trends (p < 0.05) in both topsoil and subsoil in three of four catchments, with enhanced drying in the subsoil alongside reduced evapotranspiration in future climate scenarios. This suggests negative implications for biomass and crop management, highlighting increasing needs for improved soil water management and irrigation.

title: A socio-hydrological assessment of spatial communities in an aquifer through groundwater modeling and social network analysis
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Hamoon Yousefi, Azadeh Ahmadi
abstract: Study region The Isfahan-Borkhar aquifer in central Iran, an arid region, faces severe groundwater decline, threatening local communities reliant on agriculture. Study focus This study proposes a novel approach to socio-hydrological decision-making by integrating distributed groundwater modeling with Social Network Analysis. The method examines both the relationships between communities and their interactions with the aquifer. Model outputs across nine time steps were combined, with stakeholder connections derived from their geographical proximity and water use patterns. The most influential communities were identified and analyzed from three perspectives: inter-community relations, intra-community structure, and aquifer conditions. A meta-graph representation is constructed and classified into different groups, each showing varied responses to the 2014 water withdrawal restrictions and to ongoing groundwater depletion. New hydrological insights for the region The results revealed severe groundwater depletion in the study area, with an average decline of approximately 10 m over a 9-year period, and local depletion rates reaching up to 25 m. A significant finding was the paradoxical relationship between consumption and depletion: communities exhibiting the lowest levels of local depletion were frequently the highest consumers, indicating that intensive usage in specific areas severely compromises the overall aquifer status. Furthermore, meta-graph analysis demonstrated that these high-consumption communities suffer from a lack of betweenness, leading to social isolation and limited awareness of the hydrological consequences of their actions.

title: Vine copula regional dry-wet evaluation index incorporating baseflow and XGBoost-SHAP early warning system in Huzhou, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tongtong Yu, Hao Chen, Yukun Wang, Jiaqi Tan, Zhishao Li, Yu Qiao, Jianuo Li, Saihua Huang, Yue-Ping Xu, Yuxue Guo, Hui Nie
abstract: Study region Huzhou City, Southeastern China. Study focus This study applied the Lyne-Hollick digital filter to separate baseflow and compute the baseflow index (BFI). We then used a three-dimensional vine copula to couple BFI with precipitation and evaporation, constructing a comprehensive dry-wet index (CDI). We further developed a monthly dry-wet early warning model using XGBoost and employed the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) framework to interpret the driving mechanisms. Results revealed a notable drying tendency at four of the five stations. Despite the spatially heterogeneous trend pattern, wet events across the basin consistently coincided with high baseflow periods during the rainy season. The early warning model achieved an overall accuracy of 63.5–76.0%, while SHAP analysis indicated spatial heterogeneity in the dominant driving factors across sub-regions. New hydrological insights for the region The CDI exhibits strong correlations with the standardized precipitation index (SPI), standardized evapotranspiration index (SEI), and standardized baseflow index (SBI) at multiple temporal scales. Dry-wet conditions in the basins have shifted from seasonal alternation toward more persistent states: dry periods are concentrated mainly in winter (December to February), and wet spells largely coincide with high baseflow during the rainy season. These findings provide a scientific basis for upgrading the integrated drought and flood early warning system, optimizing water resource allocation, and formulating region-specific disaster prevention strategies in Huzhou City.

title: Geodetic glacier mass balance and its hydrological implications in the Upper Indus Basin: Insights into the Karakoram Anomaly
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xiaojuan Zou, Yinsheng Zhang, Haifeng Gao, Suhaib Bin Farhan
abstract: Study Region The Upper Indus River Basin (UIB) is the most vulnerable water tower in High Mountain Asia (HMA), yet its glacier-hydrology interactions remain poorly understood. Study Focus To assess the glacier imprint on streamflow trends and quantify the depletion of non-renewable meltwater, we reconstructed multi-decadal geodetic glacier mass balance (MB Geodetic) for 1973–2018 from KH-9 Hexagon imagery, DEMs, and dh products using a photogrammetric-geodetic approach; the resulting fluxes ( ∆ S ) were compared with discharge ( Q ) within a simplified water balance framework. New Hydrological Insights for the Region UIB glaciers remained near equilibrium (−0.06 ± 0.02 m w.e. yr−1) yet exhibited pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity. Severe ice loss persisted in the Hindu Kush and western Himalaya, where negative Δ S coupled with increasing Q indicates sustained glacier overdraft and high vulnerability. By contrast, the southern Karakoram shifted from a slight gain (+0.82 ± 0.01 Gt yr−1) to a moderate deficit (−0.63 ± 0.01 Gt yr−1) around 2000, indicating that the "Karakoram Anomaly" has weakened and its core has migrated westward. Within the Karakoram, Δ S is decoupled from runoff trends ( Δ S > 0 with increasing Q ; Δ S < 0 with decreasing Q ); streamflow variability therefore stems mainly from non-glacial sources, and vulnerability is correspondingly lower. Non-renewable ice meltwater supplied < 5% of discharge in most sub-basins, and this share fell to ~2% at the UIB outlet, suggesting that glaciers modulate rather than dominate runoff, with the Karakoram buffering glacial overdraft elsewhere.

title: Heatwave-dominated changes in compound drought and heatwave events in the middle and lower Yangtze River Basin, China, during 1961–2020
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qinmian Bai, Xingdong Zhang, Chunmei Chen, Wei Wang, Aiqing Feng, Shaohong Wu, Shanfeng He
abstract: Study region The middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin, China. Study focus Compound drought and heatwave events (CDHWs) pose increasing risks to water resources, agriculture and ecosystems, but their daily-scale evolution and amplification relative to single extremes remain insufficiently understood in humid monsoon regions. Using daily observations from 66 meteorological stations during 1961–2020, this study examined the long-term changes, periodic variability, spatial patterns and amplification characteristics of warm-season CDHWs. A regression-based relative contribution framework was further used to assess whether CDHW variability was more closely associated with heatwave- or drought-related indicators. New hydrological insights for the region Warm-season CDHWs showed a clear transition around the 1990s, with decreasing tendencies before 1990 and widespread increases thereafter. High-value and significantly increasing areas were mainly concentrated in Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi and the Jiangsu–Zhejiang–Shanghai region. Compared with single heatwaves or droughts, CDHWs were characterised by stronger thermal stress, markedly lower precipitation and longer event duration, indicating an amplification of compound hot–dry extremes. Heatwave-related indicators showed larger relative explanatory contributions than drought-related indicators for CDHW occurrence days, event frequency and maximum duration, although drought duration and drought frequency were locally important in mountainous areas. These findings highlight the need to integrate heatwave monitoring with drought risk management to improve early warning and climate adaptation strategies in the Yangtze River Basin.

title: Changing controls on low flows in the Wiese catchment (southern Black Forest, Germany) under climate change
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Simon Hoeg
abstract: Study Region: The Wiese catchment (454 km2) in the southern Black Forest, Germany, is a snow-influenced mountain catchment that has undergone substantial hydrological changes during the 20th century. Understanding how the dominant controls on low-flow discharge have evolved over time is essential for sustainable water management under ongoing climate change. Study Focus: This study combines long-term discharge observations (1930–2019), process-based hydrological modelling with HEC-HMS, and bias-corrected CMIP6 climate projections to investigate historical and future low-flow discharge conditions. Historical low-flow discharge indicators (NQ, MN7Q, and Q95) were analysed together with projected changes under the SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5 scenarios (2015–2099). Historical analyses show that minimum low-flow discharge indicators increased during the late 20th century, consistent with documented land-use change, reduced industrial water use, declining agricultural irrigation, and climatic variability, although their individual contributions cannot be quantified. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: The projections indicate declining mean discharge and low-flow discharge indicators towards the end of the 21st century, with substantially stronger reductions under SSP5–8.5 than under SSP2–4.5. More importantly, the study demonstrates a shift in the dominant controls on low-flow discharge. Whereas historical low-flow characteristics are consistent with the combined influence of catchment changes, anthropogenic water use, and climatic variability, future low-flow discharge conditions are primarily associated with projected climatic forcing. This process-based perspective extends conventional climate impact assessments by linking historical hydrological change with future climate projections and provides new insights into evolving low-flow controls in mountain catchments.

title: A new watershed regulation capacity assessment approach based on scale theory and its applications
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yuqin Gao, Yijia Li, Longsheng Xu, Zhenxing Zhang, Changjun Liu, Jingang Zhang, Chenyu Yuan, Yan Wang
abstract: Study region The Qinhuai River Basin (Nanjing) Study focus Urbanization and extreme rainfall events are key factors affecting watershed regulation capacity. This study presents a basin regulation capacity assessment model based on scale theory. A power-law relationship between flow and catchment area is established to extract scale parameters, which serve as quantitative indicators of regulation capacity. Using the HEC-HMS and PLUS models, flow–area relationships under different scenarios are fitted to derive this indicator. The spatiotemporal distribution and trends of regulation capacity are then analyzed, considering various extreme rainfall and urban development scenarios. New hydrological insights for the region From 1990–2020, the basin's regulation capacity exhibited a declining trend with considerable interannual fluctuations. All regions of the basin exert a suppressive effect on flow increases, with the mid- and downstream areas relying on measures such as pumping and gate operations to maintain a relatively strong regulation capacity. Rainfall peaks were categorized as early (Type I), late (Type II), and central (Type III). Regulation capacity was weakest under Type I rainfall, whereas Types II and III exhibited the strongest regulation during a 50-year return period storm. Among four urban development scenarios, the ecological-priority scenario showed the best regulation capacity. Future basin planning should focus on ecological restoration, optimize natural retention areas, and enhance regulation measures under Type I rainfall.

title: Groundwater responses to drought and human withdrawals in the southern Andean region
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fadji Z. Maina, Sujay V. Kumar
abstract: Study region Groundwater provides a crucial buffer against drought and sustains water supply across the southern Andean region, particularly in Chile and Argentina. In recent decades, multi-year droughts combined with increasing groundwater abstraction have placed severe stress on regional aquifers, yet the joint effects of climate variability and human activities on groundwater dynamics remain insufficiently quantified. Study focus We assess groundwater storage (GWS) dynamics from 2003 to 2023 using a hydological reanalysis that integrates satellite observations of soil moisture, leaf area index, snow water equivalent, and terrestrial water storage into a land surface model forced with an improved precipitation dataset. We compare climate-driven and observation-constrained groundwater dynamics to examine how groundwater responses to multi-year droughts vary across the region. New hydrological insights for the region Results reveal three distinct groundwater response regimes. In regions with limited management, GWS exhibits delayed and prolonged declines during multi-year droughts and slow recovery after precipitation rebounds. In areas with intensive groundwater abstraction, groundwater deficits are substantially amplified and persist even after precipitation returns to near-normal conditions. In the southernmost regions, groundwater behavior is consistent with a possible cryospheric buffering influence that partially offsets precipitation deficits. These findings show that groundwater responses cannot be understood from meteorological forcing alone and highlight the need to account for human pressures and cryospheric influences when assessing aquifer vulnerability and long-term water security.

title: LSTM-based flood-stage forecasting under limited flood-event samples: Effects of forecasting scheme, spatial input configuration, and input-window length in the Pajiang River basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shanshan Li, Zhaoli Wang, Bensheng Huang, Daoyi Chen, Liangxiong Chen, Jiachao Chen, Lilan Zhang, Haibo Peng
abstract: Study region Pajiang River basin, a tributary of the Beijiang River in Guangdong Province, southern China. Study focus Using 17 historical flood events (2012–2024), this study evaluated how forecasting scheme, spatial input configuration, input-window length, and training-data availability affect 1–8 h LSTM-based downstream flood stage forecasting. Additional analyses of recursive prediction intervals, hydrological memory, upstream-downstream information transfer, and GRU models were used to interpret performance patterns and assess the consistency of the findings. New hydrological insights for the region Recent local stage observations provided the most consistent predictive information across flood events and training-data levels, whereas the benefit of upstream observations was event-dependent and became less reliable as training data decreased. Local observations directly capture the current downstream hydrological state, while the contribution of upstream observations depends on relationships that may vary among floods. When recent local observations were available, the multi-output scheme generally provided the best balance between accuracy and stability, whereas recursive forecasting deteriorated at longer lead times, with prediction-interval experiments providing indirect evidence of error accumulation. Input-window length had limited effects for local-input models but greater and less consistent effects when upstream information was included. GRU experiments reproduced the main findings for forecasting schemes and spatial input configurations. These findings support multi-output forecasting based on recent local stage observations under event-scarce conditions similar to the Pajiang River basin.

title: Balancing performance and uncertainty in multi-source evapotranspiration fusion across the Qinling–Daba Mountains, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yanhong Tang, Yi He, Rui Yan, Dejing Chen, Lei Zhu, Puxia Wu
abstract: Study region The Qinling–Daba Mountains, China. Study focus In heterogeneous mountainous regions, how weighting strategies, bias-correction references, and error dependence affect the accuracy, propagated uncertainty, and robustness of multi-source evapotranspiration (ET) fusion remains unclear. We integrated seven ET products and compared seven fusion schemes, including arithmetic averaging, linear and exponential-score weighting, and bias-corrected variants. Product performance and reliability were assessed using water-balance-derived ET (WB_ET), Kling–Gupta efficiency, and Triple Collocation-derived uncertainty. Parameters calibrated during the training period were evaluated across seven basins for monthly and seasonal accuracy, propagated uncertainty, seasonal dependence, and leave-one-out robustness. New hydrological insights for the region The ET products showed strong temporal but moderate spatial consistency. Product-mean relative uncertainty ranged from 8% to 21%, compared with 13%–16% among basins. Fused products achieved R values of 0.90–0.93, RMSE of 14–20 mm·month⁻¹, MAE of 9–15 mm·month⁻¹, and KGE mainly between 0.60 and 0.85. EWF provided the most balanced accuracy, whereas GBC schemes more effectively reduced BIAS, RMSE, and MAE. ABC-EWF yielded the lowest covariance-based relative propagated uncertainty (6.18%), although this did not consistently translate into higher validation accuracy. Accuracy gains were more stable in the dry season, while covariance-aware propagation produced systematically higher uncertainty than the independent-error assumption. LOOCV KGE deviations remained within ±0.04. Overall, fusion outcomes depended on weighting formulation, bias-correction reference, seasonal conditions, and inter-product error dependence.

title: Ecohydrological pathways linking snow cover to spring green up across Northern Hemisphere ecosystems
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jian Sun, Fengping Li, Peng Qi, Hongyan Li, Haiqing Wang
abstract: Study region Seasonally snow-covered regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Study focus Snow regulates spring ecohydrological conditions by controlling the timing of surface exposure, post-snowmelt warming, and meltwater inputs before vegetation green-up. However, the ecosystem-specific pathways through which snow cover influences the start of the growing season (SOS) remain unclear. Here, we characterized the spatiotemporal patterns of snow cover end date (SCED), snow cover duration (SCD), maximum snow water equivalent (SWEmax), and SOS across seasonally snow-covered regions of the Northern Hemisphere during 1982–2022. Partial correlation analysis was used to assess the relationships between SOS and snow cover indicators, and structural equation modeling (SEM) was applied to identify the air temperature (AT) and soil moisture (SM) pathways linking snow cover to SOS across ecosystems. New hydrological insights for the region During 1982–2022, SOS advanced by 0.11 days yr⁻¹ , accompanied by earlier SCED, shorter SCD, and declining SWEmax. SCED showed stronger associations with SOS than SCD and SWEmax. The SEM results showed that snow cover effects on SOS were primarily transmitted through a temperature pathway, whereby earlier SCED enhanced post-snowmelt warming and subsequently advanced SOS. In contrast, the soil-moisture pathway was more ecosystem dependent. In Temperate Coniferous Forests, Temperate Grasslands, Savannas and Shrublands, and Desert and Xeric Shrublands, higher SWEmax promoted earlier green-up by increasing early-season soil moisture. These findings clarify how changing snow conditions regulate spring water and energy exchanges and can improve the representation of snow–vegetation interactions in hydrological and land-surface models.

title: Urban waterlogging hazard and sponge city mitigation in the lower Bahe River Basin, Xi'an: A complementary MIKE–HEC-RAS assessment in a semi-arid to semi-humid transitional zone
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jiqiang Lyu, Xiaoyu Cai, Chen Lu, Lei Fan, Wei Qian, Tianshuo Chen, Ze Zhang, Leran Qin, Pingping Luo
abstract: Study region The Ba River Basin is a representative urban watershed in the semi-arid to semi-humid transitional zone of northwestern China, characterized by dense population, rapid urban expansion, and extensive impervious surfaces. Under intense rainfall, rapid runoff concentration in urbanized areas is primarily associated with impervious surfaces, local topographic depressions, and limited drainage capacity. Study focus This study combines MIKE FLOOD simulations with HEC-RAS hydraulic analyses to assess urban waterlogging and river-related flood hazards under multiple rainfall scenarios. MIKE was used to simulate rainfall-induced surface inundation and river–floodplain interactions, while HEC-RAS was applied to evaluate river conveyance and levee safety. The framework provides a joint assessment of pluvial inundation and river flood risk in an urbanized semi-arid basin. This study also evaluated the efficacy of sponge city initiatives in mitigating flood risk. New hydrological insights for the region Areas with gentle slopes, dense urban development, and extensive impervious surfaces are highly susceptible to severe waterlogging during intense rainstorms, with maximum ponding depths reaching 1.57 m. No river overflow was simulated under the 100-year rainfall scenario, indicating that flooding was primarily driven by inadequate drainage capacity and urbanization effects. Sponge city construction significantly reduced waterlogging hazards and the affected area. Under the 20-year return-period rainfall scenario, the high-risk area was reduced by 47.56% and 72.52% in Scenarios 2 and 3, respectively. These findings provide support for flood-resilience planning in similar regions.

title: Integrated assessment of flood and drought risk in a context of declining terrestrial water storage in Northwest China: A broad perspective analysis
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jintao Ren, Min Xu, Aihua Long, Jiawen Yu, Yunlong Wang, Jiaxi Liang
abstract: Study region Northwest China (NWC), a typical arid inland region. Study focus Based on Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) satellite data and multi-source assimilated datasets, this study analyzed the dynamics of terrestrial water storage (TWS) and assessed the associated flood and drought risks as a broad perspective analysis. The spatiotemporal variations in TWS were examined using non-parametric trend analysis methods, and the contributions of different water storage components to TWS change were quantified using partial least squares regression (PLSR). A comprehensive risk assessment framework was developed by integrating hazard probability, socioeconomic exposure, and ecological vulnerability. The associations between large-scale atmospheric circulation and hydrological extremes were explored using cross-wavelet transform analysis. New hydrological insights for the region TWS decreased by 85.54 Gt/yr in NWC from 2003 to 2023, with significant spatial heterogeneity: increasing trends in southern NWC and decreasing trends in most other regions. Groundwater storage accounted for 75.95% of the total TWS variations. Middle- to high-risk zones for drought, flood, and compound disasters were concentrated in eastern Lanzhou and areas surrounding the Tianshan Mountains. The Southern Oscillation (SO) and the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) showed exploratory associations with drought and flood variability, respectively. By linking TWS changes and atmospheric circulation with hydrological hazards, this study provides new insights for improving disaster risk identification and management in arid inland regions.

title: Lead-time-dependent effects of spatial rainfall representations on deep learning discharge forecasting in the lower Chao Phraya River
